Chapter 10 Nine capabilities, one message between them. The browser does almost all of this, which is why the two places it stops are worth naming. Nine capabilities and one message between them. Eight are the browser working normally inside the sandbox: no host round trip, no permission, nothing to negotiate, and no reason for any of it to involve a model. This is the group where Chapter 4’s principle is least ambiguous, because there is not even a plausible argument for crossing the boundary to sort a list. Two of them stop at the frame boundary, and those are the ones worth your attention: a shortcut the host may already own, and a drag that cannot leave your view. The live application needs JavaScript. Its source is in the repository under apps/ .

sections.h: How do I make dragging work?
sections.x: input.pointer Core Level 1 Platform Click, hover, drag, and capture across mouse, touch, and pen. Ground The browser inside the sandbox provides it. No host round trip. Recipes Data Explorer , Image Annotator Demo lab-input Call setPointerCapture(event.pointerId) on pointerdown . Without it the element receives events only while the pointer is inside its own box, so any drag that moves faster than the layout updates leaves the element behind and the gesture dies mid-motion. With capture, every subsequent event for that pointer id is routed to the capturing element until you release it, which means the drag survives leaving not only the element but the frame. Use Pointer Events rather than mouse events with touch handlers bolted on. They unify mouse, touch and pen, which is the whole reason they exist. Extracted from from apps/labs/lab-input/index.html dot.addEventListener("pointerdown", (event) => { dragging = true; dot.setPointerCapture(event.pointerId); offset = { x: event.offsetX, y: event.offsetY }; }); dot.addEventListener("pointermove", (event) => { if (!dragging) return; const box = pad.getBoundingClientRect(); dot.style.left = `${Math.max(0, Math.min(box.width - 22, event.clientX - box.left - offset.x))}px`; }); dot.addEventListener("pointerup", (event) => { dragging = false; dot.releasePointerCapture(event.pointerId); }); Two more details that only show up on real devices. touch-action: none on the draggable surface stops the browser interpreting a drag as a scroll, which otherwise makes touch dragging impossible. And targets need to be bigger: WCAG 2.2 sets the floor at 24 by 24 CSS pixels at AA, and 44 by 44 at AAA, which is also the long-standing platform convention. Chapter 13 gets the modality from hostContext.deviceCapabilities.touch rather than from a user agent string.

input.keyboard Core Level 2 Platform Keys, modifiers, and the platform conventions users already have. Ground The browser inside the sandbox provides it. No host round trip. Recipes Data Explorer , Spreadsheet , Code and Diff Reviewer Demo lab-input Keys, modifiers, and the platform conventions your users already have from every other application. Two rules cover most of it: read event.key rather than the long-deprecated keyCode , which reports the wrong thing on non-US layouts, and treat event.metaKey || event.ctrlKey as one modifier rather than branching on the platform. Use the platform’s modifier, not one of them. event.metaKey || event.ctrlKey is the whole of cross-platform accelerator handling and there is no excuse for getting it wrong. Read event.key rather than keyCode , which has been deprecated for a decade and reports the wrong thing on non-US layouts. Escape needs an explicit rule, because in an embedded view it has at least four plausible meanings and only one of them is yours at any moment. It can close your dialog, clear your selection, leave fullscreen, or mean something to the host that you cannot see. Calling preventDefault() unconditionally takes all four. Handle it only when you have something open, and call preventDefault() only then. Otherwise let it propagate: Illustrative, not run if (event.key === "Escape" && dialog.open) { event.preventDefault(); dialog.close(); }

input.shortcut Core Level 2 Not standardised Own an accelerator without fighting the host for it. Ground No standard mechanism exists yet. The entry carries a workaround. Recipes Document Editor , Spreadsheet Demo lab-input You can, and so can the host, and there is no way for either of you to find out which one won. Whoever calls preventDefault() first keeps the chord, and “first” depends on where focus happens to be when the key is pressed, which the user changes constantly without thinking about it. No negotiation exists anywhere in the extension. There is no list of reserved chords in hostContext , no request to claim one, and no notification when you collide. From the user’s side the symptom is not an error but an inconsistency: your find bar opens when focus is inside the frame and does not when it is not, and they have no way to predict which. Whoever calls preventDefault() first wins, and “first” is decided by whether the event reaches your frame at all, which depends on where focus is. From the user’s side this reads as an application that sometimes has a find bar and sometimes does not. Take few, and take the document ones: Bind Leave alone Cmd/Ctrl+Z, Shift+Cmd/Ctrl+Z Cmd+T, Cmd+W, Cmd+L, Cmd+R Cmd/Ctrl+C, Cmd/Ctrl+S Any bare letter with no modifier Escape, Delete, F2 in context Cmd+Shift+anything the host may own Never bind a bare letter: the user is probably typing. Recipe 4 binds four chords and shows all four on its toolbar, because a shortcut nobody can see is a shortcut nobody uses. What a mechanism would look like. The host declares reserved chords in hostContext , and the view either avoids them or requests one and is told whether it got it. Neither exists. In the demonstration, press Cmd/Ctrl+F: the view takes it, and the host it is embedded in may or may not agree.

sections.h: How do I do a context menu?
sections.x: input.longpress Core Level 2 Platform Touch equivalent of a right click. Ground The browser inside the sandbox provides it. No host round trip. Recipes File Explorer Demo lab-input input.contextmenu Core Level 2 Platform Contextual actions on right click or long press. Ground The browser inside the sandbox provides it. No host round trip. Recipes File Explorer , Workflow Builder Demo lab-input These are one intent expressed on two modalities: “give me the actions for this thing”. A mouse user right-clicks, a touch user presses and holds, and both expect the same menu in the same place with the same items. Building them as two features produces two menus that drift apart. Application behaviour. Handle contextmenu with preventDefault() and draw your own menu. Position it in the viewport, keep it inside the frame, close it on Escape and on outside click, and move focus into it so a keyboard user can reach it. On touch, a pointerdown timer of roughly 500ms with cancellation on move or up gives the same menu. The boundary. Your preventDefault() suppresses the browser’s menu inside your frame. It does not suppress the host’s, if the host has one, and it cannot tell the host that a menu is open. A host that also shows a menu on right click produces two menus, and neither party can currently detect the other. In practice hosts do not do this, but nothing in the protocol prevents it. Accessibility. A context menu that only opens on right click is unreachable for keyboard users. Give it a second route: Shift+F10, or a visible button, or both. role="menu" with role="menuitem" children, arrow key navigation, Escape to close and return focus.

sections.h: How do I do selection properly?
sections.x: input.selection Core Level 2 Platform Single, additive, range, and select-all over text and objects. Ground The browser inside the sandbox provides it. No host round trip. Recipes Data Explorer , File Explorer , Spreadsheet , Workflow Builder , Code and Diff Reviewer , Monitoring Console Demo lab-input Three gestures, and users bring all three from every other application they have ever used. They notice immediately when any is missing, because the absence does not read as a missing feature; it reads as a broken table. The implementation is about twenty lines and the demonstration below has all of it. Click replaces the selection and sets the anchor. Cmd/Ctrl-click toggles one item and moves the anchor. Shift-click extends from the anchor to the clicked item. Extracted from from apps/labs/lab-input/index.html function select(i, event) { if (event.shiftKey) { const [lo, hi] = [Math.min(anchor, i), Math.max(anchor, i)]; for (let k = lo; k <= hi; k += 1) selected.add(k); } else if (event.metaKey || event.ctrlKey) { selected.has(i) ? selected.delete(i) : selected.add(i); anchor = i; } else { selected.clear(); selected.add(i); anchor = i; } } The keyboard model is the other half: arrows move, Space toggles, Shift with arrows extends, Cmd/Ctrl+A selects everything, Escape clears. Together they are about twenty lines and they are the difference between a table and a picture of a table. Accessibility. role="listbox" with aria-multiselectable , or role="grid" , and aria-selected on each row. Announce the count on change, not the individual rows, or a screen reader user selecting forty rows hears forty announcements. The lab does exactly one announcement per change. The other reason selection matters. It is the unit of conversation. Chapter 18’s escalation carries the selection, and Recipe 8 makes a range of diff lines the thing the model is asked about. A view with no selection model has nothing precise to escalate, so its users end up describing what they mean in prose.

sections.h: How do I do drag and drop?
sections.x: input.dragdrop Core Level 2 Platform Drag and drop inside the view, with structured transfer data. Ground The browser inside the sandbox provides it. No host round trip. Recipes File Explorer , Image Annotator , Workflow Builder Demo lab-input Inside the frame, drag and drop is the HTML drag and drop API, with all of its familiar unpleasantness: dragover must call preventDefault() or the drop never fires, and dataTransfer types are the only structured channel between source and target. For reordering within one list, pointer events are usually better than the drag API: you get pointer capture, you can animate, and you avoid the drag image entirely. Recipe 7 drags nodes with pointer events and Recipe 3 uses the drag API because it needs a drop target with feedback. input.dragBoundary Extended Level 2 Not standardised Drag something out of the view and into the host, or the reverse. Ground No standard mechanism exists yet. The entry carries a workaround. Recipes none yet Demo lab-input The second boundary, and the more visible one. A file dragged from the desktop into your frame works, because the browser routes it. Anything else does not. You cannot drag a row out of your view and onto the host’s conversation. The host cannot drag one of its attachments into your view. There is no dataTransfer shared across the frame boundary and no message that carries one. Workarounds. For getting data out: copy to the clipboard, or offer ui/download-file . For getting data in: a file input, or a paste target, or a host-proxied resources/read if the thing lives on the server anyway.

sections.h: How do I do zoom and pan?
sections.x: input.zoompan Core Level 3 Platform Wheel and pinch zoom, pan, reset, fit to content. Ground The browser inside the sandbox provides it. No host round trip. Recipes Image Annotator , Workflow Builder , Media Viewer Demo lab-input For any spatial surface: wheel to zoom, drag to pan, a reset, and a fit. The reset and the fit are not optional extras. A user who has zoomed to 600% and panned into empty space has no way back without them, and in a 380-pixel frame that happens within about four wheel gestures. The detail that separates a canvas that feels right from one that fights you is zooming about the pointer rather than the origin. The transform has to be adjusted so the point under the cursor stays under the cursor. Extracted from from apps/recipes/r06-image-annotator/index.html const before = scale; scale = Math.min(6, Math.max(0.4, scale * (event.deltaY < 0 ? 1.12 : 0.89))); const rect = stage.getBoundingClientRect(); const px = event.clientX - rect.left, py = event.clientY - rect.top; panX = px - ((px - panX) / before) * scale; panY = py - ((py - panY) / before) * scale; { passive: false } on the wheel listener is required rather than optional. Browsers default wheel listeners to passive so that scrolling stays smooth, and a passive listener that calls preventDefault() is ignored with a console warning. Without the flag your zoom appears to work in development and lets the host’s conversation scroll underneath it in production. Accessibility. Every spatial gesture needs a non-spatial equivalent. Buttons for zoom in, zoom out, reset and fit, and arrow keys to pan. A canvas that can only be operated by dragging is a canvas that cannot be operated at all by a large number of people.

sections.h: The keyboard model, in one table
sections.x: This is the set users bring with them. Implementing it is about twenty lines and not implementing it is the most common reason an embedded table feels unfinished. Key In a list or grid In a menu In a dialog Arrow keys Move the active item Move the highlight Nothing Space Toggle selection Activate Activate the focused control Enter Open or activate Activate and close Submit Shift with arrows Extend the selection Nothing Nothing Cmd/Ctrl+A Select all Nothing Select the field’s text Home, End First, last item First, last item Nothing Escape Clear the selection Close, restore focus Close, restore focus Tab Leave the widget Close, then leave Cycle inside The row that matters most is the last one. A composite widget is one tab stop, and the arrow keys move within it. A table where Tab visits every cell is a table nobody can get past.

Keyboard events originating in the view are not swallowed by the host. A list of N rows presents one tab stop, not N. Shift-click and Cmd/Ctrl-click produce range and additive selection. contextmenu inside the view is not shadowed by a host menu. Pointer capture keeps a drag alive when the pointer leaves the element. A wheel listener that calls preventDefault() is honoured, so the view can zoom without the host scrolling. Every gesture in the view has a keyboard equivalent.

Nine capabilities and one line of protocol between them. The lesson is not that this group is easy; it is that the effort belongs in your view rather than in the channel. When something here does not work, the answer is almost never a message you are missing. Previous 9. Dialogs and Attention Next 11. Clipboard, Files and System Integration

Chapter 11 Two messages that exist because the sandbox closed a door, one permission, and three capabilities with no route at all. A sandboxed frame cannot navigate the browser and cannot save a file, and both restrictions are deliberate: navigation would let a hostile view move the user somewhere convincing, and unmediated downloads would let it write to disk without anyone seeing. The two escape hatches the extension provides are both here, ui/open-link and ui/download-file , and they are shaped identically because they solve the same problem: put a human in the path. Both work the same way. The view asks, the host decides, and the human can see it happen. Everything else in this chapter is either the browser working normally or a door that is still shut. The live application needs JavaScript. Its source is in the repository under apps/ .

sections.h: How do I copy to the clipboard?
sections.x: clipboard.write Core Level 2 On the wire Copy text or structured content, with a fallback when denied. Messages clipboardWrite permissions Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes Data Explorer , File Explorer , Spreadsheet , Code and Diff Reviewer Demo lab-clipboard Ship both paths, because copying is the only exit a sandboxed frame has that works without the host’s cooperation. It cannot save a file unaided, nothing can be dragged out of it, and there is no address bar to paste a URL into. The asynchronous Clipboard API is the better path when you have the permission; the execCommand fallback needs nothing but a user gesture and works in the host that granted you nothing. The asynchronous Clipboard API, navigator.clipboard.writeText , needs the clipboardWrite permission declared by your server in _meta.ui.permissions and granted by the host in the frame’s allow attribute. It is the better path: it handles multiple formats and does not touch the DOM. The execCommand("copy") fallback needs no permission at all, but it does need a user gesture and a focused selection, which is why it involves a temporary off-screen textarea. It is deprecated and it works everywhere. Extracted from from apps/labs/lab-clipboard/index.html async function copyText(text) { try { await navigator.clipboard.writeText(text); return "Clipboard API"; } catch { const area = document.createElement("textarea"); area.value = text; area.setAttribute("readonly", ""); area.style.position = "fixed"; area.style.opacity = "0"; document.body.append(area); area.select(); const ok = document.execCommand("copy"); area.remove(); if (!ok) throw new Error("both clipboard paths refused"); return "execCommand fallback"; } } Copy what the destination wants. A table copied as a single string of text is useless in a spreadsheet. Tab-separated values with newlines paste into every spreadsheet ever written, and Recipe 5 copies ranges that way for exactly that reason. CSV for a file, TSV for the clipboard. Failure modes. The whole point of the pair above is that failure is rare and recoverable. Show the confirmation once, after the copy succeeded, and do not show which path it took. The user does not care.

clipboard.read Extended Level 2 Not standardised Read what the user has on the clipboard. Ground No standard mechanism exists yet. The entry carries a workaround. Recipes Spreadsheet Demo lab-clipboard No, and it is refused twice over. The extension’s permission set is exactly camera , microphone , geolocation and clipboardWrite , so there is nothing a host could grant you even if it wanted to. Independently, navigator.clipboard.readText from an opaque origin is refused by the browser regardless of policy. Press the button in the demonstration and read the NotAllowedError it produces. What to do instead. Give the user somewhere to paste. A focused input, a textarea, or a drop zone that also handles the paste event. The browser delivers pasted content to a focused element without any permission at all, because the user’s Cmd+V is the consent. That covers the realistic use case, which is importing data, and it does not cover the unrealistic one, which is reading the clipboard without being asked. Why the door is shut. A view that could read the clipboard silently could read whatever the user last copied, which is often a password. Any proposal here needs a user gesture and a host-mediated permission, and probably a visible indication in the host’s own chrome.

sections.h: How do I let the user pick a file?
sections.x: file.open Core Level 2 Platform Open the system file picker and read what comes back. Ground The browser inside the sandbox provides it. No host round trip. Recipes File Explorer Demo lab-clipboard <input type="file"> , with no permission and no message. The sandbox does not interfere here for a reason worth understanding: the user picked the file themselves in a dialog the browser drew, so consent is unambiguous, and the bytes stay in your frame unless your code sends them somewhere. That is the same reasoning that lets paste work while clipboard reads are refused. Application behaviour. Read with FileReader or file.text() . Validate type and size before reading, not after, because a 400MB file read into a string in a frame with a modest memory budget is a crash, and a crash is not an error you can catch. Say what you accept, in the interface, before the picker opens.

sections.h: How do I accept a dropped file?
sections.x: file.dropzone Core Level 2 Platform Accept dropped files with validation, preview, and progress. Ground The browser inside the sandbox provides it. No host round trip. Recipes File Explorer , Image Annotator Demo lab-clipboard The same input by another route, and the one users reach for first when they already have the file in a window. Offer both: the picker is discoverable and the drop zone is fast, and people split roughly evenly between them. Application behaviour. Four events. dragover must call preventDefault() or the drop never fires, which is the single most common bug in every drop zone ever written. dragenter and dragleave drive the visual state, and dragleave fires when the pointer crosses onto a child element, so count depth or use pointer-events: none on the children. drop reads event.dataTransfer.files . Validate visibly. Wrong type, too large, too many: say which, name the file, and leave the zone ready for another attempt. A drop zone that silently does nothing when a file is rejected is indistinguishable from a broken one.

sections.h: How do I show the user what a document is?
sections.x: preview.document Core Level 2 Platform Show what a document is before anyone acts on it, at a chosen size. Ground The browser inside the sandbox provides it. No host round trip. Recipes File Explorer Demo r03-file-explorer A file arrives, by drop or by picker or as a link from a tool, and the user has a decision to make about it. Attach it, replace with it, delete it, send it. Every one of those decisions is easier with the document in front of them and harder with a filename in front of them, and notes.txt is a filename that could be anything. The good news is that a preview needs nothing the protocol does not already give you. tools/check_sandbox.mjs runs both routes inside a real sandboxed frame with an opaque origin, and both work: Extracted from from conformance/sandbox.json "previewDataUri": { "ok": true, "value": "rendered" }, "previewObjectUrl": { "ok": true, "value": "rendered" }, The first is a data: URI built from base64 that arrived in a tool result. The second is URL.createObjectURL on a File the user dropped, which the frame renders without the bytes going anywhere. The probe records that URL’s scheme as blob:null , which is the opaque origin appearing in the URL itself: the handle is meaningful inside this document and meaningless everywhere else, including to the host. Neither needs a permission and neither needs a CSP entry, because neither is a network request. An ordinary URL on somebody else’s origin does need a CSP entry, which makes it the one route to avoid: a preview that has to reach the network fails in the host with the strict policy, and the strict policy is the default. Size is the caller’s decision, not the document’s. The shared component takes one of three, and only the body changes between them: Extracted from from apps/lib/view.css .preview.sm .preview-body { max-height: 48px; } .preview.md .preview-body { max-height: 150px; } .preview.lg .preview-body { max-height: 360px; } Small answers “which file is this” in a list. Medium answers “is this the right one” beside a button. Large answers “what does it say” when reading is the point. The header carrying the name and type is identical at all three, because a preview whose name disappears as it shrinks has become a thumbnail. Truncate by size too. Reading four hundred kilobytes of text into a 48 pixel box costs exactly what reading it into a large one costs and shows a fiftieth of it. Recipe 3 slices at 220, 1200 and 8000 characters. Say what you cannot show. A type with no preview gets a sentence naming the type and offering the routes that do work, which are opening it and downloading it. Rendering unknown bytes as text produces mojibake, and mojibake reads as a bug in your application rather than as a file you cannot display. Accessibility. The image carries alt naming the file, because “Preview of cover.png” is what a screen reader user needs and “thumbnail” is what they already assumed. The size control is a group of toggle buttons with aria-pressed , not a <select> , because three options is below the count where a menu earns its cost and the current size should be visible without opening anything. Failure modes. Unsupported does not arise; this is platform behaviour. Denied arises when the bytes come through a server tool the host will not proxy, and the answer is the filename and metadata you already had. Failed is a tool that returned isError , and Recipe 3 shows the server’s own message in the preview’s place while leaving the tree untouched.

sections.h: How do I preview something the server only linked?
sections.x: preview.resource Extended Level 3 On the wire Preview a resource the server linked rather than embedded. Messages resource_link serverResources resources/read Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes File Explorer Demo r03-file-explorer A tool result can carry a resource_link rather than the bytes, which is the right shape when the thing is large or when the model has no use for its contents. The link carries uri , name , mimeType , size and optional icons , which is enough to render a small preview with no round trip at all. For anything larger you need the bytes, and they come through the host with resources/read , which means the host must declare serverResources . Where it does not, the metadata on the link is what you have, and a small preview built from name , mimeType and size is a genuine preview rather than a placeholder. Recipe 3’s server exposes each file as a resource as well as through a tool, because a thing with a URI is a resource and modelling it as one lets the view read it the way it reads anything else. Sending base64 image data into the model’s context through content would be tokens spent on something it cannot look at.

sections.h: How do I save a file?
sections.x: file.export Core Level 2 On the wire Draft only Hand a generated artifact to the host to save. Messages ui/download-file downloadFile Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes Data Explorer , Image Annotator , Media Viewer Demo lab-clipboard file.save Core Level 2 On the wire Draft only Persist app-generated content through the host. Messages ui/download-file resource_link Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes none yet Demo lab-clipboard allow-downloads is not in the sandbox, so an anchor with a download attribute is inert and a blob URL goes nowhere. ui/download-file is the way out, and it takes standard MCP content types. The contents array takes standard MCP resource types rather than a bespoke download format, which means the same shapes you already use in tool results. For inline content, send an EmbeddedResource : its resource.uri supplies the suggested filename and its text or blob carries the bytes. Illustrative, not run , quoted from the extension specification { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "ui/download-file", "params": { "contents": [ { "type": "resource", "resource": { "uri": "file:///deployments.csv", "mimeType": "text/csv", "text": "service,env,version\ncheckout,production,4.18.2\n" } } ] } } For something the host can fetch itself, send a ResourceLink with a URL instead. The difference matters for large files: an EmbeddedResource puts every byte through postMessage , while a ResourceLink lets the host fetch directly, with its own network identity and its own idea of what that URL is allowed to be. A refusal resolves. It does not throw. This is the single most important line in the section and the one that costs people an afternoon. McpUiDownloadFileResult carries an optional isError , and the specification uses it for a host that declined and for a user who cancelled the save dialog. The promise resolves either way: Extracted from from apps/recipes/r01-data-explorer/index.html const result = await bridge.downloadFile({ contents: [{ type: "resource", resource: { uri: "file:///deployments.csv", mimeType: "text/csv", text: csv() } }] }); if (result?.isError) { toast("The host declined to save that file."); return; } toast("Handed to the host"); A try / catch around that call catches nothing when the user cancels, so the view says the file was saved and no file exists. What a rejection does mean is that no answer arrived at all: a timeout, or the bridge going away. Both need handling and they need different sentences. ui/open-link and ui/message work the same way, with isError on McpUiOpenLinkResult and McpUiMessageResult . Pass the params object, not the contents. App.downloadFile in the extension SDK takes the request’s params , so the argument is { contents: [...] } and not [...] . Handing it the array directly leaves params.contents undefined, and a host with nothing to download does nothing at all. tools/check_sdk_api.py compares this repository’s bridge against the SDK’s signatures on every build, because the version of that helper which took a bare array is what this book used to publish. Failure modes. Absence has no fallback worth the name. If hostCapabilities.downloadFile is absent, a sandboxed frame genuinely cannot save a file. The honest response is to not show an export button, and to offer copy instead, which is what Recipe 6 does: press “Refuse downloads” in its demonstration and the export path switches to the clipboard with a sentence explaining why.

sections.h: How do I open a link?
sections.x: link.open Core Level 1 On the wire Delegate external navigation instead of attempting it. Messages ui/open-link openLinks Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes Code and Diff Reviewer , Approval Center Demo lab-clipboard Level 1, and the one capability in this chapter that a purely card-shaped view is likely to need. A summary card with no interaction at all still usually wants to link somewhere: to the ticket, the dashboard, the document it is summarising. An <a href> inside a sandboxed frame without allow-top-navigation cannot navigate, and window.open is blocked. ui/open-link asks the host to do it. The host should open in the user’s default browser or a new tab, and may refuse. Application behaviour. Check hostCapabilities.openLinks at initialisation. If it is absent, do not render links as links: render them as text you can copy, or omit them. A blue underlined word that does nothing when clicked is worse than plain text. Handle the refusal at the moment of the click as well, because a host may allow links in general and decline a specific one on policy grounds. The demonstration has a control that removes the capability so you can see both paths.

system.share Extended Level 3 Not standardised Invoke the operating system share sheet. Ground No standard mechanism exists yet. The entry carries a workaround. Recipes Media Viewer Demo no live demo system.print Extended Level 3 Not standardised Request host-mediated printing. Ground No standard mechanism exists yet. The entry carries a workaround. Recipes none yet Demo no live demo No, and for the same reason both times. navigator.share needs the web-share policy-controlled feature and window.print needs the allow-modals sandbox token; neither is in the extension’s permission set, and no message replaces either. The unpleasant part is that feature detection lies. navigator.share is a function on the object, so if (navigator.share) passes, and then the call either rejects or silently does nothing depending on the browser. Detect the capability from hostCapabilities and your own fallback plan, not from the presence of the API. navigator.share needs the web-share permission policy. window.print needs allow-modals . Neither is granted. Feature detection reports them as present and then they fail or do nothing, which is worse than absent. Workarounds. For sharing: ui/open-link with a canonical URL, or copy the URL to the clipboard. Recipe 12 does the first and falls back to the second, and says which it did. For printing: ui/download-file with a generated PDF, or accept that printing an embedded view is not a thing that happens.

sections.h: Worked example: getting a table out of a frame
sections.x:
The Data Explorer in Recipe 1 has eight rows the user might want elsewhere. Four routes exist and the recipe offers two of them, which is the right number. Copy works everywhere, needs no capability, and puts the data where the user’s next action already expects it. It is the default and it should be the first thing you build. Export through ui/download-file produces a file, needs hostCapabilities.downloadFile , and is the only way to move something too large to paste. The recipe omits the button when the capability is absent. Drag out does not exist. Chapter 10 has the gap. A link to the data on the server through ui/open-link is the fourth route, and it is worth considering before the other three: if the rows came from a system that has a URL for them, sending the user there gives them the data and the context, and costs one message. That ordering generalises. Ask what the user is going to do with the thing, then pick the route that lands closest to it, rather than picking the route that is easiest to build. Whichever route, generate the CSV properly. Three of the four end in a string somebody’s spreadsheet will open, and the line everybody writes is wrong: Illustrative, not run rows.map((r) => r.join(",")).join("
") // wrong A value containing a comma adds a column. A value containing a quote confuses the parser. A value containing a newline ends the record early. None of those produce an error: the spreadsheet opens, shows something plausible, and is false. Quote a field when it contains any of the three, and double the quotes inside it: Extracted from from apps/lib/view.js function toCsv(rows) { const field = (value) => { const text = value === null || value === undefined ? "" : String(value); return /[",
]/.test(text) ? `"${text.replace(/"/g, '""')}"` : text; }; return rows.map((row) => row.map(field).join(",")).join("
"); } CRLF between records is what RFC 4180 asks for and what Excel wants; everything else tolerates it. This book shipped the naive version until somebody asked whether the export had been checked, and the answer was that the message had been checked and the bytes never had. The fixtures contain no commas, so no demonstration would ever have shown it. The render harness now calls this function with a comma, a quote, a newline, a null and a zero, because a helper only ever called with safe input is a helper nobody has tested.

For ui/open-link , the host opens in the user’s default browser or a new tab, and may refuse. A host that opens links in a frame inside its own window has missed the point of the message, which is to get the navigation out of the sandbox and somewhere the user can see an address bar. For ui/download-file , the host should confirm, derive the filename from the last segment of resource.uri , sanitise it against path traversal, and may refuse on size or policy grounds. For a ResourceLink it fetches the content itself, which means the fetch happens with the host’s network identity rather than the view’s, and the host should treat the URL accordingly. For clipboardWrite , the host maps your server’s requested permission onto the frame’s allow attribute and reports back what it actually granted in hostCapabilities.sandbox.permissions . Requested and granted are different fields for a reason, and a view that assumes the request was honoured is a view that breaks silently in the host that declined it.

With clipboardWrite granted, navigator.clipboard.writeText succeeds inside the frame. Without it, the execCommand fallback still copies from a user gesture. ui/download-file with an EmbeddedResource produces a file named from the last segment of its URI. A declined ui/download-file resolves with isError: true and the view says the file was not saved. ui/download-file with downloadFile absent from hostCapabilities is never sent by a conforming view. ui/open-link opens outside the sandbox, or returns an error. An <a download> inside the frame does nothing, and the view does not rely on it. A file chosen with <input type="file"> is readable in the view and is not transmitted anywhere the view did not send it.

Every capability here that reaches outside the frame either has a message ( ui/open-link , ui/download-file ) or is a gap ( clipboard.read , system.share , system.print ). Everything that stays inside works. That line is the sandbox boundary, and it is worth drawing on your own requirements before you write any code. Anything that stays inside the frame costs you an afternoon. Anything that reaches outside is either one of two messages or a gap you will be working around for the life of the product. Previous 10. Keyboard, Pointer and Selection Next 12. Pickers and Dropzones

Chapter 12 Three inputs the browser has already built for every platform and locale, and one picker that has to come through the host because the view holds no connection. Use the native inputs. Three of these four capabilities are HTML input types with a decade of platform work behind them, and the effort you would spend replacing one buys you a worse version. The fourth reaches into the server’s namespace, not the user’s machine, and that one has to go through the host because your view holds no connection of its own. The live application needs JavaScript. Its source is in the repository under apps/ .

picker.date Extended Level 2 Platform Native date selection, localised by the host locale. Ground The browser inside the sandbox provides it. No host round trip. Recipes Settings and Preferences Demo lab-pickers picker.time Extended Level 2 Platform Native time selection in the host timezone. Ground The browser inside the sandbox provides it. No host round trip. Recipes Settings and Preferences Demo lab-pickers picker.color Extended Level 2 Platform Native colour selection. Ground The browser inside the sandbox provides it. No host round trip. Recipes Image Annotator , Settings and Preferences Demo lab-pickers <input type="date"> , type="time"> and type="color"> , all of which work inside the sandbox with no permission and no message. Nothing about the opaque origin interferes, because the picker is drawn by the browser rather than by your document, and the value arrives through an ordinary input event. You get keyboard support, screen reader support, the platform’s own calendar and colour panel, and localisation for every region the browser knows, which is more than your component library knows. The argument for replacing them is usually visual: they do not match the design. That is true, and the cost of replacing them is a component that has to reimplement date arithmetic, week-start conventions, month names in the user’s language, and a keyboard model, and that will still be wrong for the calendar systems you have not heard of. In a four hundred pixel card next to somebody’s conversation, the trade is not close. The one thing you have to add. The picker collects a value; you have to display values in the user’s terms, and the browser’s idea of “the user” is the machine, not the person the host is serving. Formatting comes from hostContext.locale and hostContext.timeZone , through Intl . Extracted from from apps/lib/view.js function formatters(hostContext) { const locale = hostContext?.locale || undefined; const timeZone = hostContext?.timeZone || undefined; return { number: (n, options) => new Intl.NumberFormat(locale, options).format(n), date: (value, options = { dateStyle: "medium" }) => new Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, { ...options, timeZone }) .format(value instanceof Date ? value : new Date(value)), time: (value) => new Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, { timeStyle: "medium", timeZone }) .format(value instanceof Date ? value : new Date(value)), }; } Press “Switch to ja-JP / Tokyo” in the demonstration. The pickers keep their ISO values, which is correct, and everything the view renders changes, which is also correct. A view that formats with the default locale looks right on the developer’s machine and wrong for most of its users. Accessibility. Native inputs come with the platform’s accessibility already wired. What they still need from you is a real <label> associated with the input, a hint about the expected format when there is one, and enough contrast on the border that the field is visible in a high contrast theme.

sections.h: How do I pick something the server owns?
sections.x: picker.resource Extended Level 3 On the wire Pick from resources the server exposes, through the host. Messages resources/read serverResources Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes File Explorer Demo lab-pickers Call resources/read when hostCapabilities.serverResources is present, and the host proxies it to the server and hands back the contents. The important difference from a file picker is whose namespace you are reaching into: a file picker touches the user’s machine and needs their consent, while a resource read touches the server your view came from and needs the host’s. This is different in kind from a file picker. A file picker reaches the user’s machine; a resource picker reaches the server’s namespace, and your view holds no connection to the server. Extracted from from apps/labs/lab-pickers/index.html $("#load").onclick = async () => { try { const result = await bridge.readServerResource($("#uri").value); $("#out").textContent = result.contents?.[0]?.text ?? JSON.stringify(result); } catch (error) { $("#out").textContent = `Refused: ${error.message}`; } }; The awkward part, and a live discrepancy. The specification’s list of standard MCP messages available to a view names exactly one resource method: resources/read . On a plain reading, a view can read a resource it already knows the URI of and cannot discover one. The SDK disagrees. @modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps ships App.listServerResources() , and its own documentation uses it to build a picker by filtering the returned list on MIME type. hostCapabilities also carries serverResources.listChanged , which only means something if listing is proxied at all. So the honest position is that resources/list from a view is supported by the reference implementation and unstated in the specification text, which means hosts may reasonably differ. Treat it as an enhancement: try the list, and have a fallback for a host that refuses. This book files it as a documentation gap, because the SDK’s behaviour looks like the intended one. A picker can also learn its options without listing at all: from the tool result that rendered the view, from a server tool that returns a list, or from a namespace the server documents. The last two are worth preferring anyway, because a server tool returning a list also gets you filtering and pagination. In the demonstration the options come from the host fixture, and the “missing” entry is there so you can watch a refused read. Security. This is the good path for reading server-side data, and it is worth choosing over a fetch to your own API even when you could declare the origin in connectDomains . A read through the host is visible to the host, subject to the host’s policy, and appears in the transcript. A direct fetch is a hole you asked the host to open and then used unobserved. Failure modes. Unsupported when serverResources is absent: the picker should not appear, and whatever it was going to configure needs a different route. Denied and failed both come back as JSON-RPC errors, and the error message is the host’s, so display it, and do not replace it with your own guess.

file.dropzone Core Level 2 Platform Accept dropped files with validation, preview, and progress. Ground The browser inside the sandbox provides it. No host round trip. Recipes File Explorer , Image Annotator Demo lab-clipboard Covered in Chapter 11, listed here because a dropzone and a picker are two routes to the same thing and an application that offers one should usually offer both. The picker is discoverable, the dropzone is fast, and users split roughly evenly between them. The one addition specific to this chapter: a dropzone that accepts a type of file should say so in its resting state, not only in its error state. “Drop a JSON annotation file” tells somebody what to look for. “Drop files here” followed by “wrong file type” tells them what they did wrong.

sections.h: What a picker costs at each level
sections.x: Level What you get What you build 1 Native date, time and colour inputs Formatting through the host’s locale 2 The same, plus files through file.open Validation and preview 3 Resource reads through the host The list, and a fallback when reads fail The table is worth reading as a warning about the third row. A resource picker looks like a small feature and it is the only one here that depends on a host capability, a server round trip, and a listing mechanism the specification does not describe. Budget accordingly, and consider whether a server tool returning exactly the options you need would be simpler than a general picker.

Unsupported. The native inputs cannot be unsupported; every browser has them. picker.resource is unsupported when serverResources is absent, and the correct response is to omit the picker and configure the thing some other way, usually from the tool arguments that rendered the view. Denied. Only picker.resource can be denied, as a JSON-RPC error from the host. Show the host’s message and add no guess of your own. Failed. A resource that does not exist returns an error with the URI in it. Say which resource, because a picker with three options and one broken one is a picker whose failure the user can work around. Cancelled and timeout. The native pickers cannot be cancelled from outside, and a dismissed picker simply leaves the value unchanged, which needs no handling. A resource read has no timeout of its own, so give it one.

Native date, time and colour inputs render and open their platform pickers inside the sandbox. Values are displayed using hostContext.locale and hostContext.timeZone , not the machine’s. Changing the host locale re-renders every formatted value without a reload. resources/read through the host returns content for a known URI. A read for an unknown URI returns an error, and the view reports it. With serverResources absent, the view sends no resources/read .

Two rules. Use the platform’s inputs, because they are better than the ones you would write and they are free. And format every value you display through the host’s locale and timezone, which are not the browser’s, because in this environment the browser is not where the user is.

The date input deserves one more paragraph, because the same argument generalises to every native control in Chapter 23 and it is the argument people skip fastest when a design does not match. Ask what a replacement has to know. Which day the week starts on, in the user’s region. The names of the months, in the user’s language, in the correct grammatical case for a date. Whether the region uses a non-Gregorian calendar. How to type a date rather than pick one, because most people type. What a screen reader should say when the value changes. How the picker behaves at 200% zoom, and on a touch device, and under forced colours. The browser knows all of that, for every locale it supports, and it was paid for by somebody else. A component library knows some of it for the locales its authors tested. A component you write in a four hundred pixel frame at the end of a sprint knows the first two. The visual mismatch is real and it is the only cost. In an embedded view that is already visually distinct from its host by design, it is a smaller cost than it looks. Previous 11. Clipboard, Files and System Integration Next 13. Host Environment and Theming

Chapter 13 A theming contract in three layers, seven environment signals, and the reason your view must define every colour it uses even though the host is going to send them. The host sends CSS custom properties in hostContext.styles.variables , and you use them with your own fallback defined for every single one. No component library is involved anywhere in this, and that is deliberate: the specification rejected shipping one because no single library works across every host’s aesthetic, and rejected sending spacing tokens because layouts break when spacing varies from what they were designed against. Seven capabilities describe the environment. All arrive in hostContext , all can change through ui/notifications/host-context-changed , and the most common bug in this group is reading them once at startup. That bug is quiet: the view looks correct in every screenshot and wrong only for the user who switched to dark mode with the panel already open, which is nobody on your machine and a steady fraction of everybody else. The live application needs JavaScript. Its source is in the repository under apps/ .

sections.h: What does the host actually send?
sections.x: The theming story is layered, and mixing the layers is what produces views that look almost right. The host sends a coarse signal, a set of named variables, and a set of environment facts, and each answers a different question: whether you are light or dark, what your colours should be, and how much room you actually have. The wire format is CSS custom properties in hostContext.styles.variables , with an optional block of @font-face or @import rules in styles.css.fonts . The specification standardises the names : background, text, border and ring colours in a fixed set of semantic slots, font families and weights, a type scale, border radii, and four shadow levels. The semantics are roles, not palettes. There is no “blue”. There is --color-background-primary and --color-text-primary , and the pairing is what makes contrast work. A view that uses --color-text-danger on --color-background-danger is legible in every theme; one that uses a red it picked itself on a background the host chose is legible in the theme it was built in. The adaptation is dark mode, contrast, motion and text scale, and only the first of those is on the wire. Chapter 14 covers the others, which are media queries. Spacing is deliberately absent from the variable set, and the reason is worth repeating: layouts break when spacing varies from what they were designed against. A host can change your colours safely and cannot change your rhythm safely.

sections.h: How do I follow the host’s theme?
sections.x: env.theme Core Level 1 On the wire Take the host's tokens and follow them when they change. Messages styles --color-background-primary light-dark Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes Data Explorer , Dashboard , Code and Diff Reviewer Demo lab-theme Apply the variables to the document root and define a fallback for every one you use, because a host is permitted to send all of them, some of them, or none. Falling back happens per variable, which is what makes a partial set more dangerous than an empty one. The specification warns about partial sets specifically. If a host sends a dark background and no text colour, your light-mode text fallback lands on it and the result is unreadable, which is worse than either theme applied whole. Using role pairs consistently is the defence: take --color-background-danger and --color-text-danger together, so a missing pair fails as a pair. Extracted from from apps/lib/view.css :root { color-scheme: light dark; --color-background-primary: light-dark(#ffffff, #16181d); --color-text-primary: light-dark(#15181d, #e7eaee); --color-text-info: light-dark(#0f5c8c, #63aedc); --border-radius-md: 8px; } light-dark() with color-scheme: light dark is the compact way to write a fallback that is already theme-aware, so a view with no host variables at all still respects the operating system. The host’s values, when they arrive, override it. Removing is as important as setting. When the host stops sending a variable, the view is supposed to fall back to its own value, which it cannot do while last theme’s override is still on the root element. The bridge here tracks what it applied and removes what is no longer sent. Extracted from from emulator/app-bridge.js for (const name of appliedVariables) { if (variables[name] == null) root.style.removeProperty(name); } appliedVariables = []; for (const [name, value] of Object.entries(variables)) { if (value != null) { root.style.setProperty(name, value); appliedVariables.push(name); } } Press “Send only half the variables” in the demonstration to see why this matters: with half a dark palette applied over a light fallback, the result is unreadable, and that is exactly the clash the specification warns about. The mitigation on the view side is to use pairs consistently, so that a missing background and a present foreground are both wrong together. Failure modes. No styles at all is the common case and must look deliberate. Partial styles is the dangerous case. A theme that changes while a menu is open is the fiddly case: re-render or re-read on hostcontextchanged rather than caching computed colours in JavaScript. env.fonts Extended Level 2 On the wire Load the host's typeface without loading anything else. Messages fonts --font-sans Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes Settings and Preferences Demo lab-theme Fonts arrive as a CSS block to inject, and --font-sans names the family. Inject the block into a <style> element in the head and let the variable do the rest. If the host sends the variable and not the block, or the block fails to load, your fallback stack is what people see, so make it a real stack and not a single exotic name. A view that ignores the host’s tokens reads as an advertisement

env.locale Core Level 1 On the wire Format numbers, dates, and text for the user's region. Messages locale Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes Data Explorer Demo lab-theme env.timezone Core Level 1 On the wire Render instants in the timezone the user is actually in. Messages timeZone Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes none yet Demo lab-theme hostContext.locale and hostContext.timeZone , always. Not navigator.language , which is the browser’s. Not the system timezone, which is the machine’s. A host serving a user in Tokyo from a server in Virginia sends ja-JP and Asia/Tokyo ; a view that reads the machine renders Virginia’s answer. A concrete failure. A deployment list showing “Aug 18, 2026, 4:21 AM” because the view formatted a UTC instant with the machine’s offset, while the user is in Tokyo and the deploy happened at lunchtime. Nothing errors. Everybody’s timeline is wrong by nine hours. Whose clock is it

env.platform Extended Level 2 On the wire Coarse platform shape, used sparingly. Messages platform userAgent Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes none yet Demo lab-theme env.inputMode Core Level 2 On the wire Size targets for the modality actually in use. Messages deviceCapabilities touch hover Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes Settings and Preferences Demo lab-theme platform is web , desktop or mobile , and userAgent names the host. Both are Extended, both are coarse, and both should be used sparingly. Reach for a media query or a capability check first; branch on the host name only when you are working around a known bug in a specific host, and comment it with the bug. deviceCapabilities carries touch and hover , and this pair is worth acting on. Touch without hover means every hover-revealed control is unreachable and targets want the 44 by 44 CSS pixels of WCAG’s AAA criterion, where its AA criterion requires 24 by 24. Hover means tooltips work and a compact toolbar is fine. Both can be true on a laptop with a touchscreen, so treat them as independent facts. Extracted from from apps/labs/lab-input/index.html function describeModality(device = {}) { const parts = [device.touch && "touch", device.hover && "hover"].filter(Boolean); $("#mode").textContent = `modality: ${parts.join(" + ") || "unstated"}`; } bridge.on("hostcontextchanged", (patch) => { if (patch.deviceCapabilities) describeModality(patch.deviceCapabilities); });

env.safeArea Core Level 2 On the wire Keep content out of regions the host has spoken for. Messages safeAreaInsets Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes none yet Demo lab-theme Four numbers in pixels, which you add to your outermost padding. They describe regions of the host’s window that something else already occupies: a notch, a title bar, a home indicator, a floating toolbar. Ignoring them does not truncate your layout, which is why it survives review. It puts your first button under the host’s own chrome, where it can be seen and not pressed. A native app would read env(safe-area-inset-*) . A view inside someone else’s window cannot, because those values describe the browser’s viewport and the notch is not on the iframe’s viewport, so they arrive as zero and the CSS compiles fine. The host measures the obstruction against its own window and sends the numbers, which is the only party in a position to know them. Application behaviour. Turn them into custom properties and add them to your outermost padding. The view stylesheet in this repository does exactly that, which is why pressing “Add a notch” in the demonstration visibly moves the content in from every edge. Extracted from from apps/lib/view.css body { padding-top: calc(12px + var(--safe-top, 0px)); padding-right: calc(12px + var(--safe-right, 0px)); padding-bottom: calc(12px + var(--safe-bottom, 0px)); padding-left: calc(12px + var(--safe-left, 0px)); } The controls most affected are the ones pinned to an edge: a bottom toolbar, a floating action button, a toast stack. Everything in the middle of the view is fine, which is why this bug survives testing on a desktop and appears on the first phone.

The standardised set is long and the grouping is what makes it usable. There are four families, and a view that uses one member of a family should use the rest of it, because the host chose them together and a background from one family under text from another is how you get grey on grey in exactly one theme. Backgrounds and text come in pairs by role: primary, secondary, tertiary, inverse, and the status roles info, success, warning, danger, plus disabled. The pairing is the contrast guarantee. --color-text-danger on --color-background-danger is legible in every theme a host can send; a red you chose on a background the host chose is legible in the theme you tested. Borders and rings mirror the same roles. The ring set exists because focus indication needs to be distinguishable from a border, and a host with an unusual palette needs to be able to say so. Typography carries families, four weights, a text scale in four sizes and a heading scale in seven, each with a matching line height. Using the size without its line height is the most common way to end up with cramped text in a host that sends a larger scale than you designed against. Radii, border width and four shadow levels are the shape vocabulary. These are the ones most likely to be absent, because many hosts do not have opinions about them, so their fallbacks matter more than the colours’. Spacing is deliberately absent, and the specification says why: layouts break when spacing varies from what they were designed against. Your rhythm is yours, and the practical consequence is that a view can look native in colour and typography while keeping a layout it can actually test, because the two things that shift under it are the two things CSS custom properties handle without a reflow.

No styles at all. The common case, and it must look deliberate. Every view in this book renders correctly with an empty hostContext , which is the test worth running first. Half the variables. The dangerous case, and the one the specification warns about. Use role pairs consistently so a missing background and a present foreground fail together. A theme that changes mid-interaction. Re-read rather than cache. Anything you computed in JavaScript from a variable is stale the moment ui/notifications/host-context-changed arrives. A font block that does not load. Your fallback stack is what people see, so make it a real stack. A single exotic family name with no fallback is a view rendered in whatever the browser picks.

hostContext carries theme , locale and timeZone in the initialize result. Style variables are applied to the document root and removed when the host stops sending them. A theme change arrives as a partial ui/notifications/host-context-changed and the view re-renders without a reload. The view renders correctly with no styles at all. safeAreaInsets moves content away from every edge it names. deviceCapabilities.touch produces targets of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, and 44 by 44 where the design allows it.

Read the environment in a function, not in a constant. Define a fallback for every variable you use. Format through the host’s locale and timezone. Those three habits cover almost everything in this chapter, and the demonstration above will break a view that lacks any of them within three button presses. Previous 12. Pickers and Dropzones Next 14. Accessibility

Chapter 14 Three preferences the host never sends, one live region you have to build, and the reason an embedded frame makes all of this harder than a page. Accessibility is a section in every entry of this book, because that is the only arrangement that survives a deadline. A chapter at the end gets read once and cut first; a section in the entry you are already reading gets implemented while you are implementing the entry. This chapter carries the four capabilities that fit nowhere else, and the problems that come specifically from running inside someone else’s window. The live application needs JavaScript. Its source is in the repository under apps/ .

sections.h: What is harder inside a frame?
sections.x: Four things, none of which are your fault and all of which are your problem. They come from the frame boundary, and knowing them changes what you build rather than merely what you test. Your view is a document inside a document. A screen reader user reaches it by moving into the frame, and inside it your headings start again at whatever level you chose. Use a sensible internal hierarchy and give the frame a meaningful title, because the title is what the host can expose as the frame’s accessible name. You cannot see the host’s landmarks. You do not know whether the conversation is a main , whether there is already an h1 , or what else has role="status" . Assume your announcements are competing with the host’s. Focus cannot cross the boundary. A keyboard user who tabs in must be able to tab out, so no focus traps outside <dialog> and no roving list that cycles forever. Chapter 8 has the gap. The user’s preferences reach you by a different route than the theme. The host sends colours. The operating system sends motion, contrast and text size, through media queries. Those two can disagree, and the demonstration above has a control that makes them disagree on purpose.

sections.h: How do I respect reduced motion?
sections.x: env.reducedMotion Core Level 2 Platform Respect a stated preference for less movement. Ground The browser inside the sandbox provides it. No host round trip. Recipes Dashboard , Media Viewer , Settings and Preferences Demo lab-a11y prefers-reduced-motion: reduce works inside the sandbox and reflects the operating system setting directly. Nothing is proxied and no host involvement is needed, which also means the host cannot override it for you: if the user asked their machine for less motion, that preference reaches your frame whatever the host thinks. Application behaviour. The blunt instrument is a stylesheet rule that collapses every animation and transition, and it is the right default: Extracted from from apps/lib/view.css @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { *, *::before, *::after { animation-duration: .001ms !important; transition-duration: .001ms !important; } } The finer instrument is to check the query in JavaScript where motion is functional. A dashboard that repaints a sparkline every 1.4 seconds is not decorating; it is moving, continuously, in somebody’s peripheral vision. Recipe 2 slows its polling to four seconds under a reduced motion preference, which is a different response from removing an animation and a more honest one. What to keep. Reduced motion does not mean no feedback. Replace slides with crossfades, replace crossfades with instant changes, and keep the state change legible. A toast that appears instantly is fine; a toast that never appears is a regression.

env.contrast Core Level 2 Platform Survive forced colours and high contrast. Ground The browser inside the sandbox provides it. No host round trip. Recipes Image Annotator , Settings and Preferences Demo lab-a11y prefers-contrast: more and forced-colors mode both work inside the frame without the host’s involvement, and forced colours is the one that breaks views. It replaces the entire palette, including the host’s variables, so any state you signalled with a background colour stops being visible at the exact moment the user most needs contrast. The embedded-specific trap. In forced colours, the operating system replaces the palette. Anything you drew with a background image, a gradient, or a box-shadow to indicate state loses that indication entirely, because those properties are not overridden and the colours around them are. State has to be carried by something that survives: a border, an outline, text, or an icon. The same applies to your own custom properties. A view that indicates selection only by background: var(--color-background-info) shows no selection at all under forced colours. Recipe 1 sets both a background and an aria-selected attribute, and the attribute is what makes it survive.

env.textScale Core Level 2 Platform Stay usable when text is two sizes larger than you designed for. Ground The browser inside the sandbox provides it. No host round trip. Recipes Settings and Preferences Demo lab-a11y Size in relative units so the root scale carries through, never fix a pixel height on anything containing text, and let the frame grow through surface.resize . The third one is the embedded-specific part: a page reflows into the space it already has, while your view has to ask for more, and a view that reports a stale height at 200% zoom clips its own content. The difference from a page is the width you have to work with. In a page, enlarged text reflows into a column that is usually still comfortable. In a 380 pixel frame at 200% zoom you have the effective width of a phone held sideways, and a two-column layout gets about three words per line before it becomes unreadable. WCAG 2.2 asks for usability at 200% zoom and reflow at 320 CSS pixels of width. Both are testable with the browser’s own zoom, and a four hundred pixel card at 200% is roughly a phone, so testing one gets you most of the other.

sections.h: How do I announce a change nobody caused?
sections.x: a11y.announce Core Level 2 Yours to build Tell assistive technology that something changed. Ground The view implements it. Nobody else can. Recipes Data Explorer , Spreadsheet , Approval Center , Settings and Preferences Demo lab-a11y One polite live region, created once and reused, updated by setting its text. Creating a region per announcement does not work, because a screen reader announces changes to a region it already knows about, and a freshly inserted element is often missed entirely. Everything in an agentic application is a change nobody caused. A tool result arrives. The agent highlights a row. A log gains forty lines. A sighted user notices; nobody else does unless you say so. Use polite , not assertive . Assertive interrupts whatever is being read, and in an application where results arrive continuously that is unusable. Extracted from from apps/lib/view.js function announce(text) { let region = $("#live-region"); if (!region) { region = h("div", { id: "live-region", class: "sr-only", role: "status", "aria-live": "polite" }); document.body.append(region); } region.textContent = ""; setTimeout(() => { region.textContent = text; }, 30); } The clear-then-set with a small delay is not superstition. Screen readers announce changes to a live region, and setting the same string twice is not a change, so the second identical event is silent without it. Announce the outcome, not the event. “Six of forty selected” rather than one announcement per row. Where events arrive faster than a person can listen, the announcement belongs on a timer: Recipe 9’s log is aria-live="off" with a five second summary, because a politely live log at five lines a second reads out continuously and tells the user nothing. “Import failed. Row 812 has a malformed date.” rather than “error”. The demonstration announces at phase boundaries only, which is what a sighted user actually perceives from a progress bar. What not to announce. Hover. Scroll position. Anything the user did deliberately and can already feel. A live region that narrates the mouse is worse than no live region.

sections.h: Two things this environment makes harder
sections.x: Announcing agent activity. In an ordinary application, changes the user did not cause are rare enough to be exceptional. Here they are the normal case: a tool result arrives, the agent highlights a row, a proposal appears. Each one needs an announcement, and together they need a budget, or the live region becomes a narration nobody can follow. The rule that works is to announce outcomes that change what the user can do and to stay silent about everything else. An agent proposing a rewrite is worth announcing, because there is now a decision to make. An agent highlighting a row is worth announcing once, briefly. A tool result that only refreshes numbers already on screen is not. Naming things the user did not name. A screen reader reads names, and in an agentic interface many elements exist because a model produced them. A row labelled only by its data reads as a string of values; the same row with an aria-label that names what it is reads as a thing. Recipe 2’s tiles carry “Checkout p95, 412 milliseconds” rather than a heading and a number in separate nodes, and that single change is the difference between a dashboard that can be listened to and one that cannot.

sections.h: The checklist that fits on a card
sections.x: Every recipe in Part V is built against this list, and Appendix C turns it into assertions. Every interactive element is reachable by Tab and operable by Enter or Space. Every composite widget is one tab stop with arrow key navigation inside it. Every control has a name, and the name is what a person would call it. State changes that were not caused by focus are announced. Focus is visible, and the ring is not clipped by an overflow: hidden ancestor. Nothing depends on colour alone. Nothing depends on hover alone. Every spatial gesture has a button or a key equivalent. Text stays usable at 200%. Motion respects the preference. Ten lines, and running axe-core against your view will confirm perhaps half of them. The other half need a keyboard and five minutes, which is a cheaper test than most of the automated ones in Part VI and catches more.

Tab order covers the view and leaves it, with no element skipped and none reachable only by pointer. A list of N rows presents one tab stop for all N. prefers-reduced-motion suppresses animation and slows anything that repaints continuously. Under forced colours, selection and status remain distinguishable without relying on background colour. Text at 200% remains usable, and the view reports its new height. A change the user did not cause is announced once into a polite live region. No announcement is produced by hover or scroll. Previous 13. Host Environment and Theming Next 15. Lifecycle and Connectivity
