Chapter 15 Your view will be destroyed without warning, hidden without notice, and disconnected without an event. One request in the whole protocol gives you time to react. Assume you will be destroyed at any moment, with one request of warning, and assume the warning may not arrive. Every design decision in this chapter falls out of that: autosave rather than save, server state rather than view state, and cheap by default rather than suspending on a signal you may never receive. A page gets beforeunload . You get ui/resource-teardown , if the host is well behaved, and the interval before you answer it is the only time you are guaranteed to still exist. The live application needs JavaScript. Its source is in the repository under apps/ .

sections.h: Can I tell when nobody is looking?
sections.x: Every view in this book starts the same way, and the lifecycle wiring is four lines of it: Extracted from from apps/lib/view.js async function boot(appInfo, appCapabilities, onReady) { const bridge = new global.McpApp.AppBridge(appInfo, appCapabilities); const result = await bridge.connect(); global.McpApp.applyHostStyles(bridge.hostContext); applySafeArea(bridge.hostContext.safeAreaInsets); bridge.autoResize(document.body); bridge.on("hostcontextchanged", (patch) => { global.McpApp.applyHostStyles(bridge.hostContext); if (patch.safeAreaInsets) applySafeArea(patch.safeAreaInsets); }); await onReady(bridge, result); return bridge; } onReady runs after connect() resolves, which is after the handshake, which is the earliest moment anything is allowed to happen. The hostcontextchanged listener is registered before the application’s own code runs, so a theme change arriving during the first render is still handled. Applying host styles in both places, once at boot and once per change, is what keeps the two paths from diverging. lifecycle.visibility Core Level 3 Platform Know when the view is on screen and when it is not. Ground The browser inside the sandbox provides it. No host round trip. Recipes Dashboard , Monitoring Console , Media Viewer Demo lab-lifecycle Partly, and the part it misses is the one that happens. The Page Visibility API fires inside your frame when the host’s whole tab or window is hidden, which is real and worth handling, and covers none of the cases where the tab stays visible. It does not cover the case that actually happens: the tab is visible and your frame has scrolled out of the conversation. document.hidden stays false, and your sparkline repaints every 1.4 seconds for nobody. Press “Hide the frame” in the demonstration and watch all three panes. The frame disappears from the page, the transcript records nothing at all, and the poll counter inside the view keeps climbing. Nothing told the view it had stopped being visible, because from its own point of view nothing changed. Workaround. IntersectionObserver against the view’s own viewport does not help either, because the clipping is happening in a document you cannot see. What does help is being cheap by default: poll on demand rather than on a timer, coalesce updates, and let the server push through ui/notifications/tool-result instead of asking repeatedly. What a mechanism would look like. The host already sends ui/notifications/host-context-changed for display mode. A visibility field in the same notification would cost nothing and would let a view suspend honestly. This is the third variation of the same missing signal, after surface.reveal and notify.attention , and they may all be one feature.

sections.h: How do I stop doing work nobody sees?
sections.x: lifecycle.suspend Core Level 3 Yours to build Stop doing work nobody is looking at. Ground The view implements it. Nobody else can. Recipes Monitoring Console , Media Viewer Demo lab-lifecycle Yours to build, and worth building even though the signal you would trigger it from is unreliable. The discipline that survives a missing signal is to be cheap by default: poll on demand rather than on a timer, coalesce updates, and let the server push through ui/notifications/tool-result rather than asking repeatedly. Application behaviour. Keep a list of the things that consume resources while nobody is looking: timers, animations, observers, in-flight polling. Have one function that stops them and one that restarts them, and call the stop from visibilitychange and from ui/resource-teardown . Recipe 12’s player pauses on hide, which is both a resource decision and a courtesy: audio continuing from an invisible frame is genuinely alarming. The general principle is that a view should be able to do nothing. A view that requires a heartbeat to stay correct will be wrong every time it is backgrounded, and it will be wrong silently.

lifecycle.connectivity Core Level 3 Platform Show online, offline, and reconnecting honestly. Ground The browser inside the sandbox provides it. No host round trip. Recipes Monitoring Console Demo lab-lifecycle navigator.onLine and the online and offline events work inside the frame. They tell you whether the browser thinks it has a network, which is weaker than it sounds and still worth using. What they cannot tell you is whether the host still has its connection to the server. That connection is the host’s, and there is no message reporting its state. Your evidence is indirect: a tools/call that fails, or one that never answers. Application behaviour. Three states, honestly labelled. Live means something arrived recently. Reconnecting means a call failed and a retry is scheduled. Offline means the browser says so or retries have run out. The crucial part is what the data looks like in the last two states. Recipe 9 keeps the last lines it received and says so in a banner, because a monitoring console that clears its screen when the connection drops has destroyed the evidence at the exact moment somebody needs it. Stale data with a timestamp is more useful than no data, as long as the interface never lets the user mistake one for the other.

sections.h: How do I track unsaved work?
sections.x: lifecycle.dirty Core Level 2 Yours to build Track uncommitted local state and say so. Ground The view implements it. Nobody else can. Recipes Document Editor , Settings and Preferences Demo lab-lifecycle Yours to track, and it costs a boolean and a chip. What you can do with it inside the view is the obvious part: enable Save, enable Discard, show a marker. What you cannot do is tell the host, which is why the teardown handshake below matters more here than anywhere else. Inside the view, a dirty flag drives the obvious things: enabling Save, disabling Discard, showing a marker. The chip in the demonstration goes from “saved” to “unsaved changes” on the first keystroke and back on save. Across the boundary, there is nothing. No message tells the host that this view has unsaved work, so the host cannot warn the user before switching conversations, and cannot include the view in its own “you have unsaved changes” logic if it has any. Workaround. Autosave, so that dirty is a state that lasts seconds rather than minutes. Then the teardown handshake below is enough to close the gap. The lifecycle, as a sequence

sections.h: What do I do when the host closes me?
sections.x: lifecycle.beforeClose Core Level 2 On the wire Get one chance to finish before the frame goes away. Messages ui/resource-teardown reason Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes Document Editor Demo lab-lifecycle The one guarantee in the whole lifecycle, and the reason the missing dirty signal is survivable. The host cannot know you have unsaved work, but it does have to ask before it takes the frame away, and that question is your opportunity. Chapter 7 introduced this message from the view’s side of the pair. Here is what it is worth: the interval between the host asking and your code answering is the only interval in the whole protocol during which a view is guaranteed to still exist and to have the host’s attention. Everything you were going to lose has to be flushed inside it. Extracted from from apps/recipes/r04-document-editor/index.html bridge.on("teardown", async ({ reason }) => { $("#log").textContent = `Host is closing this view: ${reason}`; if (dirty) { $("#log").textContent += " Flushing unsaved changes first."; await save(); } }); Rules for the window. Do the smallest possible thing. This is a flush, not a save dialog: you cannot ask the user a question, because the host is waiting and the user is already leaving. Bound it. A host that waits forever for a view that never answers is a host that will stop waiting, and different hosts will stop at different times. And answer even on failure, because an unanswered request is indistinguishable from a hung view. Failure modes. A host that does not send the request at all takes your work with it, which is why autosave matters more here than in a page. A host that sends it and does not wait looks identical from the inside, and the only way to know is to measure. The demonstration’s teardown control reports how long the view took to answer, which is the same measurement a conformance test makes.

sections.h: How do I ask to be closed?
sections.x: The other direction is ui/notifications/request-teardown , covered as surface.close in Chapter 7. It is worth restating the asymmetry here, because the pair is the whole lifecycle contract: the view asks with a notification that may be ignored, and the host tells with a request that must be answered. Neither side can force the other, and the protocol is deliberately arranged so that the party who owns the window has the last word.

sections.h: Worked example: one second in the document editor
sections.x: Recipe 4’s document editor is the clearest illustration of this whole chapter, because every decision in it is a response to not being able to rely on a signal. It cannot know when it is invisible, it cannot tell the host it has unsaved work, and it may be destroyed at any moment. What it does instead is keep the window of loss short and bounded by a constant it chose itself. The user types. A timer starts. After 900 milliseconds of quiet the view commits an undo transaction and calls save_document , which is an app-only tool, so the model neither sees the save nor can trigger one. The chip goes from amber to green. Now the host tears the view down. ui/resource-teardown arrives with a reason. If the chip is green, the view answers immediately and the frame goes away with nothing lost. If it is amber, the view saves first and then answers, and the demonstration reports how many milliseconds that took, because that number is the thing a host either waits for or does not. Worst case you lose 900ms of typing, and that bound is a constant the view chose, and nothing the protocol promises. Pick a bound, keep it small, and assume the teardown warning may not arrive.

Send ui/resource-teardown before removing a frame, for any reason, including reasons the user initiated. Give the reason, because a view can behave differently for “the user closed the conversation” and “this view is being replaced by a newer result”. Wait for the response, with a deadline that is generous. A view flushing to a server needs a network round trip, and a host that waits 200 milliseconds has effectively not waited. Answer ping . It is the only way a view can check that the channel is still there, and a host that ignores it leaves the view unable to distinguish a slow call from a dead one. Do not send anything before ui/notifications/initialized arrives. A host that sends ui/notifications/tool-input early is talking to a view that has not registered its handlers yet, so the notification is dropped on the floor and no error is raised on either side. The view then renders empty and waits forever for data that has already been sent.

ui/resource-teardown is sent before the frame is removed, with a reason. The host waits for the response, and a view that takes 600 milliseconds is not cut off. Nothing is sent to the view before ui/notifications/initialized . ping is answered. Hiding the host’s tab fires visibilitychange inside the frame. A view that is scrolled out of view receives no signal, which is the gap in Appendix B.

Assume you will be destroyed at any moment with one request of warning, and that the warning may not come. Every design decision in this group follows from that: autosave rather than save, server state rather than view state, cheap by default rather than suspend on a signal you may not receive. Chapter 16 The sandbox took away your storage and the extension has not replaced it. Undo, on the other hand, was always yours, and in an agentic application it matters more than it ever did in a page. You have no storage worth the name, so persist through a server tool instead. That is not a stylistic preference: the sandbox gives your document an opaque origin, and an opaque origin has no durable storage partition to write to. Undo is a different story: nobody can build it for you, and in an application where a model can also edit the document it is the mechanism that makes that acceptable. A user who knows one keystroke reverses anything the agent did will let the agent try things. A user who does not will read every proposal twice and eventually stop asking, which is the same outcome as the feature not existing. The live application needs JavaScript. Its source is in the repository under apps/ .

state.save Core Level 3 Not standardised Persist view state keyed to the view's identity. Ground No standard mechanism exists yet. The entry carries a workaround. Recipes Document Editor , Spreadsheet , Settings and Preferences Demo lab-state state.restore Core Level 3 Not standardised Come back up where the user left off. Ground No standard mechanism exists yet. The entry carries a workaround. Recipes Document Editor Demo lab-state On the server, through a tool call, keyed by something the server already knows: a conversation identifier, a document id, or the tool arguments that rendered the view. There is no other durable place, and pretending otherwise produces a view that appears to remember during development and forgets in production. localStorage.setItem throws SecurityError inside the frame, or hands you a partition that is discarded along with the frame, and which of the two you get depends on the browser. Neither is usable. The demonstration probes it at startup and prints the result, which is a more reliable way to find this out than reading a specification, because the behaviour varies. There is no message either. No ui/set-state , no ui/get-state , nothing in hostContext that round-trips. The OpenAI Apps SDK has setWidgetState , which is exactly this feature, and the extension’s own “Future Considerations” lists state persistence as deferred. The workaround is a server tool. Persist through tools/call , keyed by something stable that the server knows: a conversation identifier, a document id, the tool’s own arguments. Recipe 4 does this, with a save_document tool marked visibility: ["app"] so the model neither sees it nor can call it. Extracted from from apps/recipes/r04-document-editor/server.js save_document: { description: "Persist the draft. Called by the view, not by the model.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { html: { type: "string" } }, required: ["html"] }, visibility: ["app"], run: ({ html }) => { document = html; saves += 1; return { content: [{ type: "text", text: `Saved revision ${saves} at the server.` }] }; }, }, What it costs. A round trip per save, so Recipe 4 debounces at 900ms rather than saving per keystroke. Scroll position and which panel is open end up on a server, which is absurd and is what the gap forces. And with hostCapabilities.serverTools absent you get no persistence at all. What a mechanism would look like. ui/set-view-state from the view, and a viewState field in the initialize result coming back, scoped to the view identity the host already tracks and capped at a size the host enforces. It is cheap to specify, obviously useful, and already proven by prior art on both sides of this ecosystem. Design around it in the meantime. Ask what genuinely has to survive a teardown. A document does. A sort order does not, and reconstructing it from the tool arguments costs nothing. The recipes here persist documents and preferences and deliberately forget everything else, which started as a compromise forced by the gap and turned out to be a better design than the one that saved everything.

history.transaction Core Level 3 Yours to build Group mutations into one undoable unit. Ground The view implements it. Nobody else can. Recipes File Explorer , Document Editor , Spreadsheet , Workflow Builder Demo lab-state A stack of transactions, where each transaction knows how to apply itself and how to reverse itself. The distinction sounds academic until an agent is editing the same document: a snapshot undo restores the whole document to an earlier moment and silently discards anything the agent contributed in between, while a transaction reverses exactly its own change and leaves the rest standing. Extracted from from apps/labs/lab-state/index.html const past = []; const future = []; function apply({ label, forward, back }) { forward(); past.push({ label, forward, back }); future.length = 0; draw(); announce(label); } Three properties of that shape carry the weight, and each shows up as a specific bug when it is missing and not as a general degradation. Undo is usually discussed as a quality, something an application has more or less of. It is three invariants, and each one you drop produces a reproducible complaint you can write a test for. future.length = 0 on every new action. Keeps the history a line, which is what users expect. A label per transaction. Lets you announce “Undid delete Contracts” and never a bare “Undid”. When an agent also writes, the label is how the user knows whose change they are reversing. Closures, not snapshots. A snapshot undo restores the whole document and silently reverts anything the agent did in between. back() reverses exactly its own change. Grouping. One transaction per meaningful unit, not per event. Typing gets grouped by pause: Recipe 4 commits a transaction after 900 milliseconds of inactivity. Dragging gets one transaction on drop, not one per pointermove. The test is whether a user pressing Undo once gets back to a state they recognise. One undo stack, two authors

sections.h: What belongs in the undo stack?
sections.x: history.undo Core Level 3 Yours to build Revert the last transaction, including the agent's. Ground The view implements it. Nobody else can. Recipes File Explorer , Document Editor , Spreadsheet , Image Annotator , Workflow Builder Demo lab-state history.redo Core Level 3 Yours to build Reapply what was reverted. Ground The view implements it. Nobody else can. Recipes Document Editor Demo lab-state The operations themselves are four lines each once the transaction model exists, so the design effort goes entirely into deciding what belongs in the stack and what does not. Selection does not. Scroll position does not. A filter probably does, because a user who filters, edits and presses Ctrl+Z expects the edit back and not the filter. Those judgements are the work, and they are the part no library makes for you. Include the agent’s changes. This is the argument of Chapter 21 arriving early. When an agent rewrites a paragraph, that rewrite goes on the same undo stack as the user’s own edits, so a single Cmd+Z takes it back. An agent whose changes cannot be undone is an agent people will not let near their document, and correctly so. Recipe 4 pushes exactly one transaction when the user accepts a proposed rewrite, so a single Cmd/Ctrl+Z restores the human’s words in one step, without unwinding through the agent’s paragraph. It is nine lines of code, it is the entire safety argument for letting a model edit a document, and check_render.mjs asserts it: accept the proposal, press undo, expect the original text. Do not include selection, scroll, or view state. Undo that restores a scroll position feels broken, because the user’s model of undo is about content. Some editors undo selection changes as part of restoring context, which is a defensible variant, but undoing a pure selection change as its own step is not. Bind the shortcuts. Cmd/Ctrl+Z and Shift+Cmd/Ctrl+Z, with the caveats from Chapter 10 about the host possibly owning them. Provide visible buttons too, because a shortcut the user cannot see is a shortcut most users do not have. Accessibility. Announce the label, both ways. A screen reader user pressing Undo needs to hear what was undone; a silent stack change is indistinguishable from a key that did nothing.

Undo depth is state that cannot survive a teardown, because forward and back are closures and closures do not serialise. A view that persists its document and not its history returns with a document it cannot un-edit. That is usually the right trade. Serialising a transaction stack means representing every operation as data, which is a substantially larger design, and the value of undoing something from before a reload is low. But it should be a decision you made. Recipe 4 persists the document, drops the history, and says so.

Because every save costs a round trip, the useful discipline is to sort your state into three buckets before writing any persistence code at all. Two of the three buckets turn out to need nothing. Reconstructible. Anything derivable from the tool arguments or the tool result. A sort order, a filter, which tab is open, the current page. All of it comes back for free on the next render, and persisting it is work that buys nothing. Worth a round trip. Documents, drafts, annotations, preferences. Things a person made. These go to a server tool, and the cost is real, so debounce them and save on pause rather than on change. Deliberately forgotten. Undo history, scroll position, transient selections. Losing them is mildly annoying and keeping them is disproportionate work, particularly for undo, where serialising a stack of closures means redesigning the whole transaction model as data. Recipes 4 and 13 persist exactly the second bucket and say so in their entries. The value of writing the buckets down is that it turns “we should save state” into three short lists, one of which is empty work.

The shape is small enough to state completely in a paragraph, and every recipe in this book that has undo uses exactly it without modification. There is no library involved and no reason to reach for one: the whole model is two arrays and three functions. A transaction is an object with a label, a forward closure and a back closure. apply() runs forward, pushes it onto the past, and clears the future. undo() pops the past, runs back, and pushes onto the future. redo() does the reverse. Four methods, about twenty lines, and no library. Three refinements the recipes add on top of that shape, each of which was added because its absence produced a specific bug in a demonstration on this site, and each of which is cheap enough that there is no reason to defer it. None of them changes the transaction model; they change what gets pushed onto the stack and when. Coalescing by pause. Typing produces one transaction per quiet period, because undo that steps back a character at a time is undo nobody uses. Capturing by value, not by reference. A back closure that restores an array must have captured a copy, or it restores a reference to the array that was mutated. This is the bug that makes undo appear to work and then not. Recording the index. Removing an item and putting it back at the end is not an undo. Recipe 3’s move records where the node came from, which is the difference between reversing a change and approximating it.

localStorage inside the frame either throws or is discarded with the frame, and the view does not depend on it. A view’s persisted state survives a teardown and a re-render, through whatever server tool it uses. An app-only save tool is absent from the agent’s tool list. Undo reverses exactly the last transaction and leaves later changes alone. A new action clears the redo stack. An agent-initiated change is undone by one Cmd/Ctrl+Z. Undo and redo announce what they did.

Persistence is a gap with a workable but heavy workaround, so keep the set of things that must survive as small as you can defend. Undo is not a gap, it is a design, and in an agentic application it is the mechanism that makes it safe for a model to touch a document at all. Previous 15. Lifecycle and Connectivity Next 17. Media, Progress, Cancellation and Errors

Chapter 17 Playback the platform gives you, immersion the host gives you, and four capabilities about work that takes long enough for somebody to change their mind. Two groups joined by one theme: the user is waiting, may stop waiting, and is owed an accurate account either way. Media takes time and the platform handles almost all of it for you. A tool call takes time and the protocol handles some of it, leaving the interface to cover the rest. The live application needs JavaScript. Its source is in the repository under apps/ .

sections.h: How do I play audio or video?
sections.x: media.playback Extended Level 3 Platform Play, pause, seek, rate, volume, captions. Ground The browser inside the sandbox provides it. No host round trip. Recipes Media Viewer Demo lab-media <video> and <audio> work inside the sandbox with no host involvement at all. Controls, seeking, playback rate, volume and caption tracks through <track> are platform behaviour, and the accessibility of the native control set is better than anything you will write in an afternoon. Three embedded-specific notes. Media has to come from somewhere. The restrictive default CSP is media-src 'self' data: , so a view loading video from a CDN must declare that origin in resourceDomains , and a host may decline it. Data URIs work and are impractical past a few hundred kilobytes. Autoplay will not work, and should not. Autoplay policies require a user gesture or a muted element, and a view that starts playing sound inside somebody’s conversation without being asked is an actively bad citizen. Start paused, always. Custom transports need the keyboard. If you replace the native controls, you inherit the accessibility contract: Space to play and pause, arrows to seek, a labelled slider with a real aria-valuetext , and a caption toggle with aria-pressed . Recipe 12 does this, and the honest note is that the native controls do it better with less code, so replace them only when you have a reason.

sections.h: How do I go fullscreen for media?
sections.x: media.fullscreen Extended Level 3 On the wire Go immersive through the host, not through the Fullscreen API. Messages ui/request-display-mode fullscreen Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes Media Viewer Demo lab-media Through ui/request-display-mode , not Element.requestFullscreen() . The obvious API is the wrong one here. requestFullscreen needs the fullscreen permission policy, and the extension’s permission set is exactly camera , microphone , geolocation and clipboardWrite . A host has no defined way to grant it. The supported route is ui/request-display-mode with "fullscreen" , which is the same mechanism Chapter 7 describes. The host takes over its own window and tells you the resulting mode. That is better in an embedded context: the host knows what “fullscreen” means in its own chrome, and your view stays a view. Application behaviour. Declare fullscreen in appCapabilities.availableDisplayModes , check the host’s list before asking, and re-layout on the mode you actually get. A player at 200 pixels tall and one at 800 need different control sizes, and the host tells you which you are in through ui/notifications/host-context-changed .

op.progress Core Level 2 Core MCP Determinate and indeterminate progress with a phase name. Messages notifications/progress progressToken Ground Core MCP defines it; the view inherits it. Recipes Dashboard , Agent Control Center Demo lab-media Core MCP defines notifications/progress , carrying a progressToken , a progress number, an optional total and an optional message . The token is what ties a stream of these to the specific request they describe, which matters as soon as two calls are in flight: without it a view has no way to know which task advanced. The catch. The extension’s list of messages a view may receive does not name notifications/progress . In practice hosts that proxy tools/call can forward it, and the demonstration’s fixture host does, but you cannot rely on it. Treat progress as an enhancement, not as the basis of your interface. Application behaviour. Determinate when you have a total , indeterminate when you do not, and a phase name in both cases. “Building the index” is worth more than a percentage, because it tells the user whether the thing that is slow is the thing they expected to be slow. The demonstration shows four named phases moving a bar, and the phase text is what makes the wait legible. Accessibility. role="progressbar" with aria-valuenow , or a live region that announces phase changes only. Not both, and not every tick. Chapter 14 has the reasoning.

op.cancel Core Level 2 Core MCP Interrupt work that is still running. Messages notifications/cancelled requestId Ground Core MCP defines it; the view inherits it. Recipes Agent Control Center Demo lab-media Core MCP again: notifications/cancelled with the requestId of the request you are abandoning and an optional reason. The SDK sends it when you abort the AbortSignal you passed to a request, so cancellation costs you an AbortController and nothing else. What it does not buy is a guarantee: the notification is advisory, the server may already have committed the work, and your interface has to say “stopping” until a result or an error actually arrives. The part people get wrong is the interface, not the message. Cancelling is easy. Returning the view to a state that matches reality is not. If a tool call was cancelled after three of five steps, the correct interface does not show a progress bar at zero and does not show one at sixty percent either. It says the operation stopped after three steps, and it says whether those three steps changed anything. Extracted from from apps/recipes/r11-agent-control/index.html function cancel(task) { task.controller?.abort(); task.state = "cancelled"; task.steps.push("cancelled by the user"); task.error = `Stopped after ${task.done} of ${task.total} steps. ` + "Completed steps were not rolled back."; draw(); bridge.notify("notifications/cancelled", { requestId: task.requestId, reason: "The user cancelled" }); } The other direction. The host can cancel you, through ui/notifications/tool-cancelled with a reason. That happens when the user asks the agent something else, when a classifier intervenes, or when sampling fails. Your view must handle it, and the right handling is almost always to keep the last good state and explain, rather than to blank the view. op.pause Extended Level 3 Yours to build Suspend and continue long work. Ground The view implements it. Nobody else can. Recipes none yet Demo no live demo Extended, yours to build, and rarer than it looks. Most long operations cannot be paused, only cancelled and restarted. Offer pause only when the underlying work genuinely supports resumption, because a pause button that quietly means cancel is worse than no pause button.

sections.h: How do I offer a retry?
sections.x: op.retry Core Level 2 Yours to build Retry without making the user rebuild the interaction. Ground The view implements it. Nobody else can. Recipes Dashboard , Monitoring Console , Agent Control Center Demo lab-media The measure of a retry is whether the user has to rebuild the interaction. A button next to the failure that repeats the same call with the same arguments, against a form still holding what they typed, costs nothing to build and saves everything they did. A failure that clears the form is the same failure with a punishment attached. A retry button next to the failure, which repeats the same call with the same arguments and the same form still filled in, costs nothing and saves the user’s work. A failure that clears the form and returns the user to the start is the same failure plus a punishment. Application behaviour. Keep the arguments. Keep the last good data on screen. Make the retry idempotent, or make it obvious that it is not. For automatic retries, back off exponentially and cap it, and stop after a small number, because hammering a service that has told you it is unwell.

sections.h: How do I report a failure?
sections.x: op.error Core Level 2 Core MCP Draft only Structured errors: what failed, whether to retry, what to do. Messages isError isError Ground Core MCP defines it; the view inherits it. Recipes Data Explorer , Spreadsheet , Workflow Builder , Approval Center , Agent Control Center , Settings and Preferences Demo lab-media A tool result can fail in two different ways, and the difference is worth knowing. A JSON-RPC error means the call did not happen: unknown tool, bad arguments, host refused. A result with isError: true means the tool ran and failed, and its content is a message intended to be read. A structured error carries three facts. What failed, whether retrying could help, and what the recovery action is. The fixture in the demonstration returns this: Extracted from from apps/labs/lab-media/demo.js return { isError: true, content: [{ type: "text", text: "The index volume is full, so nothing was written. " + "Free space and retry." }] }; Three facts in nineteen words: what happened, what the consequence was (nothing was written, so no partial state to worry about), and what to do. Compare it with “Error: operation failed”, which has none of them and is what most tools return. Show it where the action was. An error about an export belongs next to the export button, not in a toast that vanishes and not in a banner at the top of a view the user has scrolled past. Keep the last good state. Recipe 1’s table keeps its rows when a reload fails and says the data is from the previous successful call. An empty table with an error above it has thrown away information the user still needed.

sections.h: The four states of a long operation
sections.x: Every operation in this chapter moves through the same small state machine, and naming it is what stops each application in a product inventing a slightly different one. Users learn a state machine once; they do not learn it four times. Idle. No work in flight. The control that starts it is enabled, and whatever the last run produced is still on screen. Running. Determinate or indeterminate progress, a phase name, and a cancel control that is enabled. The control that started it is disabled or idempotent. Settled. Done, failed, or cancelled. All three are terminal, all three leave something on screen, and the difference between them is what the interface says. Done keeps the new result. Failed keeps the previous one and explains. Cancelled keeps the previous one and says how far the work got. Retrying. A distinct state, because it is not idle: the arguments are still there, the failure is still visible, and the user is deciding. Recipe 11 renders all four states with a chip whose text is simply the state name. It is unglamorous, it survives forced colours because the state is in words, and in practice it is the most legible thing in that interface.

notifications/progress from a server reaches the view, or the view degrades to indeterminate progress. notifications/cancelled from the view carries the id of the request being abandoned. ui/notifications/tool-cancelled from the host leaves the last good state on screen. A tool result with isError: true is rendered as a readable message. A retry re-sends the same arguments without the user re-entering them. ui/request-display-mode with fullscreen is the route a media view takes, and requestFullscreen is not called. Media never autoplays.

Four obligations while somebody waits, and each is a different message. Progress says how far it has got. notifications/cancelled says where it stopped and whether anything was left behind. A result with isError: true says what failed and what to do about it. Retry re-sends the same arguments without making anyone retype them. Do all four and the application feels reliable when the server is not, because every state the user can be in has a sentence attached and a control that still responds. Do none and it feels broken when everything worked: the same slow tool call reads as a hang, the same transient error reads as data loss, and the user’s next move is a reload that throws away state the server had already accepted. Chapter 18 Three ways for a view to reach the conversation, one of which is quiet, one of which starts a turn, and one of which skips the conversation entirely. Three ways to reach outward, and they are roughly an order of magnitude apart in cost from each other. Choosing between them is the main design decision in this part of the protocol, and the cost that matters is not tokens: it is whether the user sees it happen and whether it can be taken back. Publish state quietly. Ask for a turn in the conversation. Or call a model directly and keep the answer. Picking the wrong one is the most common design error in this part of the protocol. The live application needs JavaScript. Its source is in the repository under apps/ .

Context update is push, and it is quiet. The view says what is currently true. Nobody is asked to do anything, no turn starts, and the fact is available when the next thing the user says needs it. Message is a turn. The view puts content into the conversation and expects the agent to respond. This is heavy and should be traceable to a deliberate user action. Sampling skips the conversation. The view asks the host’s model for a completion and gets a result back privately. No turn, no visible exchange, and the answer belongs to the view. Reaching for the wrong one is the most common design error in this part of the protocol. A view that sends a message every time a selection changes has turned a mouse into a conversation partner. A view that only ever publishes context and never offers a way to ask about it has built something the user cannot get an answer out of.

sections.h: How do I tell the model what is on screen?
sections.x: agent.contextUpdate Core Level 4 On the wire Draft only Publish the part of view state the model should reason over. Messages ui/update-model-context updateModelContext Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes Data Explorer , Dashboard , Code and Diff Reviewer , Approval Center Demo lab-agent Send ui/update-model-context , carrying content , structuredContent , or both. It replaces whatever you published before rather than adding to it, which is the single most important thing to know about this message: the model sees one payload from your view, not a history of them. Replacement is the important word. The specification is explicit: each request overwrites the previous context from this view, hosts may deduplicate identical updates, and if several arrive before the next user message the host should send only the last. The design assumes a view that publishes a current state , not a stream of events. Extracted from from apps/labs/lab-agent/index.html function update() { if (!bridge?.hostCapabilities.updateModelContext) return; if (!selected.size) return; const payload = { content: [{ type: "text", text: `The user has ${selected.size} ticket(s) selected:\n${selectionText()}` }], structuredContent: { selected: [...selected].map((i) => ({ id: ROWS[i][0], owner: ROWS[i][1], ageDays: ROWS[i][2], state: ROWS[i][3] })), }, }; bridge.updateModelContext(payload); } Publish state, not events. “Three tickets are selected, here they are” is state. “The user clicked row 4” is an event, and by the time the model reads it the user has clicked six other things. Publish the minimum that changes an answer. The demonstration has a control that starts publishing hover position, which is the reductio: it works, the host accepts it, and it makes every answer worse by burying the selection under noise. Failure modes. Unsupported when updateModelContext is absent, which is a real Level 1 host, so the interface must still be usable: the escalation button carries the selection in its text instead. Denied comes back as a JSON-RPC error and should not be fatal; the view keeps working, the model knows less.

sections.h: How do I put something in the conversation?
sections.x: agent.escalate Core Level 4 On the wire Put the current selection into the conversation as a request. Messages ui/message message Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes Data Explorer , Code and Diff Reviewer Demo lab-agent ui/message puts content into the conversation with a role. This is how the user says “talk about this”, and the important design property is that it is a user action with a visible consequence. Application behaviour. Carry the selection and the question, and stop. Recipe 8’s “Explain this change” sends the selected diff lines. Recipe 1’s “Ask about these” sends the selected deployments as CSV. Neither summarises the whole view, because the whole view is not what the user pointed at. Say what will happen. A button labelled “Ask about these” is honest about starting a turn. A view that quietly sends a message when a row is clicked has taken an action on the user’s behalf in a conversation they are reading. Host behaviour. The host should add the message with the role given, and may ask for consent. That last clause is worth designing for: your promise may sit in front of a confirmation dialog for a second or two. Failure modes. Unsupported when hostCapabilities.message is absent, and this one hurts, because escalation is the main route from a view back into the conversation. The fallback is to make the selection copyable, so the user can paste it themselves. It is worse, and it is not nothing.

sections.h: Can I send a verb and a target?
sections.x: agent.intent Core Level 4 Not standardised Name a semantic action rather than describing it in prose. Ground No standard mechanism exists yet. The entry carries a workaround. Recipes Workflow Builder Demo lab-agent No. You can send a sentence through ui/message , and the agent parses a verb and a target back out of it with whatever accuracy that model has on that phrasing. The loss is real and it varies between models, which also means it varies between hosts and between days. When a user clicks “Explain this node” your view knows two things exactly: {"intent": "explain", "target": "node-17"} . What you can put on the wire is prose. That round trip through prose is lossy, and it is lossy in a way that varies between models. It also makes the interaction untestable: an assertion about “the agent understood the user wanted to explain node 17” is an assertion about a sampled token. The workaround that almost works. Register a tool. A view that exposes explain_node(id) gives the agent a precise entry point, and Chapter 19 is about exactly that. What tools cannot express is the direction : tools are the agent calling the view, and intent is the view telling the agent what the user just meant. In practice, views send a message with a structured payload alongside the prose and hope the model reads it. What a mechanism would look like. ui/intent with a verb, a target and arguments, delivered to the agent as a structured turn. Appendix B has it.

sections.h: Can I call a model directly?
sections.x: agent.sampling Extended Level 4 On the wire Draft only Ask the host's model for a completion from inside the view. Messages sampling/createMessage sampling Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes Document Editor Demo lab-agent Yes, with sampling/createMessage , when hostCapabilities.sampling is present. You send messages and get a completion back, and the conversation never sees it. That privacy is the whole distinction from escalation: the user does not watch the question being asked and does not get the chance to correct it before the answer lands in your interface. This is genuinely different from the other two. Escalation asks the user’s agent, in front of the user, and the answer appears in the chat. Sampling asks a model, privately, and the answer comes back to your code. When it is right. Work that belongs to the view. Drafting a suggestion into a text field. Classifying a free-text field. Summarising a selection for a label. Recipe 4 uses it to draft a rewrite, which is then shown as a proposal, for the user to accept. When it is wrong. Anything the user should see being asked. If the answer is going to be the substance of what the user does next, it belongs in the conversation where they can push back on it. Host behaviour. The host chooses the model, and should rate limit, apply cost controls, and involve a human. Your call may be slow, may be refused, and may return something from a smaller model than the conversation uses. Failure modes. Check hostCapabilities.sampling before offering the feature, and hostCapabilities.sampling.tools before including tools in the request. Press “Withdraw sampling” in the demonstration: the button stays, and explains that the view cannot reach a model on its own and that escalation is the alternative. That is the honest degradation, because the underlying user need has not gone away.

sections.h: What a good context payload looks like
sections.x: Both channels, filled from the same data: Extracted from from apps/recipes/r01-data-explorer/index.html bridge.updateModelContext({ content: [{ type: "text", text: `The user selected ${picked.length} deployment(s): ` + picked.map((r) => `${r.service}@${r.version} in ${r.env}`).join(", ") }], structuredContent: { selected: picked }, }); The content string is what the model reads and reasons over, so it is a sentence and not a dump. The structuredContent object is what a tool call can be built from afterwards, so it is the rows themselves with nothing elided. Sending only the first makes the model guess at identifiers; sending only the second makes it read JSON where a sentence would do. Three properties, and the demonstration has a control that breaks each one so you can watch what the model actually receives when it goes wrong. Getting them right costs nothing at write time and is very hard to diagnose afterwards, because a badly shaped payload produces worse answers, and never an error you can see. It is a state, not an event. Present tense, complete, and true right now. “Three tickets are selected, here they are” survives being read two turns later; “the user clicked row 4” does not. It has both halves. content for the model to read as language, and structuredContent for anything the model may need to quote back exactly. Identifiers, numbers and dates belong in the structured half, because a model copying an identifier out of prose is a model that occasionally copies it wrong. It is small. Not because there is a limit, but because it is displacing conversation. Publishing four selected rows is proportionate. Publishing the whole table on the grounds that the model might want it is spending somebody else’s context window on a table the view has already rendered.

Unsupported. Check hostCapabilities for message , updateModelContext and sampling separately; a host may have any combination. The demonstration withdraws each one so you can watch the view rearrange itself. Denied. All three can return a JSON-RPC error, and none of them should be fatal. A view whose escalation was refused still has a selection the user can copy. Deferred. Specific to context updates, and easy to mistake for a failure. The host may hold your update until the next user message, so a model that “does not know” about a selection published half a second ago may simply not have been asked anything yet. Slow. Specific to sampling. The host chooses the model, applies rate limits, and may involve a human, so a sampling call is not a function call with a predictable latency. Show that something is happening and offer a way out.

A selection change sends exactly one ui/update-model-context . A second change replaces the first. Nothing is published for hover, scroll or sort. ui/message is sent only in response to a deliberate user action. With message absent, the escalation control is not rendered. With sampling absent, no sampling/createMessage is sent. sampling/createMessage includes tools only when hostCapabilities.sampling.tools is present.

Three routes, and the cost rises steeply along them. A context update is a line of JSON that might improve the next answer. A message is a turn with a model behind it. Sampling is a model call your view pays for and the user never sees. Most applications need the first constantly, the second on a button, and the third rarely. An application that has reached for the third for something the first would have handled is an application that has misunderstood what the conversation is for. Previous 17. Chapter 19 The host cannot see inside your frame, so an agent that wants to act on your interface has to be given a vocabulary. Registering tools is that vocabulary, and it turns out to be the same mechanism accessibility and testing need. Register tools, and let the host call them through tools/list and tools/call in the host-to-app direction. That is the entire mechanism, and it exists because the alternative was rejected on security grounds: the host cannot read your DOM, and giving it a way to would hand every host a route into content that came from a server it does not trust. The host cannot read your DOM, and should not be able to. So an agent that wants to highlight a row or propose a value has no way to reach in. Instead the view reaches out: it registers tools, and the host calls them. The live application needs JavaScript. Its source is in the repository under apps/ .

sections.h: How does the agent act on my view?
sections.x: app.tools Core Level 4 On the wire Draft only Expose the view's operations as tools the agent can call. Messages appCapabilities tools/list notifications/tools/list_changed Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes Workflow Builder , Agent Control Center Demo lab-apptools Declare tools in appCapabilities at startup. The host then sends tools/list , you answer with standard MCP tool descriptors, and it sends tools/call to invoke one. Send notifications/tools/list_changed when the set changes. Extracted from from apps/labs/lab-apptools/index.html bridge.registerTool({ name: "highlight_line_item", description: "Draw the user's attention to one line item by index", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { index: { type: "integer", minimum: 0, maximum: 3 } }, required: ["index"] }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: true }, }, async ({ index }) => { tab = "b"; draw(index); return { content: [{ type: "text", text: `Highlighted ${ITEMS[index][0]}.` }], structuredContent: { item: ITEMS[index][0], amount: ITEMS[index][1] } }; }); Three properties of app tools distinguish them from server tools, and all three follow from where the code lives. They are ephemeral. They exist while the frame does. Hosts must not persist the registrations across sessions, and calling a tool from a closed app returns an error. They are untrusted. The code came from a server and runs in a sandbox. Descriptions may not describe side effects honestly, names may collide with server tools, and results should be validated. The specification recommends clear attribution in the host’s UI, per-app or per-server approval, name prefixes, resource limits, and an audit trail. They are the only introspection route. The host has no DOM access, and a view may nest cross-origin frames of its own. If the model is to know anything about the view’s state, the view has to say so, either by pushing with ui/update-model-context or by answering a pull through a tool. Annotate honestly. readOnlyHint: true is the one claim a host will act on, by auto-approving. Marking a mutating tool read-only is the single most consequential lie available in this system.

ui.highlight Core Level 4 Yours to build Let the agent point at a row, a node, or a hunk. Ground The view implements it. Nobody else can. Recipes Document Editor , Workflow Builder , Code and Diff Reviewer Demo lab-apptools “Draw attention to this thing”, where the thing is a row, a node, a line, or a region. It is the lightest agent action and the one that makes a conversation about a view feel connected to it. Application behaviour. Implement it as a tool that takes a stable identifier, not a coordinate or a CSS selector. highlight_line_item(index) survives a re-render; highlight("#row-3 > td:nth-child(2)") does not, and hands the agent a way to poke at your internals. Make the highlight obviously temporary and obviously the agent’s. Recipe 7 puts a glow on the node and says “agent: highlighted Classify” in the corner, so a user who looks away and back knows who moved what. Accessibility. A highlight that is only visual is invisible to a screen reader user, and this is a change they did not cause. Announce it, once, into the live region from Chapter 14.

sections.h: Navigate: open the panel being discussed
sections.x: ui.navigate Core Level 4 Yours to build Let the agent open the panel it is talking about. Ground The view implements it. Nobody else can. Recipes Dashboard , Workflow Builder Demo lab-apptools “Open the panel you are talking about.” The agent changes view state: switches a tab, expands a section, scrolls to a result, selects a row. The rule that keeps this safe is that every agent-initiated navigation must be something the user could have done themselves with the mouse, and must be visible when it happens. An agent that silently changes what the user is looking at while they are reading is worse than one that does nothing. Design the tool around the user’s vocabulary , not your component tree. show_panel("items") is a tool the model can use correctly from a description. set_state({activeTabIndex: 1}) is one it will use wrongly, and one that breaks when you reorder the tabs.

ui.prefill Core Level 4 Yours to build Let the agent propose values, never submit them. Ground The view implements it. Nobody else can. Recipes Document Editor Demo lab-apptools The agent proposes values into inputs and never submits them. That distinction carries the whole entry, because prefilling is genuinely useful and submitting is genuinely dangerous: the agent has read the ticket and can fill six fields the user would have typed, but the signature at the bottom of the form has to be a human’s. That distinction is the whole entry. Prefilling a form is enormously useful: the agent has read the ticket, the invoice, the previous three messages, and can fill in six fields the user would have typed. Submitting the form is taking an action in the user’s name, and the signature on it has to be theirs. Application behaviour. Fill the field, mark it visibly as proposed, focus it so the user’s next keystroke is in the right place, and leave the submit button alone. The demonstration shows “Proposed by the agent. Review before submitting.” next to the field until a human presses the button. Extracted from from apps/labs/lab-apptools/index.html bridge.registerTool({ name: "propose_reason", description: "Propose wording for the adjustment reason, for human review", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { text: { type: "string" } }, required: ["text"] }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: false }, }, async ({ text }) => { $("#reason").value = text; $("#proposed").hidden = false; $("#reason").focus(); return { content: [{ type: "text", text: "Proposed. The user has not submitted it." }] }; }); Note the return value. The tool tells the agent what actually happened, including the part the agent might otherwise assume: the user has not submitted it. An agent that receives “done” will report to the user that it has been done. In a document , the same rule produces a diff or a proposal card rather than a silent replacement. Recipe 4 shows the rewrite as a proposal with Accept and Decline, and accepting is one undo transaction.

sections.h: Let the agent read the view
sections.x: The fourth thing to register is not an action at all. get_state lets the agent ask what is currently on screen, which is the pull half of a pair whose push half is ui/update-model-context . Push keeps the model current on the facts that always matter; pull lets it ask about the ones that only occasionally do, without you spending context on them every turn. Extracted from from apps/labs/lab-apptools/index.html bridge.registerTool({ name: "get_state", description: "Read the view's current state", annotations: { readOnlyHint: true }, inputSchema: { type: "object" }, }, async () => ({ content: [{ type: "text", text: `Panel ${tab}, reason ${ $("#reason").value ? "drafted" : "empty"}.` }], structuredContent: { panel: tab === "a" ? "summary" : "items", reason: $("#reason").value, submitted: false }, })); This is the pull half of the pair whose push half is ui/update-model-context . Push keeps the model current on the things that always matter; pull lets it ask about the things that occasionally do. Most views want both, and the deciding question is whether a fact is worth spending context on every turn.

The same four tools serve three different callers, which is what justifies the effort of writing them at all. An agent uses them to act. An assistive technology or voice interface uses them to reach operations the pointer would otherwise own. And tools/check_render.mjs uses them to drive the view in tests, which is why Recipes 4, 7 and 10 are the ones checked most deeply. Agent action. The subject of this chapter. Accessibility and voice. A user who cannot point still needs to open the panel. An agent driving show_panel on their behalf is doing exactly what the mouse would have done, through an interface designed for it. Testing. A sandboxed frame cannot be driven from outside by a test harness, because the harness cannot reach its DOM either. It can be driven through the same tools. The conformance harness in Part VI drives views this way, and the golden transcripts for this chapter’s demonstration are recordings of a test doing exactly what an agent would do. Three requirements, one mechanism, one set of tools to write. That is unusual enough to be worth designing around: if you are choosing which parts of your view to expose, choose the ones that would make all three easier.

sections.h: How many tools, and what shape?
sections.x: A view with twenty registered tools is a view whose tools the model will choose between badly. Four to six is the range the recipes here settle on, and the way to get there is to design the surface as a vocabulary. Name operations, not implementation. show_panel("items") reads from a description; set_state({activeTabIndex: 1}) does not, and breaks when the tabs are reordered. Take stable identifiers. Names and ids that survive a re-render. Never selectors, never coordinates, never array positions that depend on the current sort. Return what happened, not what was asked. “Held. The user is editing” and “Proposed. The user has not submitted it” are both outcomes an agent needs, and both are outcomes a naive implementation would report as success. This is the single highest-value habit in the chapter: an agent that receives “done” will tell the user it is done. Include one read tool. get_state costs almost nothing and removes the need to publish everything through ui/update-model-context every turn. Annotate honestly. readOnlyHint: true is the claim that earns automatic approval, so it is the claim that must be true.

Unsupported. The view declares tools and the host never sends tools/list . Everything still works by pointer; nothing works by agent. Do not build a view whose only route to a function is a tool. Unknown tool. Return an error naming the tool, so the agent can correct itself. Invalid arguments. Validate before acting. The SDK does this from the schema; the bridge in this repository does not, which is a real difference between a teaching implementation and a production one. Called after teardown. The frame is gone and the host must return an error. Tools are tied to the render, and hosts must not persist registrations.

A view declaring tools receives tools/list and answers with descriptors. tools/call for a registered tool runs it and returns its result. tools/call for an unknown name returns an error. Registering or removing a tool sends notifications/tools/list_changed when the view declared listChanged . App tools disappear when the frame is torn down. A prefill tool changes an input and does not submit it. Every agent-initiated change is visible and reversible.

The agent cannot see your interface, and giving it a set of named, stable, honestly annotated operations is both the safest and the most useful thing you can do about that. Every one of them should be something a user could have done, should be visible when it happens, and should be reversible. Chapter 21 is what happens when it is not. Previous 18. UI to Agent Next 20. Chapter 20 The view can call server tools without the model's involvement, receive arguments before they finish arriving, and take delivery of a result it was rendered for. Your view can call server tools itself, with no model between the click and the call. This is the capability most applications under-use, because it is easy to assume that anything leaving the frame is a conversation, and most of what leaves the frame should not be. tools/call from a view is not asking the agent to do anything. It is a straight line: view, host, server, view. Nothing is sampled and nothing enters the conversation. The live application needs JavaScript. Its source is in the repository under apps/ .

sections.h: How do I refresh my data?
sections.x: tool.invoke Core Level 4 On the wire Call a server tool from a button, through the host. Messages tools/call serverTools visibility Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes Data Explorer , Dashboard , Agent Control Center Demo lab-tools Send tools/call . When hostCapabilities.serverTools is present the host proxies it to the server and returns a standard CallToolResult , the same shape the model would have received. Nothing is sampled, nothing is added to the conversation, and the round trip is a network call. The design decision here is tool visibility. A tool’s _meta.ui.visibility array controls who can call it. ["model", "app"] is the default and means both. ["app"] means the view only: the host must not show it in the agent’s tool list, and cross-server calls are blocked. Extracted from from apps/recipes/r13-settings/server.js save_preferences: { description: "Persist preferences. Called by the view.", inputSchema: { type: "object" }, visibility: ["app"], run: (values) => { Use ["app"] for anything that exists to serve the interface: refresh, save, validate, load a page of results. Two benefits, and both are larger than they sound. The model’s tool list stays short, which measurably improves its choice among the tools that remain. And a save that the model cannot call is a save that the model cannot decide to call. Application behaviour. Check the capability at initialisation; a view whose refresh button cannot work should not have one. Disable the control while a call is in flight, or make it idempotent, because users press buttons twice. Keep the last good data on screen while the new call runs. Failure modes. Unsupported means no serverTools , and the view is reduced to whatever arrived in its initial tool result. That is a real Level 1 host and every recipe here still renders under it. Denied is a JSON-RPC error from the host. Failed is a result with isError: true , which means the tool ran and did not work, and its text is meant to be read by a person.

sections.h: How do I render before the arguments arrive?
sections.x: tool.partialInput Core Level 4 On the wire Render something useful while arguments are still streaming. Messages ui/notifications/tool-input-partial ui/notifications/tool-input Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes Agent Control Center Demo lab-tools The host sends ui/notifications/tool-input-partial zero or more times while the model is still writing the arguments, and then exactly one ui/notifications/tool-input with the complete set. Both halves of that are optional in practice: a host may send no partials at all, and a view may ignore every one it receives, and both remain conformant. The partial arguments are best-effort recovered JSON: the host closes unclosed brackets and braces to produce a valid object. So fields appear, change, and occasionally disappear between notifications. Extracted from from apps/labs/lab-tools/index.html bridge.on("toolinputpartial", ({ arguments: args }) => { $("#title").textContent = args?.region ? `Weather in ${args.region}` : "Weather in"; $("#args").textContent = "Arguments still arriving: " + JSON.stringify(args ?? {}); }); bridge.on("toolinput", ({ arguments: args }) => { $("#title").textContent = `Weather in ${args?.region ?? "nowhere"}`; }); What this is worth. It is the difference between an application that feels instant and a spinner that lasts as long as the model takes to write a JSON object. Press “Stream the tool input” in the demonstration and watch the title fill in as "Nor" becomes "Nordics" . The rules. Never act on partial arguments. Never fire a request, never write anything, never treat a field as final. Render a skeleton and fill it in. Handle fields appearing and changing between notifications without throwing. The whole thing is optional in both directions: a host may send none, and a view may ignore all of them, and both are conformant.

sections.h: How does the result reach me?
sections.x: tool.result Core Level 4 On the wire Take delivery of the result that this view was rendered for. Messages ui/notifications/tool-result ui/notifications/tool-cancelled Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes Data Explorer , Dashboard , Monitoring Console Demo lab-tools ui/notifications/tool-result carries the standard CallToolResult for the call that rendered this view, and ui/notifications/tool-cancelled arrives instead, with a reason, if the call never completed. Exactly one of the two arrives, so a view that renders a spinner until the result lands must handle both or it will spin forever on a cancelled call. The two channels, again. content is what the model reads; structuredContent is what your view reads and never reaches the model. Chapter 2 made the case; here is the concrete version from a working server: Extracted from from apps/recipes/r01-data-explorer/server.js return { content: [{ type: "text", text: summarise(rows) }], structuredContent: { deployments: rows }, }; summarise(rows) produces “8 deployments. Worst p95 is 1290ms on billing.” The eight full records go in structuredContent . The model gets a sentence it can reason with; the view gets the data it can render; nobody pays for eight rows of JSON in the context window. Cancellation is not an error. Keep the last good state, say what happened, and do not blank the view. The demonstration’s cancellation control leaves the table populated and explains that the call was stopped. tool.cancel Core Level 4 Core MCP Cancel a call the user has stopped caring about. Messages notifications/cancelled Ground Core MCP defines it; the view inherits it. Recipes Agent Control Center Demo lab-tools Cancelling a call the user has stopped caring about is core MCP’s notifications/cancelled , carrying the id of the request being abandoned. The view sends it, the host relays it, and the server stops if it can. Chapter 17 covers what the interface has to do afterwards, which is the harder half: a cancelled call leaves the view holding an optimistic state that never became true, and rolling it back honestly means saying how far the work actually got. Input streams to the view. Output does not.

sections.h: Can the server stream results to me?
sections.x: tool.partialOutput Core Level 4 Not standardised Update stable elements as results arrive, not after. Ground No standard mechanism exists yet. The entry carries a workaround. Recipes Monitoring Console , Agent Control Center Demo lab-tools No, and this is the most consequential gap in Part III, because it is the one that changes what you can build and not merely how you build it. A tool result arrives exactly once, when the tool finishes. There is no ui/notifications/tool-result-partial anywhere in the specification. Input streams to you through ui/notifications/tool-input-partial , and output does not stream back, which is an asymmetry that is hard to justify from the view’s side: the model’s arguments arrive progressively and the server’s answer does not. For anything that produces results progressively, a log tail, a long generation, a scan over many objects, the view has three options and none of them is good. Poll. Call an app-visible tool on a timer. Simple, works everywhere, wastes a call whenever nothing changed, and the interval is a guess. Push through repeated results. A host that re-sends ui/notifications/tool-result as new data arrives gives you a stream, which is what Recipe 9’s demonstration does. Nothing forbids it, and nothing requires it, so it is not something you can build on across hosts. Chunk into many calls. Ask for a page at a time. This turns a stream into pagination, which changes the interface and is sometimes fine. notifications/progress helps a little, because it carries a message string, but it is a progress report and the extension does not list it among the notifications a view receives. What a mechanism would look like. A ui/notifications/tool-result-partial mirroring the input side, with the same “never rely on it, always get a final one” contract. The asymmetry between input and output streaming is hard to justify from the view’s point of view: the model streams its arguments to you and the server cannot stream its results to you. Design around it. Update stable elements in place. Recipe 9 appends rows and never redraws the list, so selection and scroll survive. Whatever your streaming mechanism turns out to be, that discipline is what keeps it usable, and it is the discipline the conformance checks assert.

It is worth putting the whole tool picture in one place, because four different things in this book are all called “a tool call” and they are not the same. Direction Message Needs Used for View to server tools/call hostCapabilities.serverTools Refresh, save, load Model to server tools/call Nothing from the view The call that rendered you Model to view tools/call appCapabilities.tools Agent acting on the interface View to model sampling/createMessage hostCapabilities.sampling Private completions The second row is the one people forget is different. Your view exists because the model called a server tool; the result arrives as a notification, and the view never sent anything. Everything else in the table is a call your code makes or answers.

Unsupported. No serverTools means no refresh, no save, no pagination. The recipes all render from their initial tool result under this condition, which is worth testing. Denied. The host may refuse a specific call on policy grounds even with the capability present. Report its message. Failed. isError: true with readable text. Keep the last good state. Cancelled. Either direction. Keep the last good state and say where it stopped. Timeout. Give every call a deadline. A host that never answers is indistinguishable from a slow server, and a spinner with no end is the worst of the five failure modes because it never resolves into anything the user can act on.

tools/call from the view reaches the server and its result returns. A tool with visibility: ["app"] is absent from the agent’s tool list. A cross-server call for an app-only tool is refused. ui/notifications/tool-input arrives exactly once, after any partials. Partial arguments are recoverable JSON and never a fragment. ui/notifications/tool-result carries the standard result shape. With serverTools absent, the view sends no tools/call .

tool.invoke is the workhorse of Part III and the one most applications under-use, because it is easy to think of every server round trip as a conversation. It is not. A refresh button that calls an app-only tool is cheaper, faster, more reliable and more testable than anything routed through a model, and it is the mechanism that lets a view be an application rather than a rendering of one turn. Previous 19. Agent to UI Next 21. State Ownership and Concurrency
