Chapter 21 Two parties can write to the same document and neither knows what the other is doing. Declare who owns what before it happens, because afterwards there is no good default. Label every region of your state user-owned, agent-owned or shared before you write any code. It takes about ten minutes and it converts an argument about merge semantics into a short list of decisions, most of which turn out to be obvious once the regions are named. This is not about merge algorithms. The agent is not another user: it is fast, it works in bursts, it cannot see the screen, it does not know the human is mid-sentence, and it cannot be asked to wait. The live application needs JavaScript. Its source is in the repository under apps/ .

state.ownership Core Level 4 Yours to build Declare who owns each region when both parties can write. Ground The view implements it. Nobody else can. Recipes Document Editor , Workflow Builder Demo lab-ownership Every region of application state gets exactly one of three labels, and the labels should be visible in the interface. A user who can see that the risk score belongs to the agent and the note belongs to them can predict what will change under their cursor. User-owned. The agent may read it and may propose changes to it in conversation. It may not write it. Personal notes, drafts the user has not shared, anything where the point is that a person said it. Agent-owned. The agent computes it and the view displays it. The user does not edit it directly; if they disagree, they change the inputs. Risk scores, classifications, generated summaries that are labelled as generated. Shared. Both may write, and therefore a conflict policy is required. This is where all the difficulty lives, and the useful discipline is to keep the shared set small. The demonstration has one region of each, and the labels are visible in the interface. That visibility is not decoration: a user who can see that the risk score is the agent’s and the note is theirs can predict what will change under them. Write the map down before the code. It takes ten minutes and it converts an argument about merge semantics into a list of decisions. Recipe 4 declares its map in the recipe entry, and the map is what determined which tools the view registers. Three regions, three owners, one conflict policy each

state.conflict Core Level 4 Yours to build Decide what happens when they both do. Ground The view implements it. Nobody else can. Recipes Document Editor Demo lab-ownership For each shared region, pick one policy and make it visible. The four are not equally safe, and the choice is worth making deliberately, before the first time two writes land in the same second. Reject. The write fails and the writer is told. Appropriate when the region is small and the loss is cheap. The tool returns isError: true with an explanation, which the agent can relay. Last writer wins. The later write applies. Simple, and dangerous exactly when the human is the earlier writer, because they lose work they can see on screen. Acceptable only with a visible notice and an undo. Merge. For structured state where writes touch different fields, apply both. Requires that your state actually be structured, and no blob of HTML, which is a good reason to structure it. Ask. Hold the write, show both versions, let the human choose. The heaviest and the safest, and the right default when the human is actively editing. The demonstration implements the last one with a rule that costs eight lines: while the human has typed within the last 1.5 seconds, hold the agent’s write and offer it when they stop. The number is a guess and the mechanism is not. Anything between one and three seconds behaves the same way to a user, and the property that matters is that the agent’s text never appears under a moving cursor. Extracted from from apps/labs/lab-ownership/index.html bridge.registerTool({ name: "rewrite_summary", description: "Replace the shared summary text", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { text: { type: "string" } }, required: ["text"] }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: false }, }, async ({ text }) => { if (userTyping) { pending = text; setOwner("Agent write held: the human is typing.", "warn"); return { content: [{ type: "text", text: "Held. The user is editing; the change will be offered to them." }] }; } offer(text); return { content: [{ type: "text", text: "Offered to the user for review." }] }; }); Two things to notice. The tool tells the agent what actually happened, so it does not report to the user that the summary has been rewritten when it has not. And “held” and “offered” are different outcomes with different words, because an agent that reads “held” can decide to wait and try again.

sections.h: How do I say no to the agent?
sections.x: The user-owned region needs a registered tool as well, and that tool’s entire job is to refuse usefully. Not registering one is worse: a model that cannot find a way to write the note will try adjacent tools, or will report to the user that it updated the note when nothing happened. Extracted from from apps/labs/lab-ownership/index.html bridge.registerTool({ name: "write_note", description: "Attempt to write the user-owned note", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { text: { type: "string" } }, required: ["text"] }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: false }, }, async () => ({ isError: true, content: [{ type: "text", text: "The internal note is user owned. Propose a change in the " + "conversation instead of writing it." }], })); The alternative, not registering the tool at all, is worse. A model that cannot find a way to write the note will try adjacent tools, or will tell the user it has updated the note when it has not. An explicit refusal that names the correct route is a better interface for a model in exactly the way it is for a person.

The other concurrency problem has nothing to do with the agent. It is between your view and the server, and it appears the moment you show a change before the call that makes it has returned. A view that applies a change locally and then calls a tool has committed to an outcome it does not have yet. When the call fails, or is cancelled, or the frame is torn down mid-flight, the interface is showing something that never happened. The rule. Optimistic updates need a compensating action recorded at the same moment they are applied, which is the same transaction shape as Chapter 16’s undo. On failure, apply the compensation and say why. On cancellation, apply the compensation only for steps that did not complete, and say how far it got: Recipe 11 reports “stopped after three of five steps, completed steps were not rolled back”, which is unglamorous and true. The unrecoverable case. If the frame is torn down while a write is in flight, nobody rolls anything back. The server may have applied it. This is why writes that matter should be idempotent and keyed, so the next render can ask what actually happened.

sections.h: Put the agent on the undo stack
sections.x: The single most important rule in this chapter, and mechanically it costs nothing, because it belongs to Chapter 16’s transaction stack and that stack already exists. Every agent write goes through the same apply path a human edit goes through, carrying a label that names the agent, and Ctrl+Z reverses it like anything else. Every agent write goes onto the same undo stack as the user’s own edits, as one transaction, with a label that names the agent. One Cmd+Z restores the human’s words. Recipe 4 does this for accepted rewrites, and the whole safety argument for agent-assisted editing rests on it: a change you can take back in one keystroke is a change you can afford to let a model make. An agent whose changes are outside the undo stack is an agent whose changes are permanent, and users respond to permanent changes by not using the feature. This is the cheapest trust mechanism in the book and the one most often skipped, because agent writes usually arrive through a different code path than user edits and joining the two paths is a refactor nobody scheduled.

A shortcut for picking one, since this choice is usually made under time pressure and the wrong default is expensive to unwind once views depend on it. Four questions, in order, and the first one that gets a yes decides it. Write the answer next to the region in the code, because the next person to touch it will otherwise re-derive it from the behaviour and get it wrong. Is losing this write cheap? Reject. The tool says no with a reason and the agent can relay it. Is the region a field? Merge, if writes touch different fields, and last-writer-wins with a notice if they do not. Is a human likely to be editing it right now? Ask, as defined above. This is the default for anything a person types into, and the cost of getting it wrong is somebody watching their sentence disappear as they write it. Is the region computed? Agent-owned. There is no conflict, because the user does not write it; if they disagree they change the inputs. The demonstration implements Ask with a 1.5 second idle timer, which is crude and works. A more careful version would key on whether the field has focus, and would still need the timer for the case where somebody types and then looks away.

An agent write to a user-owned region returns isError: true with a reason. An agent write to a shared region while the user is typing is held. A held write is offered to the user rather than dropped. The tool result distinguishes held, offered and applied. Every applied agent write is one undo transaction. A failed optimistic update is rolled back and the reason is shown. A cancelled multi-step operation reports how far it got.

Three labels, four policies, and a decision made before the code. Keep the shared set small, hold agent writes while a human is typing, tell the agent what actually happened, and put everything the agent does on the undo stack. That is the entire chapter, and every part of it is cheaper to build than the merge algorithm you were considering. Previous 20. Tool Invocation and Streaming Next 22. Approval, Elicitation and the Context Boundary

sections.t: Approval, Elicitation and the Context Boundary
sections.x: Chapter 22 Two capabilities the extension does not have, one principle it depends on, and an argument about what the model should never be told. This is where the protocol runs out. Human approval has no message. Structured questions from a view have no message. Both are things real applications need, and both have partial answers elsewhere in MCP that stop short of the view: core MCP has elicitation, which flows server to host, and core MCP has a consent model that hosts implement for tool calls. Neither reaches a ui:// document. What this chapter describes is the shape you build in their absence, and how much of a security property that shape actually carries. The chapter closes with the principle that has been implicit since Chapter 4: UI state is not model context, and the default is silence. That default is easily lost, because publishing feels free and helpful, and each individual update looks reasonable in isolation. The live application needs JavaScript. Its source is in the repository under apps/ .

sections.t: Approval, Elicitation and the Context Boundary
sections.h: How do I require a human signature?
sections.x: approval.request Core Level 4 Not standardised Require a human signature on a sensitive action. Ground No standard mechanism exists yet. The entry carries a workaround. Recipes Approval Center Demo lab-approval Put the gate on the server. Core MCP is built on user consent, and the specification is clear that hosts must give users control over what is authorised. What the Apps extension does not give you is a way for a view to demand it. Your Approve button is an ordinary button in an untrusted iframe: nothing signs the click, nothing attests that a human made it, and the host never learns that an approval happened. The button’s only effect is the tool call your own code makes next, which the server would have had to trust anyway. What that means in practice. Approval today is a convention, and its integrity depends on where the enforcement lives. The enforceable design is: The server holds the gate. A refund tool does not perform a refund; it queues one and returns a queue id. A separate tool performs it, and that tool is visibility: ["app"] so the model cannot call it, and it requires the queue id. The view calls it after a human presses a button. The view shows provenance. Who asked, on whose behalf, using which tool, with which arguments, and what the consequence is. Recipe 10’s card carries five provenance fields, and the reason is that an approval card without them is a dialog with a lever attached, and users learn to pull levers. Extracted from from apps/recipes/r10-approval-center/server.js provenance: { "asked by": "the agent, in this conversation", "on behalf of": "sam@meridian.example", tool: "billing.refund", arguments: "invoice=2026-0814 amount=1240.00 currency=USD", "prior approvals": "none for this customer", }, The last field is the one that does the most work and is almost never present. “None for this customer” is what turns a routine approval into a pause, because it is the only line on the card that says anything about whether this request is unusual. Everything above it describes the request; that line describes the pattern the request sits in. The host shows the boundary. prefersBorder and whatever chrome the host provides are what tell a user that this rectangle came from a server. The specification names phishing inside a view as a threat for exactly this reason. The tool that refuses. Recipe 10 registers an approve tool whose only behaviour is to decline: Extracted from from apps/recipes/r10-approval-center/index.html bridge.registerTool({ name: "approve", description: "Approve a queued action", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { title: { type: "string" } } }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: false }, }, async () => ({ isError: true, content: [{ type: "text", text: "Approval requires a person. This view does not accept approvals over " + "the tool interface." }], })); Registering a tool in order to refuse it looks strange until you consider the alternative. An agent that finds no approval tool will try something else, and what it tries may be a server tool that does not have the gate. An explicit refusal that states the rule is a better interface for a model in the same way it is for a person. What a mechanism would look like. ui/request-approval from the view, answered by the host after the host itself asks the user, returning something the server can verify. The host is the only party in a position to render an authentic consent surface, because it is the only one the user has a trust relationship with.

sections.t: Approval, Elicitation and the Context Boundary
sections.h: Can I ask a structured question?
sections.x: elicit.request Core Level 4 Not standardised Ask the user a structured question mid-operation. Ground No standard mechanism exists yet. The entry carries a workaround. Recipes Approval Center Demo lab-approval Core MCP has elicitation, which lets a server ask the host to collect structured input from the user in the middle of an operation. It also has a URL mode for out-of-band interactions, with a hard requirement that credentials never be collected in form mode: passwords, API keys, tokens and payment details must go through a URL the user can inspect. That flows server to host. There is no view-to-host equivalent, so a view with a mid-operation question has two options. Ask in its own UI, which works and carries no more weight than any other pixels in an untrusted iframe. Or send ui/message and wait for a turn, which costs the flow. The rule that survives regardless. Never collect credentials in a view. The elicitation specification’s prohibition on form-mode credential collection applies with more force here, not less: a form inside an untrusted iframe asking for a password is the phishing attack in the threat model, drawn by the application itself. If your flow needs authentication, it needs URL-mode elicitation from the server, or a link opened through ui/open-link into a real browser context where the user can see the address bar. What crosses the context boundary, and what does not

sections.t: Approval, Elicitation and the Context Boundary
sections.h: What should the model never be told?
sections.x: agent.boundary Core Level 4 Yours to build Keep hover, scroll, and sort out of the model's context. Ground The view implements it. Nobody else can. Recipes Approval Center Demo lab-approval The Context Boundary. UI state is not automatically model context. Hover, scroll position, open menus, focus, local sort order and transient selection stay private to the interface. None of them changes what a reasonable answer to the next question would be. Only state that changes what a reasonable next answer would be should cross, and it crosses explicitly through ui/update-model-context and never by accident. Explicitly is the operative word: nothing about your interface is published unless a line of your code publishes it. ::: The demo has two counters: local events, and ui/update-model-context calls. Move the mouse over the card and drag the scrollbar for ten seconds. The first passes a thousand, because pointermove and scroll fire at the display’s refresh rate. The second stays at the number of decisions you made, which on that card is zero until you press Approve or Deny. The ratio between the two counters is the point of the whole section, and it is roughly three orders of magnitude in any interface a person actually uses. Why the default is silence. Three reasons, and only the first is about cost. Context is finite and shared with the conversation, so anything you publish displaces something else. Published state is not deletable in the way it feels: hosts may hold the last update until the next user message, and the model may reason from it for several turns. And some UI state is information the user did not intend to disclose. What somebody hovered over before deciding is a record of their hesitation, and a view that publishes it has told the model something the user would not have said. The test. Would this change a reasonable answer to the next question? State Publish? Selection Yes. It answers “why are these slow”. Decision made Yes. Recipe 10 publishes approve or deny. Sort order Only if the user may ask “what is at the top”. Hover, scroll, focus Never. Two failures. Under-publish and the assistant does not know what “these” means, which reads as stupidity. Over-publish and the window fills with near-identical snapshots, and answers degrade as the session runs. The second is harder to spot because nothing looks broken.

sections.t: Approval, Elicitation and the Context Boundary
sections.h: Why the view cannot enforce it
sections.x: Be precise about this, because the queue-and-perform pattern looks like security and is only a convention. Knowing exactly what it does and does not buy is the difference between using it correctly and trusting it too far. The view is HTML from a server, running in a sandbox, and its Approve button is an ordinary button. Nothing signs the click. Nothing attests that a human made it. A compromised view, or a view whose server was compromised, can call the performing tool directly without rendering anything at all, and the server cannot tell the difference because the call arrives over the same channel with the same credentials. The pattern buys three things, and they hold under different assumptions. The first holds as long as the host honours visibility . The second holds as long as the server’s log is trustworthy. The third holds only as far as the user reads what is in front of them: The model cannot approve, because the performing tool is visibility: ["app"] and the host must not put it in the agent’s tool list. That closes the case where a model talks itself into an action. The audit trail is coherent, because queueing and performing are separate server-side events sharing an id, so the record shows what was requested, when it was authorised, and by which path it executed. The gap between those two timestamps is the only durable evidence anywhere in the system that a human paused, and it lives on the server, which is one more reason the gate has to live there too. The user sees provenance, which is the difference between an approval and a reflex. Five fields naming who asked, on whose behalf, using which tool, with what arguments, and what was approved before, is enough for somebody to notice that this is the first refund ever issued to this customer. What it does not buy is protection from a hostile view, and that requires the host to render the consent surface, which requires a message that does not exist. That is the finding, and it belongs upstream.

sections.t: Approval, Elicitation and the Context Boundary
sections.x: A view’s approval control has no protocol effect, and the enforcing gate is on the server. The tool that performs a gated action carries visibility: ["app"] . An approval tool exposed to the agent refuses. No credentials are collected in a view. Context updates carry decisions and outcomes, not interaction traces. Hover, scroll and sort produce no messages.

sections.t: Approval, Elicitation and the Context Boundary
sections.h: What to remember from Part III
sections.x: Both parties can act and neither can see the other. The view cannot read the conversation. The host cannot read the view’s DOM, because allow-same-origin is absent and the frame’s origin is opaque. The agent cannot see the screen at all; every fact it holds about your interface arrived because a line of your code sent it. Every capability in Part III passes a small, explicit, auditable amount of information across that gap: ui/message to start a turn, ui/update-model-context to replace a standing summary, tools/call in both directions for work that needs no turn, and sampling/createMessage for language the view needs but cannot generate. Four messages, each carrying a payload you wrote by hand. approval.request and elicit.request did not get one, because both need the host to render a consent surface, and a message that lets a view demand host chrome is a message that lets a hostile view demand host chrome. That is a harder specification problem than it looks, which is a reason for its absence and not an excuse for building around it in private. Previous 21. State Ownership and Concurrency Next 23. Components I: Overlays, Controls and Text

sections.t: Components I: Overlays, Controls and Text
sections.x: Chapter 23 What each component composes, which ARIA pattern governs it, and the embedded-specific detail that makes it different from the version you have built before. Capabilities are too small to build an interface out of and applications are too large to reuse, so components are the layer in between: the pieces with names a designer already uses, assembled from capabilities and assembled into recipes. Every entry answers three questions: what it composes, which Authoring Practices Guide pattern governs its keyboard behaviour, and what changes because it lives in someone else’s window. The third question is the one that makes this part worth writing. The first two are answered better by the APG itself, and every entry here links to it instead of paraphrasing it. The third question is the only reason these chapters exist. Plenty of references tell you how to build a combobox. None tell you how to build one that is four hundred pixels wide, inside an opaque origin, next to a model that may fill it in. The recipes are built from two files: apps/lib/view.css and apps/lib/view.js , about 500 lines together, and all thirteen share them. That is small enough to read in a sitting and is the whole component layer behind every demonstration on this site. There is no framework underneath it and no build step over it, which is a claim you can check by viewing source on any recipe.

sections.t: Components I: Overlays, Controls and Text
sections.x: Component Composes APG pattern Alert dialog.alert , surface.focus Alert Dialog Confirmation dialog.confirm , surface.focus , input.keyboard Alert Dialog Modal surface.displayMode , surface.focus , input.keyboard Dialog (Modal) Sheet, drawer surface.focus , input.pointer , env.reducedMotion Dialog (Modal) Popover surface.focus , input.keyboard Disclosure Tooltip input.pointer , env.inputMode Tooltip Context menu input.contextmenu , input.longpress , surface.focus Menu Use <dialog> and showModal() . It gives you the focus trap, the inert background, the Escape handling and the aria-modal semantics. A hand-rolled overlay gives you none of them, and in a frame a keyboard user cannot escape from, the difference is not cosmetic. This is the whole confirmation component the thirteen recipes share. Every behaviour a hand-rolled overlay would have to reimplement is inherited from the element, and the promise makes it usable from an await : Extracted from from apps/lib/view.js // window.confirm is blocked in a sandbox without allow-modals, and blocking // the thread would freeze the bridge anyway. This is the in-view version: // same semantics, one promise, focus trapped by <dialog>. function confirmDialog({ title, body, confirm = "Confirm", cancel = "Cancel", destructive = false }) { return new Promise((resolve) => { const dialog = h("dialog", {}, h("h2", { text: title }), body ? h("p", { class: "muted", text: body }) : null, h("div", { class: "row", style: "justify-content:flex-end" }, h("button", { class: "quiet", text: cancel, onclick: () => { dialog.close(); resolve(false); } }), h("button", { class: destructive ? "danger" : "primary", text: confirm, onclick: () => { dialog.close(); resolve(true); } }))); dialog.addEventListener("cancel", () => resolve(false)); dialog.addEventListener("close", () => dialog.remove()); document.body.append(dialog); dialog.showModal(); }); } The cancel listener is the one people leave out. It fires when the user presses Escape, and without it the promise never settles and the code awaiting the answer waits forever in a frame that looks fine. Everything is clipped by the frame. A popover that would overflow the viewport in a page just overflows; here it is cut off by the iframe’s edge and there is no way to render outside it. Position with the frame’s bounds, not the screen’s, and prefer flipping to a different side over letting the content extend past the boundary. A dropdown that opens downward at the bottom of the frame is a dropdown nobody can read. Tooltips need a second route. They are hover-only by construction, and hostContext.deviceCapabilities.hover tells you when hover does not exist. On a touch device, move the content into the label, a popover triggered by tap, or a description that is always visible. Context menus need a keyboard route. Shift+F10, a visible button, or both. Chapter 10 has the details. Why <dialog> and not a div The list of what a hand-rolled overlay loses is longer than people expect, and hand-rolled overlays are still the common case, usually because somebody needed one animation the native element did not offer. Each item below is a behaviour you are then committing to re-implement, and most of them are invisible until somebody uses a keyboard or a screen reader. showModal() puts the dialog in the top layer, which means it renders above everything regardless of stacking context, and no z-index arms race is needed. It makes the rest of the document inert, so clicks and focus cannot reach it. It gives you ::backdrop as a real pseudo-element. It handles Escape, firing a cancel event you can intercept. It restores focus to the previously focused element on close. And it carries the modal semantics assistive technology needs without a single ARIA attribute. A div with position: fixed gives you none of those, and the versions people write typically reimplement two of them badly. The one thing to remember is the cancel event: a dialog whose promise is only resolved by its buttons hangs forever when the user presses Escape, and in an application that awaits the answer, a hung promise is a frozen interface.

sections.t: Components I: Overlays, Controls and Text
sections.x: Component Composes APG pattern Button input.pointer , input.keyboard Button Checkbox, radio input.keyboard , input.selection Checkbox, Radio Group Toggle input.keyboard Switch Slider input.pointer , input.keyboard Slider Stepper input.keyboard Spinbutton Segmented control input.keyboard , input.selection Radio Group Filter chip input.selection , input.keyboard Checkbox Dropdown input.keyboard , surface.focus Listbox Combobox input.keyboard , input.selection , surface.focus Combobox Start from the native element. <button> , <input type="checkbox"> , <input type="range"> , <select> all work, all come with keyboard and screen reader support, and all are one CSS file away from matching your design. The recipes use native elements everywhere except the combobox, which does not exist natively. Target size is a host-dependent decision. WCAG 2.2 requires 24 by 24 CSS pixels at AA and 44 by 44 at AAA, and deviceCapabilities is where you find out whether you are on touch. A toolbar designed at 28 pixels clears AA and is still unpleasant on a phone, and you cannot detect a phone by width when the same width is a side panel on a desktop. Disabled controls carry an obligation. A disabled button is a promise that something could enable it, and the user is entitled to know what. If the reason is a missing host capability, do not disable, omit: Chapter 1’s argument. If the reason is state, say so. The combobox is the one worth buying. It is the most complex pattern in the APG, it involves a listbox that must be positioned within the frame, and getting the aria-activedescendant and expanded state right takes longer than any other component here. If a plain <select> or a text input with a datalist will do, take it.

sections.t: Components I: Overlays, Controls and Text
sections.x: Component Composes APG pattern Text field input.keyboard , surface.focus (native) Search field input.keyboard , input.shortcut (native) Multiline editor input.keyboard , history.transaction (native) Autocomplete input.keyboard , input.selection Combobox Token input input.keyboard , input.selection , clipboard.write Combobox Rich text editor history.transaction , input.selection , ui.prefill (none) Code editor input.keyboard , clipboard.write , input.selection (none) Validate on blur and on submit, never on keystroke. Telling somebody their email is invalid while they are typing the at sign is the fastest way to make a form feel hostile. Recipe 13 tracks a touched flag per field and only shows an error after the field has been left once. Extracted from from apps/recipes/r13-settings/index.html if (!email && (!live || $("#email").dataset.touched)) { $("#email").setAttribute("aria-invalid", "true"); $("#email-err").hidden = false; $("#email-err").textContent = "That is not an address this will reach."; ok = false; } else { $("#email").removeAttribute("aria-invalid"); $("#email-err").hidden = true; } Two attributes do the accessibility work. aria-invalid is what a screen reader announces when focus lands back on the field, and the error element is referenced by aria-describedby so the message is read as part of the field and not as a stray paragraph. Toggling hidden on the message rather than emptying its text keeps the layout from jumping as the user moves through the form. Undo grouping is per pause, not per keystroke. Chapter 16. In a rich text editor this is the difference between an undo stack somebody can use and one that steps back a character at a time. Search fields want a shortcut and cannot safely have one. Cmd/Ctrl+F is the convention and the host may own it. Bind it, expect to lose it sometimes, and always provide the visible field. Rich text is where the agent shows up. A text field can be prefilled and the user sees the value change. A document cannot: the agent’s rewrite has to appear as a proposal, with the original still visible, and accepting it has to be one undo transaction. Recipe 4 is the worked example, and the proposal card is a component in its own right that Chapter 25 lists. Code editors are a decision about weight. A real editor is a large dependency inside a frame with a restrictive CSP and no CDN unless the server declares one. A <pre> with syntax highlighting done server-side covers reading, which is most of what a review interface does. Recipe 8 renders a diff with no editor at all.

sections.t: Components I: Overlays, Controls and Text
sections.x: A quick reference, because the trade is genuinely different from a page. In a page an overlay costs the user a moment; in a 380 pixel frame it costs them the entire interface for as long as it is open. Component Cost in a four hundred pixel frame Use when Alert Blocks everything, clipped by the frame Almost never; usually a toast Confirmation Blocks, but small The action is destructive and not undoable Modal Covers the whole view The task genuinely needs the whole surface Sheet or drawer Covers most of the view, animates A secondary task the user returns from Popover Clipped at the frame edge Short content anchored to a control Tooltip Unreachable without hover Never the only route to information Context menu Clipped, needs a keyboard route Per-item actions, with a visible alternative The pattern in the right-hand column is that the answer is almost always “smaller than you think”. A modal inside a card is a card that has become unusable for the duration; a sheet that covers eighty percent of a small frame is a modal wearing a different animation.

sections.t: Components I: Overlays, Controls and Text
sections.h: The one component worth not building
sections.x: The combobox, and it is worth being specific about why. It is the most complex pattern in the Authoring Practices Guide. It needs a listbox positioned within a frame that clips it. It needs aria-activedescendant , an expanded state, a value that may or may not be one of the options, and typeahead that does not fight the input. And it needs all of that to work with a virtual list once the option count passes a few hundred. Recipe 1 uses a plain <select> for its environment filter for exactly this reason. The filter has four options. A combobox would be worse in every dimension including the one it exists to improve, because typing to filter four items is slower than reading four items, and the native control already opens above or below depending on where the frame sits in the host’s window.

sections.t: Components I: Overlays, Controls and Text
sections.x: Every component in this chapter is smaller than the version you have built before, and the reduction is not proportional. Halving the width does not halve what fits, because labels, padding and touch targets do not scale down with it. A toolbar of nine buttons becomes four and an overflow menu. A three-column form becomes one column. A 600 pixel modal has to work at 380. None of that is new to anyone who has built a responsive layout; what is new is that the narrow case is the common case here, because an inline card in a chat transcript is narrower than a phone and the host chose the width, not the user. The useful discipline is to design at the narrowest width you will accept, and to let surface.resize report the height. Everything in this book is built at 380 pixels first, and the recipes look the same at 900 because the layout only ever had one column to lose.

sections.t: Components I: Overlays, Controls and Text
sections.x: Every overlay traps focus while open and restores it on close. Escape closes any overlay and resolves whatever was awaiting it. No overlay renders outside the frame’s bounds. Native controls are used where they exist, and replacements carry the same keyboard behaviour. Hit targets clear 24 by 24 CSS pixels everywhere, and 44 by 44 when deviceCapabilities.touch is set. Validation errors appear on blur and on submit, not on keystroke. Every error is associated with its field through aria-describedby . Previous 22. Approval, Elicitation and the Context Boundary Next 24. Components II: Navigation, Data and Visualization

sections.t: Components II: Navigation, Data and Visualization
sections.x: Chapter 24 Structure without a URL bar, tables that survive streaming, and charts in a frame that cannot load a charting library. These are the components that carry data, and all three groups run into the same two walls. There is no address bar, so nothing about navigation state can live in a URL and the back button belongs to somebody else. And there is very little room, so the column budget runs out long before the data does.

sections.t: Components II: Navigation, Data and Visualization
sections.x: Component Composes APG pattern Tabs input.keyboard , surface.focus , ui.navigate Tabs Breadcrumbs input.keyboard Breadcrumb Tree input.keyboard , input.selection , input.contextmenu Tree View Accordion input.keyboard , surface.resize Accordion Sidebar input.keyboard , surface.viewport (layout) Toolbar input.keyboard , env.inputMode Toolbar Command palette input.shortcut , surface.focus , input.keyboard Combobox Split view input.pointer , surface.viewport (layout) There is no URL. Everything a URL normally does has to be done some other way. You cannot deep link into a view. The user cannot bookmark a state. The back button belongs to the host and does not know your tabs exist. Pressing it leaves the conversation, which is a considerably worse outcome than going back one tab. Three consequences. Navigation state has to be shallow, because there is no history to unwind. Every panel needs a visible way back, because the browser’s is not available. And navigation state is one of the few things worth publishing to the model, because “the user is looking at the line items panel” changes what a good answer looks like. Tabs are the default and the tree is the exception. In four hundred pixels, a tab strip with more than four labels wraps or scrolls, and both look like a mistake. If you need more than four, you probably need a different structure. A tree is one tab stop. role="tree" with roving tabindex, arrows to move and expand, Home and End, and typeahead if the tree is large. Recipe 3 builds one, and the roving tabindex is what keeps a hundred-file tree from being a hundred tab stops. Toolbars overflow. A wrapped toolbar changes the height of the view on a resize, which triggers surface.resize , which changes the frame, which can change the wrap. Put the extras behind a menu. A command palette is the best answer to a narrow surface , and it is also the component most likely to lose its shortcut to the host. Give it a visible entry point.

sections.t: Components II: Navigation, Data and Visualization
sections.x: Component Composes APG pattern List input.selection , input.keyboard Listbox Virtual list surface.scroll , input.selection Listbox Table input.selection , input.keyboard , clipboard.write Grid Editable grid input.selection , history.transaction , clipboard.write Grid Pagination input.keyboard (native) Comparison grid input.selection Grid Property list input.selection , clipboard.write (definition list) This is the group most MCP applications are actually made of, and it has the most predictable failures of anything in Part IV. Four of them account for nearly everything that goes wrong, and all four are about what survives an update. Column budget. Four columns is comfortable at 380 pixels, six is the ceiling, and beyond that the answer is a property list per row. Recipe 1 shows six and drops to a card layout under 480 pixels. Sort, filter and page locally. Chapter 4. All three are answerable from data already in the frame. Selection is the unit of conversation. Chapter 10 has the gesture model, Chapter 18 has what to do with it. A table without a selection model gives its users nothing precise to ask about. Streaming updates must not rebuild the list. Appending a row is fine. Replacing the container’s children destroys selection, focus and scroll position at the same time, and the user notices all three. Recipe 9 appends and trims, never redraws, which is what makes selecting a log line survive a thousand lines arriving after it. Virtualise past a few thousand rows , and be aware that virtualisation and surface.resize interact badly: a virtual list has a fixed height by design, so it wants a fixed container, which means telling the host a stable size and scrolling inside it. Copy as the destination wants it. TSV for the clipboard, CSV for a file. Chapter 11.

sections.t: Components II: Navigation, Data and Visualization
sections.x: Six columns at 380 pixels is the practical ceiling, and getting there takes deliberate work. Each of the following buys you roughly half a column, and you need all of them. Right-align every number and use tabular figures, which buys a character of width per column and makes outliers scannable. Put units in the header: “p95 ms” once beats “412ms” eight times. Use chips for enumerated values, because a chip reads at a glance and a word does not. Format dates to the shortest form that is still unambiguous, which usually means dropping the year for anything inside the current one. And put anything that is only occasionally needed behind row expansion. When that is not enough, the answer is not a horizontal scrollbar. It is a different component: a property list per row, which turns a wide table into a tall list and is what every mobile client does with the same problem. Recipe 1 switches at 480 pixels.

sections.t: Components II: Navigation, Data and Visualization
sections.x: Component Composes APG pattern Chart surface.viewport , env.theme , input.pointer (image or table) Timeline input.zoompan , input.selection (image or table) Heatmap input.pointer , env.contrast (image or table) Progress visualization op.progress , env.reducedMotion Progressbar Status indicator env.contrast (status) You probably cannot load a charting library. The default CSP is default-src 'none' . A CDN means declaring that origin in resourceDomains , and a host that declines leaves you with no chart. Bundling means a few hundred kilobytes of JavaScript in an HTML string on every resources/read . Inline SVG is the answer for most of what embedded applications actually need. A sparkline is nine lines. A bar chart is fifteen. Recipe 2’s sparklines are generated with createElementNS and no dependency at all, and Recipe 12 draws its media thumbnails the same way, which is also how the demonstrations avoid declaring any external origin. Theme through variables, not through constants. A chart with #0f5c8c baked in is invisible in a dark theme. stroke="var(--color-text-info)" works inside SVG and follows the host. Colour alone is never the encoding. Forced-colors mode replaces your palette. A status that is only a green dot becomes a dot. Pair every colour with a shape, a label, or text. Charts need a text equivalent. A <table> behind a disclosure, or an aria-label carrying the figures. Recipe 2 writes “Checkout p95, 412 milliseconds, up 18 percent since the 4.18.2 deploy” under each tile, which more readers use than the sparkline. Progress that never moves is worse than no progress. An indeterminate spinner with a phase name beats a determinate bar whose number is invented. Chapter 17.

sections.t: Components II: Navigation, Data and Visualization
sections.x: Selection state lives on the row as aria-selected , so one attribute drives both the screen reader announcement and the highlight, and neither can drift from the other: Extracted from from apps/lib/view.css tbody tr[aria-selected="true"] { background: var(--color-background-info); } tbody tr:hover { background: var(--color-background-secondary); } td.num, th.num { text-align: right; font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; } font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums is the line that makes a column of latencies scannable. Without it the digits have proportional widths, so 412 and 1290 do not line up and the eye cannot compare them down the column. The four properties that separate a table people can work in from a table people take screenshots of. All four appear in Recipe 1, and none of them is more than a few lines. Selection survives updates. Keyed by identifier, not by row index. A table that re-sorts and keeps three rows selected is behaving; one that keeps rows three, four and five selected is not. Scroll survives updates. Append and patch. Recipe 9 appends up to a cap and never rebuilds, which is what makes a log tail usable at five lines a second. Focus survives updates. The consequence of the first two, and the one users feel most sharply. A grid that rebuilds on every tick moves focus to the document body twice a second, which makes keyboard operation impossible. Numbers are aligned and tabular. text-align: right and font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums . Two declarations, and they turn a column of figures into something you can scan for an outlier. This is not accessibility and it is not decoration; it is the reason the table exists.

sections.t: Components II: Navigation, Data and Visualization
sections.x: A bar is two elements and eleven lines of CSS, and it is the entire visualisation layer behind Recipe 2’s tiles: Extracted from from apps/lib/view.css .bar { height: 6px; border-radius: var(--border-radius-full); background: var(--color-background-tertiary); overflow: hidden; } .bar > span { display: block; height: 100%; background: var(--color-text-info); transition: width .2s ease; } Both colours come from the host’s variables, so the bar re-themes with everything else and needs no branch for dark mode. The transition is suppressed wholesale by the reduced-motion rule at the foot of the same file, which is why no chart in this book animates for a user who asked it not to. Three shapes cover most of what an embedded view actually needs, and all three are cheap enough in inline SVG that a dependency is hard to justify. A sparkline is a polyline whose points are the series scaled to the box. Nine lines, no axes, no labels, and it belongs next to a number, never in place of one. Recipe 2 builds one per tile. A bar chart is a loop of rects with a shared scale. Fifteen lines. The work is in the labels, not the bars, and in a narrow frame the labels usually have to go under the bars. A status strip is not a chart at all: a row of chips with text in them. It is what most dashboards actually need, it is legible at any size, and it survives forced colours because the state is in the words. Beyond those three, ask whether the view is the right place. A six-series chart at 380px is unreadable; a table plus a ui/open-link to the real dashboard is usually better.

sections.t: Components II: Navigation, Data and Visualization
sections.x: The URL bar and the CDN are the two things this chapter keeps running into, and they are the two things a page has that a view does not. Design navigation that does not need history, and visualisation that does not need a dependency, and most of the rest of your components will port over unchanged. Previous 23. Components I: Overlays, Controls and Text Next 25. Components III: Spatial, Media and Agent-Native

sections.t: Components III: Spatial, Media and Agent-Native
sections.x: Chapter 25 Canvases in a small frame, transports you should probably not replace, and five components that exist only because there is a model in the room. Two familiar groups, then five components with no precedent anywhere in web design. Spatial and media components you have built before and mostly port unchanged. The last five could not have existed before there was a second party acting on the interface, so there is no established pattern to copy and every agentic application ends up inventing them badly at least once.

sections.t: Components III: Spatial, Media and Agent-Native
sections.x: Component Composes APG pattern Canvas input.pointer , input.zoompan , surface.viewport (application) Node graph input.dragdrop , input.selection , input.zoompan (application) Bounding box editor input.pointer , input.zoompan , history.transaction (application) Image annotation input.pointer , file.dropzone , file.export (application) Minimap input.pointer , surface.viewport (decorative) Report a fixed height and scroll inside it. Recipe 6 uses 260px, Recipe 7 uses 280px, both chosen to work at 380px wide. A canvas that grows with its content fights surface.resize and loses. Pointer capture, touch-action: none , and zoom about the cursor. All three in Chapter 10, and all three are the difference between a canvas that feels right and one that fights. Add a minimap. Recipe 7 draws one into a 220 by 148 <canvas> in eleven lines: fillRect per node, strokeRect for the viewport. Every gesture needs a button. Zoom in, zoom out, reset, fit, and arrow keys to pan. A canvas operable only by dragging cannot be operated at all by a significant number of people, and this is the component group where that failure is both most common and least noticed, because the developer testing it always has a pointer. Undo per gesture, not per frame. A drag produces one transaction on pointerup, not sixty during pointermove. Recipe 7 records the start position on pointerdown and pushes a single transaction at the end.

sections.t: Components III: Spatial, Media and Agent-Native
sections.x: Component Composes APG pattern Player transport media.playback , input.keyboard Toolbar, Slider Scrubber media.playback , input.pointer Slider Caption selector media.playback , input.keyboard Listbox Thumbnail strip input.selection , input.keyboard Tabs, Listbox Use the native controls unless you have a reason. <video controls> handles keyboard, screen readers, captions, picture-in-picture and playback rate in zero lines. Replace them and you inherit the contract: Space to play, arrows to seek, aria-valuetext on the slider in minutes and seconds, and aria-pressed on the caption toggle. Recipe 12 does all of that in about 40 lines and is still worse than the native set. The aria-valuetext line is the one that is always missing: Extracted from from apps/recipes/r12-media-viewer/index.html $("#seek").max = String(clip.seconds); $("#seek").value = String(at); // A range input announces its raw value, so a seek bar reads as "1601" to a // screen reader unless you say what the number means. This is the most // common defect in custom transports. $("#seek").setAttribute("aria-valuetext", `${clock(at)} of ${clock(clip.seconds)}`); A <input type="range"> announces its numeric value and nothing else, so a seek bar at eighty seconds reads as “80” with no unit and no total. The render harness asserts the announced string, which is the only way this stays fixed: the visible clock and the announced text are computed from the same clock function, so they cannot disagree. Pause when hidden. Chapter 15. Audio continuing from a frame nobody can see is genuinely alarming, and it is the fastest way to make a user close a conversation. Fullscreen goes through the host. ui/request-display-mode , not the Fullscreen API, because fullscreen is not in the extension’s permission set. Chapter 17. A thumbnail strip is a tab list. Give it roving tabindex, aria-current on the selected item, and real labels, and no image alt text that says “thumbnail”.

sections.t: Components III: Spatial, Media and Agent-Native
sections.x: An approval card is a rendering problem with a content problem underneath it. Recipe 10’s server sends five fields per request, and the card’s whole job is to make them readable in the order a person decides in: Extracted from from apps/recipes/r10-approval-center/server.js id: "refund-8841", title: "Refund 1,240.00 USD", risk: "high", at: "2026-08-18T09:12:00Z", description: "Refund invoice 2026-0814 to Meridian Systems in full.", consequence: "The money leaves today and cannot be recalled from here.", question: "Which invoices does this refund cover?", consequence and question are the two that separate this from a notification. The first says what becomes true and whether it is reversible; the second is a prompt the card can hand to the conversation, so a user who is not ready to approve has somewhere to go other than Deny. These five have no conventional web precedent because the situation they address is new: an interface with a second actor in it that the user cannot see and cannot interrupt. Each one exists to make some invisible part of that situation visible. Component Composes Where it appears Approval card approval.request , dialog.confirm , agent.contextUpdate Recipe 10 Tool status chip tool.invoke , op.progress , op.cancel , op.error Recipes 9, 11 Streaming log tool.partialOutput , input.selection , a11y.announce Recipe 9 Context inspector agent.contextUpdate , agent.boundary Every demonstration Proposal card ui.prefill , history.transaction , state.ownership Recipes 4, 7 The approval card is a heading, a consequence sentence, a <dl> of five provenance fields, and two buttons. Recipe 10 renders “asked by”, “on behalf of”, “tool”, “arguments” and “prior approvals”. High risk adds a second confirmDialog . Without those fields users learn to click through it. The tool status chip carries a name, one of five states, a progress value and exactly the controls that state allows. Queued has none. Running has Cancel. Failed has Retry. Cancelled and Done have neither. Recipe 11 puts the state name in text, not only in colour. The streaming log is the append-only list from Chapter 24 with the selection and follow behaviour that terminals taught everybody: follow the tail until the user scrolls up, then stop following and say so. Recipe 9 turns following off automatically when the user scrolls away from the bottom, which is the behaviour nobody notices when it is right. The context inspector shows what the view has published to the model. It is a debugging tool that deserves to ship. A user who can see that the assistant knows about three selected rows and nothing else can predict what it will say, and the same panel is how a developer finds out that their view has been publishing hover state for a week. Every demonstration in this book has one, in the form of the “Show what the model was told” control. The proposal card is the shape that makes agent editing safe. The agent’s version, visible next to the current one, with Accept and Decline, and accepting recorded as one undo transaction. Chapters 19 and 21 both arrive at it, from prefill and from conflict policy respectively, which is a decent sign that it is the right primitive.

sections.t: Components III: Spatial, Media and Agent-Native
sections.x: No reference implementation exists for any of these five, and no design system has a page about them, so here is a definition of done for each. They are all small; the difficulty is knowing what to include. Approval card. Renders a title, a risk level, a consequence sentence, and a provenance list of at least four fields. Approve and Deny are both single actions; high risk adds a confirmation. Every decision produces exactly one context update carrying the outcome and nothing else. It never accepts an approval over its own tool interface. Tool status chip. Carries a name, one of five states, a progress value when it has one, and exactly the controls that state allows. Queued has none. Running has Cancel. Failed has Retry. Cancelled and Done have neither. The state name is visible as text, not only as a colour. Streaming log. Appends, trims to a cap, and never rebuilds. Follows the tail until the user scrolls away, then stops and shows that it has stopped. Selection is by identifier so it survives the next thousand lines. Context inspector. Shows the last payload published to the model, verbatim, and says when nothing has been published. It is one control and about ten lines, and it is the fastest way to find out that a view has been leaking hover state for a week. Proposal card. Shows the agent’s version next to what is currently there, with Accept and Decline. Accepting is one undo transaction. The tool that created it returns “proposed, not applied”, so the agent does not report a change that has not happened.

sections.t: Components III: Spatial, Media and Agent-Native
sections.h: What all five have in common
sections.x: Every agent-native component makes an invisible thing visible. What the model was told. What it is doing. What it is proposing. What it wants permission for. What it has been told before. That is the design brief for this whole layer, and it comes out of the same constraint the rest of the book keeps hitting: the two parties cannot see each other. The user cannot see the model’s context. The model cannot see the screen. Components that surface one to the other are the ones that make an agentic interface feel like a place.

sections.t: Components III: Spatial, Media and Agent-Native
sections.x: A spatial surface reports a stable height rather than growing with its content. Every pointer gesture has a button or key equivalent. A drag produces one undo transaction, not one per pointer event. Media pauses when the frame is hidden. Immersive playback goes through ui/request-display-mode . An approval card renders provenance, and its decision produces exactly one context update. A streaming log appends and trims, and never rebuilds its container. Every agent-initiated change is announced once and is reversible. Previous 24. Components II: Navigation, Data and Visualization Next Recipe 1. Data Explorer

sections.t: Why Recipes Are the Test Suite
sections.x: Chapter 26 Capabilities pass in isolation and fail in composition. The thirteen applications exist to find out which, and the completeness test is what they answer. The recipes are the test suite, and being illustrations is a side effect. That ordering is the decision the rest of Part VI follows from, and it constrains what a recipe is allowed to be. A recipe whose behaviour depends on what a model happened to say cannot assert anything, so none of them depend on that: the model decides when a tool is called, and the recipe decides what the tool does.

sections.t: Why Recipes Are the Test Suite
sections.h: Why testing capabilities alone is not enough
sections.x: A host can implement every capability in Parts II and III correctly, one at a time, and still fail to run any of the recipes. Composition is where the failures live, and they are specific and repeatable: Focus fails inside fullscreen , because the mode change re-parented the frame and the browser dropped focus with it. Drag and drop conflicts with host scrolling , because the conversation scroller and your drag gesture want the same pointer. Shortcuts collide , because the host bound Cmd+F before your view existed and Chapter 10 has no mechanism to find out. Streaming updates destroy selection , because a view that rebuilds its list on each batch has a selection that lasts one batch. Resizing loses scroll position , because the frame changed height and the scroll container was measured against the old one. Cancellation leaves optimistic state behind , because the compensating action was never recorded. Every one of those is two capabilities that both work correctly on their own. A capability harness cannot find any of them, because it exercises one capability at a time and none of these failures exists inside one. Only a recipe puts two of them in the same frame, at the same moment, with a user in the middle doing something ordinary. The failure that reports nothing

sections.t: Why Recipes Are the Test Suite
sections.x: The question the recipes answer. Can a host construct conventional, native-like applications entirely from a small, well defined set of reusable UI capabilities? There are only two ways a recipe can fail, and both produce a finding. That is the property that makes the exercise worth the effort of building thirteen applications. If a recipe cannot be built from the primitives in Parts II and III, it has found a missing capability. Appendix B is where the sixteen current findings live, and Chapter 29 describes what turning one into a proposal involves. If a recipe can be built but does not run in a particular host, it has found a conformance failure. That is a finding about an implementation, and the checklist in Appendix C is what turns it into a bug report with a specific line in it. No third outcome exists. A recipe either cannot be expressed, which indicts the capability model, or can be expressed and does not run, which indicts an implementation. Both answers are more useful than a chapter arguing about whether the model is complete.

sections.t: Why Recipes Are the Test Suite
sections.h: Why an empty delta is fatal
sections.x: Every recipe carries a delta: the capabilities it exercises that no earlier recipe does, generated from the registry rather than asserted in prose. A recipe whose delta comes out empty gets merged or deleted, because it is teaching nothing and testing nothing that is not already covered. Thirteen recipes that each exercised the same twelve capabilities would demonstrate nothing about whether the model is sufficient. That rule is what stops thirteen recipes from being thirteen views of the same six capabilities. It is also what determined the order: the Data Explorer is first because its delta is the baseline, and Settings is last because its delta is the picker set and the accessibility requirements, which need everything before them to be in place. The deltas are generated from the registry rather than asserted in prose, so a recipe whose delta becomes empty because an earlier recipe grew will show it in the build output.

sections.t: Why Recipes Are the Test Suite
sections.x: Three kinds of assertion, in increasing order of what they catch and of how much work they are to write. The handshake happened. ui/initialize went out, a result came back, ui/notifications/initialized followed. This is the cheapest check in the whole suite and it catches the worst failure: a view with a syntax error never runs, so it never sends anything, so the frame sits there empty with nothing logged anywhere. Every demonstration in this book is checked for it, and it is the reason a missing handshake is a hard failure in the harness. Extracted from from tools/check_demos.mjs // The handshake, or nothing else matters. await waitFor(() => session.eval( `(() => { const rows = [...document.querySelectorAll('.demo-row .method')] .map(n => n.textContent); return rows.includes('ui/initialize') && rows.includes('ui/notifications/initialized'); })()`), 12000); It reads the transcript out of the page rather than instrumenting the bridge, which means it is checking the same thing a reader sees. The twelve second deadline is what turns “never sent” into a failure instead of a hang, and a timeout here is the signal that the view did not run at all. The observable behaviour is right. The table has eight rows. Sorting changes the order. Undo restores the node at its original index. These are ordinary assertions about a running application. Those are written as data, not as code, so a case is a list of selectors and expected values against the live DOM: Extracted from from conformance/render/r12-media-viewer.json { "label": "the gallery renders", "expect": [ { "selector": ".strip button", "count": 3 }, { "selector": "#clock", "text": "0:00 / 1:36" }, { "selector": "#frame", "attr": { "name": "aria-label", "value": "Assembly line, wide" } }, { "selector": "#caption", "hidden": true }, { "selector": "#seek", "attr": { "name": "aria-valuetext", "value": "0:00 of 1:36" } } ] }, Every value in that file came out of the recipe’s real server, and the last line asserts an accessible name that no screenshot would ever show. A reader can check any of them by opening the same page, and changing the interface without changing the entry fails the build. The transcript is right. Selecting a row sent exactly one ui/update-model-context . Selecting a second one replaced the first. Withdrawing downloadFile means no ui/download-file is ever sent. This is the layer that catches protocol regressions, and it is the layer that only exists because the whole conversation is JSON-RPC over postMessage and therefore recordable.

sections.t: Why Recipes Are the Test Suite
sections.h: How is any of this deterministic?
sections.x: An agentic application looks untestable at first glance. A model is involved, models are stochastic, and an assertion about a sampled token is not an assertion at all. Every test in this repository would be flaky if the model were in the loop. The way out is that the model is never in the loop of a recipe test. Every tool result is a recorded fixture. Every stream is a scripted sequence. Every failure is injected on purpose. The agent’s side is played by the harness calling the view’s registered tools, which is exactly what an agent would do and is completely deterministic. That is a design constraint on the recipes themselves, not just on the tests. A recipe whose behaviour depends on what a model happened to say cannot be a test, so the recipes are built so that it does not. The model decides when to call connect_steps ; the recipe decides what connect_steps does. Chapter 4’s local-first principle turns out to be the same rule as testability, which is a good sign that it is the right rule.

sections.t: Why Recipes Are the Test Suite
sections.x: The exercise is only worth anything if it produced findings, so here are the ones building thirteen applications against eighty-nine capabilities turned up. None of them was predicted from reading the specification. An empty red banner, visible in the Data Explorer. The error element had the hidden attribute set and was displayed anyway, because an author rule with a class selector beats the user agent’s [hidden] rule. Every component in the shared stylesheet that sets display had the same defect. Found by looking at a screenshot, fixed with one declaration, and the comment explaining it is still in apps/lib/view.css . A transcript that changed on every run. The workflow builder minted node ids from Date.now() , and those ids travel to the agent in a tool result, so the recorded transcript differed every time the suite ran. The fix was a counter. The finding is that anything reaching the wire has to be deterministic or the whole of Layer 1 is noise. Module scripts do not load from an opaque origin. The first version of the view bridge was an ES module, which is a CORS request from a sandboxed frame, which a static file host will not answer. It is a classic script now, and the reason is a comment at the top of the file. Dynamic import resolves against the module, not the page. The demo widget loaded each demonstration’s fixture with a relative specifier and got a 404 on every page except the harness. Both of these are the kind of thing that is obvious once seen and costs an hour when not. Half a theme is worse than none. Applying host style variables without removing the ones the host has stopped sending leaves the previous theme’s overrides in place, so a view that switches from a dark host to a bare one is unreadable. The specification warns about partial variable sets; this is the same hazard from the view’s side, and the bridge now tracks and clears what it applied. A spreadsheet full of #VALUE . Every text cell rendered as an error, because the evaluator passed its contents through Number() and the view rendered the resulting NaN . It had been that way in every screenshot and nobody had looked at the top-left cell. Accepting the agent’s rewrite could not be undone. Recipe 4 recorded its transaction by comparing the document against itself, which it did before replacing the text, so the comparison found no change and pushed nothing. One undo did not restore the human’s words. This is the safety property Chapters 15 and 20 both argue is the whole reason it is acceptable to let a model edit a document, and the recipe asserting it did not have it. The monitoring console showed every line twice. It received the tool result it was rendered for and also called the tool itself on mount, so two rows shared an identifier and selecting one selected both. Eight findings, seven of them in shipped code. The last three are the interesting ones, because they were invisible to every check that existed before: the messages were all correct, and the interface was wrong. They came from the layer described in the next chapter, which starts a real server, renders the view that server delivers, and then looks at the result.

sections.t: Why Recipes Are the Test Suite
sections.x: Two things this suite cannot do, both of which limit what the rest of Part VI is entitled to claim. It cannot drive the view’s own interface from outside. The frame is sandboxed with an opaque origin and the harness cannot reach its DOM, which is the same property that stops a host reading it. So view-initiated behaviour is driven through the tools a view registers, which covers the recipes that register tools and does not cover the ones that do not. Chapter 27 says exactly which. And it cannot tell you whether an application is any good. Every check in this book is about whether a thing works, not about whether it should exist. Chapter 4 is the only defence against building a well tested application that nobody wants, and it is not a test. Previous Recipe 13. Settings and Preferences Next 27. The Verification Layers

Chapter 27 Six layers, from a schema to a cross-host dashboard, and an honest account of which of them this repository actually runs. Six layers, because the failures are layered. A malformed message, an inaccessible combobox and a host that ignores display mode requests are three different problems, they are discovered by three different kinds of machinery, and no single check finds all three. A suite with one layer therefore has a blind spot the size of the other five, and the usual missing layer is the one that looks at pixels. Five of the six run here. The sixth needs hosts this repository does not control, and it is the one that would matter most. For each layer this chapter says what this repository runs today and what it does not. The second half matters: describing an aspirational test pyramid and shipping none of it is exactly what Chapter 26 argues against.

Capability manifests and every bridge message validate against JSON Schemas derived from the extension specification, so nothing untyped ships. This is the cheapest layer to build and the one that catches the errors nobody notices: a field renamed in a draft, a message shape that drifted, an identifier that exists in the prose and nowhere else. What runs here. The registry is generated from a single Python source and every downstream artifact reads the generated JSON, so an identifier that exists in one place and not another is impossible by construction. tools/check_claims.py goes further and greps the pinned specification text for every message name the registry claims exists: seventy-one claims, checked on every build. That check has already earned itself. It reports which anchors exist in the current draft but not in the last dated release, and the answer is eight: ui/download-file , downloadFile , ui/notifications/request-teardown , updateModelContext , sampling/createMessage , notifications/tools/list_changed , resource_link and isError . A book that did not check would have described all eight as though they were settled. What does not run. Full JSON Schema validation of every message against the SDK’s generated schema. The bridge here validates shape by construction.

Because every message is JSON-RPC over postMessage , a scenario can be replayed and its message log diffed. That is a stronger property than it sounds: the wire is the whole interface between a view and its host, so a transcript that has not changed is a view that behaves identically from the host’s side. A transcript diff in a pull request is a protocol change somebody has to explain. What runs here. tools/check_demos.mjs drives all thirty demonstrations in headless Chrome over the DevTools Protocol, waits for the handshake, clicks every host control in order, and records the normalised message log to conformance/transcripts/ . Timings and request ids are stripped, object keys are sorted, and the result is compared byte for byte with the committed file. A missing handshake is a hard failure, for the reason Chapter 26 gives: a view that never sends ui/initialize is a view whose script never ran, and nothing else about it can be meaningfully checked. Any console error that is not a missing favicon fails the run as well.

One minimal application per capability group, driven inside a reference host, with assertions on both the observable behaviour and the message log. The point of keeping them minimal is diagnostic: when a lab fails there is one capability in it, so the failure names itself. What runs here. The seventeen labs are that harness. Each exercises a single chapter’s capabilities, carries a fixture host with controls for the things only a host can do, and has a recorded transcript that the build diffs. Keeping each lab one chapter wide is what makes a failure legible: when one breaks, the set of things that could have broken it is small enough to read. What does not. They run against the emulator in this repository, not against the basic-host that ships with the official SDK. Running the same labs against that host is the obvious next step and would convert a set of assertions about this book’s host into assertions about a reference one.

An axe-core audit of every recipe, run inside the sandboxed frame after the interactions rather than on load, so it sees the interface the interactions produced. axe-core is vendored into tools/vendor/ rather than installed, because this repository has no npm dependencies and an accessibility audit is a poor reason to acquire the first one. Rules that assume a page are disabled by name, with a reason each. A view is a fragment inside somebody else’s document. The host owns <main> , the landmark structure and the heading outline, so landmark-one-main , page-has-heading-one and region are not defects here; a view that declared its own <main> would be adding a second one to the host’s page. The list is four rules long and each carries its reason in the source, which is a different thing from a suppression file nobody reads. Anything else that fires fails the build, and a per-case allowance that stops firing also fails, so an allowance cannot quietly outlive the defect it excused. What it found on the first run. Five defects across four recipes. The monitoring console put aria-selected on plain div elements, which no role there permits, and its scrolling log had no keyboard focus. The diff reviewer’s line numbers were under 4.5:1 against the tinted add and delete rows. The spreadsheet’s corner cell was an empty column header. And the image annotator’s labels used a fixed white on a background the user picks, so any light annotation colour produced unreadable text; that one is now computed from the chosen colour’s relative luminance. What still does not run. The components are a shared stylesheet and helper file, and there is no component library with stories, so each component is audited only in the recipes that use it. Screen reader output was walked by hand and is recorded per recipe rather than claimed in aggregate here, because no automated tool reports what a screen reader actually says.

Reaching into a frame with an opaque origin needs one Chrome DevTools Protocol call, and without flatten: true the sandboxed frame’s execution context is not addressable at all: Extracted from from tools/check_render.mjs await browser.send("Target.setAutoAttach", { autoAttach: true, waitForDebuggerOnStart: false, flatten: true }); await browser.send("Page.enable"); await browser.send("Runtime.enable"); That the harness has to go outside the page to see inside the frame is the same fact Chapter 5 states as a security property. The sandbox is doing its job; a test is simply another party the boundary keeps out, and the way in is a debugger rather than a hole in the sandbox. The layer the first edition of this suite did not have, and the one the book is actually about. Everything above verifies messages. This verifies the interface the messages produce, which is the thing a user sees and the thing none of the other layers can observe. It found four defects on its first run, and three of them were invisible to every message-level check in the suite. For each of the thirteen recipes, tools/check_render.mjs runs the whole chain with no recording anywhere in it. Six steps, and the fourth is the one that makes the rest meaningful: Start the recipe’s MCP server as a child process over stdio. Perform the host’s initialize , declaring the UI extension, so a server is free to register different tools when it is absent. Call tools/list and read _meta.ui.resourceUri off the tool. Fetch the view’s HTML through resources/read . That is what the frame renders. Nothing is read from apps/ or from the built site. Call the tool. Deliver the arguments and result as notifications. Proxy the view’s own tools/call back to the same server, and forward that server’s progress notifications onward. Then it asserts on the DOM inside the sandboxed frame: row counts, cell text, which element carries aria-current , whether the error banner is hidden. 124 assertions across the thirteen recipes, followed by an axe-core audit of each. Reaching inside that frame at all takes Target.setAutoAttach with flatten: true , because the frame has an opaque origin and no ordinary evaluation crosses into it, which is the same boundary Chapter 5 describes doing its job. Captured output from node tools/check_render.mjs r01-data-explorer: 18 assertion(s) on rendered output r04-document-editor: 12 assertion(s) on rendered output r07-workflow-builder: 15 assertion(s) on rendered output 13 case(s), 108 assertion(s) against real servers, 13 audited by axe-core, 0 failing No model appears in those six steps. A host connects to servers, allocates surfaces and mediates privileged operations, and none of that requires an LLM. A host driven by conformance/render/r01-data-explorer.json is the same architecture as a host driven by a person, which is why the surface is testable at all. How it reads into the frame. Over the DevTools Protocol, not from page script. Page script cannot: the frame has an opaque origin, which is precisely the property that stops a host reading a view, and Chapter 5 is about why that is correct. A debugger is not page script, and attaching to the child frame gives a session that can evaluate inside it. The sandbox that ships is not weakened; the harness is simply outside the model the sandbox defends against. That also closes a limitation this chapter used to state. The harness can click inside the view, so a recipe no longer has to register tools in order to be driven. Cases in conformance/render/ interleave three kinds of step: a click inside the frame, a call to one of the view’s registered tools, and a change to the host context, each followed by assertions.

Each recipe end to end against a scripted mock agent, with recorded tool results, deterministic streaming and deliberate fault injection. The fault injection is the part that earns its keep: capabilities withdrawn mid-session, servers that fail, calls cancelled halfway, teardown with unsaved work. What runs here.
