All thirteen recipes are driven by the same harness as the labs, with fixtures recorded from their real servers by tools/record_fixtures.mjs . The fault injection is real: controls that break the server, withdraw capabilities, cancel mid-flight, and tear the view down are part of every recipe’s demonstration and are exercised by the harness. What each of the two browser layers covers. The transcript layer drives the published demonstrations from the host side, which is what verifies the message log. The render layer drives the recipes from a live server and reaches inside the frame, which is what verifies the interface. Between them a recipe is checked on both halves of the promise it makes. Registering tools is still worth doing, and Chapter 19 gives three reasons that survive: an agent can drive the view, an accessibility tool can drive it, and a test can express an intention. A case that calls connect_steps says what it means; a case that clicks a coordinate says where a button happened to be.

The same suite run against several hosts, with results published per host and per capability the way the public web platform test dashboards do it. That format matters as much as the results: a per-feature, per-implementation grid is what lets somebody write portable code without guessing. What does not run. Nothing. This book runs against one emulator. The basic-host in the extension SDK, the MCP-UI client, and the production hosts that implement the standard are all candidates, and the checklists in Appendix C are written so that they could be run against any of them. The reason this matters more than the missing Layer 3 is that cross-host results are the only evidence that would answer the completeness test in Chapter 26. One host running thirteen recipes proves the recipes work. Several hosts running them unmodified proves the capability model is general, which is the claim the whole book is making.

node tools/check_demos.mjs starts a static server over docs/ , launches headless Chrome, and for each of the thirty demonstrations opens the harness page, waits for ui/initialize and ui/notifications/initialized to appear in the log, clicks every host control in order with time to settle, and then reads the transcript back out of the DOM. The log is normalised before comparison: request ids and timings are dropped because they vary, and object keys are sorted because insertion order is not meaningful. What is left is a list of direction, method and payload, which is the part that is supposed to be stable. Captured output from node tools/check_demos.mjs lab-surface: 10 messages lab-theme: 11 messages r01-data-explorer: 9 messages r07-workflow-builder: 20 messages r13-settings: 11 messages 30 demos driven, 0 transcripts written, 0 failing “0 transcripts written” is the assertion. The harness runs in a mode where a matching transcript writes nothing, so a demonstration whose behaviour changed fails the run and leaves the diff of its transcript file as the description of what the change actually was. Regenerating is a deliberate command, which keeps an accidental behaviour change from silently becoming the new baseline.

sections.h: The checks that are not about the protocol
sections.x: Four more checks run on every build, and between them they catch a class of error that no browser test can see: prose that has drifted from the code, the specification, or the repository it describes. check_refs.py verifies that every figure the prose asks for exists, that every capability in the registry has exactly one defining entry, and that every @demo names a directory that is really there. It found the missing tool.cancel entry. check_listings.py takes every code block tagged extracted from a file and checks it against that file line by line. It found two listings that had been quietly abridged and presented as extracted, which is the specific failure mode of a book that quotes its own repository: the code was real when it was copied, somebody shortened it for the page, and nothing anywhere recorded that the two had diverged. check_counts.py recomputes every number the prose asserts about the repository and fails when the prose disagrees. It found the Core capability count wrong in Chapter 1, which had been written from an estimate, and it found the level 3 total wrong in two appendices after a capability moved between levels. Both are the kind of error that no reader would catch and every reader would be misled by. check_identifiers.py pulls every protocol identifier out of the prose and requires it to appear in the pinned specification, the SDK, or this repository’s own source. Two hundred and three identifiers, and the reason it exists is that a plausible-looking field name reads as a fact and is not one.

sections.h: The layer that is not on the list
sections.x: Human usability sessions. None were run for this edition, and none of the design claims here are backed by watching somebody use these applications. The recipes are built to a set of principles with arguments behind them, and the arguments could be wrong in ways no automated check would detect. That is the largest single gap in this book’s evidence, larger than Layers 3 and 5 combined, because those two would confirm that the applications work while this one would tell you whether they should exist in that shape at all. Previous 26. Why Recipes Are the Test Suite Next 28. The Coverage Matrix and the Checklists

sections.t: The Coverage Matrix and the Checklists
sections.x: Chapter 28 What eighty-nine capabilities by thirteen recipes actually shows, why the matrix is generated, and what a host is claiming when it claims a level. Two artifacts come out of the registry on every build, and both are more useful as diagnostics of the book than as references for a reader. A row of the matrix with no marks in it is a capability this book described and never demonstrated, which is a gap in the evidence, and it is visible only because the matrix is generated rather than written.

sections.t: The Coverage Matrix and the Checklists
sections.x: Appendix A carries the full capability by recipe matrix. It is generated from the registry, never hand-maintained, and reading down a column tells you what a recipe needs while reading across a row tells you how well covered a capability is. The extremes are where the matrix says something. The middle of it is unsurprising and mostly confirms that recipes use the capabilities their entries say they use. Rows with no marks at all. A capability that no recipe exercises is a capability this book has described and not demonstrated. There are several, and they cluster: op.pause , system.print , and the environment signals that have no visible consequence in a small view. Each is either genuinely rare or a recipe that should exist and does not. Rows with a mark everywhere. surface.resize , env.theme and host.capabilities are in every recipe, which is what “Level 1” means in practice. If a host gets those three wrong, nothing in Part V renders. Columns that are unusually short. A recipe that touches few capabilities is either focused or thin. Recipe 5’s column is short and it is focused; Recipe 2’s is short and could carry more. The delta diagonal. Reading the deltas in order shows the book’s argument as a shape: the first recipe claims sixteen capabilities, and by the thirteenth the deltas are down to a handful each. That taper is the evidence for the completeness claim. If the thirteenth recipe still needed six new primitives, the model would not be converging.

sections.t: The Coverage Matrix and the Checklists
sections.x: A hand-maintained matrix is wrong within a week and nobody notices, because nothing reads it. A generated one is wrong only if the registry is wrong, and the registry is what everything else reads. The generation also enables checks that a document cannot make. The build reports capabilities with no entry in any chapter, which is how the missing tool.cancel entry in Chapter 20 was found. It could equally fail on a Core capability with no covering recipe, which is the check a mature version of this suite would run in CI. The matrix itself is twelve lines. Every cell is a set membership test against the registry, so a mark on the page means a recipe declared that capability and nothing else can put one there: Extracted from from tools/build_site.py def matrix_block() -> str: recipes = REGISTRY["recipes"] head = "".join(f'{html.escape(r["name"])}' for r in recipes) rows = [] for cap in REGISTRY["capabilities"]: cells = "".join( f'' f'{"✕" if r["id"] in cap["recipes"] else ""}' for r in recipes) rows.append(f'' f'{cap["id"]}{cells}') The check that found tool.cancel is four lines in a different file, and it runs on every build: Extracted from from tools/check_refs.py for cap in sorted(CAPS - set(seen_caps)): problems.append(f"capability {cap} has no entry in " f"{CAP_CHAPTER[cap]}") A registry that names a capability the prose never explains is a book with a badge and no entry behind it, which is the failure a generated artifact makes easy to introduce and easy to catch. Capabilities per level, split by where they come from

sections.t: The Coverage Matrix and the Checklists
sections.x: Appendix C turns each level into a checklist of observable behaviours. The translation from capability to check is mechanical, and the phrasing is deliberately in the form an assertion takes. A host claiming Level 1 is claiming that a view renders, that ui/notifications/size-changed resizes the frame, that hostContext carries a theme and a locale, that ui/open-link works or is honestly absent from hostCapabilities , and that ui/initialize returns a capability set that matches what the host will actually do. That last clause fails most often, so state it as a rule. A capability advertised and not implemented is worse than one never advertised. A host that lists downloadFile and then ignores ui/download-file breaks every view that checked hostCapabilities and rewards every view that did not. Level 2 adds the interactive set, and the checks are mostly about the host staying out of the way: that keyboard events reach the frame, that the frame’s focus ring is not clipped by host styling, that a context menu inside the frame is not shadowed by the host’s own. Level 3 is where hosts diverge most. Display modes, lifecycle signals, and the persistence gap all live here, and a host can be excellent at Levels 1 and 2 while implementing none of Level 3. That is a legitimate position for a host whose views are all cards. Level 4 is the agentic set, and it has the largest gap between what the checklist asks and what the specification provides. Ten Core capabilities across all levels have no standard mechanism, and Appendix C marks each of them, because a checklist that asked hosts to implement something unspecified would be worthless.

sections.t: The Coverage Matrix and the Checklists
sections.h: If you are building a host
sections.x: The useful order is not top to bottom. It is: Make the handshake truthful. Every other recommendation in this book assumes it. A capability listed in hostCapabilities and not implemented breaks precisely the views that checked properly and rewards the ones that never checked. Get surface.resize right , including the zero-height first render. More views look broken because of this than because of anything else in the protocol. Get ui/resource-teardown right , including waiting for the response. This is the only data-loss defect in the protocol that a view cannot work around. Then work down the levels , and publish which one you pass with the date of the run. That order is not the order of the checklist, and it is deliberately not the order of the levels. Those three come first because a failure in any of them makes the levels above meaningless: a view that never sized itself correctly does not care how good your display mode support is.

sections.t: The Coverage Matrix and the Checklists
sections.h: If you are building an application
sections.x: The order is different. Assume Level 1, check for everything above it, and make the check the thing that decides whether a control exists. Then use the failure column of the recipe entries in Part V as a design prompt. Every one of those tables was written by asking, for each capability, what the application looks like without it. That exercise takes an hour and produces most of the progressive enhancement work you were going to do anyway, before the code makes it expensive.

sections.t: The Coverage Matrix and the Checklists
sections.x: The delta column is the load-bearing part of the matrix, and reading it in recipe order is the closest thing this book has to evidence for its own premise. Recipe 1 claims sixteen capabilities, because it is the baseline: a table, a selection, an export, an escalation. Recipes 2 and 3 add roughly a dozen each, because monitoring and hierarchy are genuinely different surfaces. By Recipe 7 the deltas are down to three or four, and by Recipes 11 to 13 most of what each one needs is already in the model. That taper is what convergence looks like. If the thirteenth recipe still needed six new primitives, the honest conclusion would be that eighty-nine is not enough and the model is still growing. It does not, which is weak evidence that the surface has been covered. Weak, and worth being precise about why. The recipes were written by the same person who wrote the capability list, against one emulator, in one sitting. Convergence under those conditions could equally mean the recipes were chosen to fit. The test that would settle it is Layer 5 from Chapter 27: someone else’s application, someone else’s host, and a delta that still comes out small.

sections.t: The Coverage Matrix and the Checklists
sections.h: The matrix is evidence, not proof
sections.x: One last use. The matrix is the closest thing this book has to a proof, and it is not one. What it shows is that thirteen recognisable applications were built from eighty-nine named primitives, that the primitives were sufficient for all thirteen, and that sixteen of them had to be worked around because no mechanism exists. That is evidence for the completeness test in Chapter 26 and not an answer to it. The answer needs Layer 5 from Chapter 27: the same recipes, unmodified, running in hosts that were not built alongside them.

sections.t: The Coverage Matrix and the Checklists
sections.h: Using this on your own project
sections.x: The exercise transfers, and it is cheap. Take your application, list the interactions it has, and map each one to a capability identifier from Appendix A. Three things fall out within an hour. The host dependency list. Everything you mapped to a wire capability is something a host has to support, and the level column tells you which hosts those are. That list is what you test against, and it is usually shorter than people fear. The gap list. Anything you mapped to a not standardised capability is a place where you are about to invent a private convention. Better to know before the code than after the second host. The work list. Everything mapped to yours to build is real engineering that no protocol will do for you, and it is typically the largest of the three. Undo, dialogs, toasts and the whole attention system live here. An interaction that maps to nothing is the interesting case. Either you have found something the eighty-nine do not cover, which belongs upstream as a finding, or you have described an interaction in terms of your implementation, and never what the user does. Chapter 29 is about telling those two apart. Previous 27. The Verification Layers Next 29. The Missing Primitive Loop, and the Live Book

sections.t: The Missing Primitive Loop, and the Live Book
sections.x: Chapter 29 How a gap gets found, what a good proposal looks like, and how a static site runs thirty applications next to their own source without hosting anything. Two subjects in one chapter, because the second is what makes the first credible. A list of missing capabilities is an opinion until somebody can run the applications that needed them and watch the workaround happen. Anyone can assert that sixteen capabilities are missing. A book whose demonstrations run in your browser, with transcripts showing exactly where each workaround happens, has shown you. Appendix B names the recipe behind every one of the sixteen, and every one of those recipes is on this site with its message log open, so the sentence “there is no message for this” is checkable in the place it is made.

sections.t: The Missing Primitive Loop, and the Live Book
sections.x: Primitives compose into components. Components compose into applications. Applications become coverage tests. A test that cannot be written names a missing primitive. The last step is the one that does the work. A conformance check is a sentence about observable behaviour, and a sentence you cannot phrase without inventing a message is a gap with a name attached. The loop only works in that direction. Starting from “what should the protocol have” produces a wish list. Starting from “build the thirteen applications people actually ask for” produces sixteen findings, each attached to a recipe that needs it and a workaround somebody had to write. Every gap in this book arrived that way. state.save was found by the Document Editor needing to survive a reload. tool.partialOutput was found by the Monitoring Console needing a log tail. notify.attention was found by an error arriving at three in the morning in a view nobody was looking at. approval.request was found by asking what the Approve button actually guarantees, and finding that the answer is nothing.

sections.t: The Missing Primitive Loop, and the Live Book
sections.x: Four parts, and Appendix B carries all four for each of the sixteen gaps. A finding missing any of them is a complaint: the recipe pins it to something real, the cost stops it being a wish, the mechanism makes it arguable, and the threat-model note is what stops it being naive. The recipe that needs it. Not a hypothetical. A named application, in this repository, that a reader can run. What the workaround costs. Every gap has one, and stating the cost is what separates a finding from a complaint. Persistence through a server tool costs a round trip and stops working at Level 1. Streaming through repeated tool results costs portability. Approval through a queue-and-perform convention costs the guarantee. A concrete mechanism. One request, one notification, or one context field, specific enough to argue with: ui/set-view-state plus a viewState field in the initialize result; a visibility field on ui/notifications/host-context-changed ; ui/request-attention with a severity and a label. What it reopens. Chapter 5’s threat model, applied to the proposal. A mechanism that reopens one of the five attacks needs a better story than convenience, and saying which attack in the proposal saves everybody an argument later.

sections.t: The Missing Primitive Loop, and the Live Book
sections.x: Upstream, as issues against the extension specification. A host-specific mechanism for view state solves the problem for one host and fragments it for everybody else, which is exactly the outcome this extension was created to prevent. The counter-argument is real: sometimes a host has to ship something before a specification exists. The mitigation is to ship it as an experimental capability, which both hostCapabilities and appCapabilities already reserve a slot for, and to file the finding at the same time.

sections.t: The Missing Primitive Loop, and the Live Book
sections.x: Everything on these pages runs, and the arrangement behind it is simpler than it looks. There is no backend, no build server and no runtime: the whole site is static files served by GitHub Pages, which is possible only because an MCP application needs neither a model nor a server in order to render. What it needs is something willing to answer the host side of a postMessage conversation, and that fits in 250 lines of JavaScript. One source tree, three views of it. The application is executed, in a sandboxed iframe. Its source is read, fetched from the same directory the iframe loaded it from. And the conversation between them is narrated, in the transcript pane, as it happens. The code pane cannot drift from the running code, because they are the same file over the same URL. That is the entire mechanism, and it replaces a build step that extracts listings and a discipline that keeps them current. The host is an emulator, not a mock. About two hundred and fifty lines implementing the host half of the bridge: it answers ui/initialize , applies capability rules, resolves tools/call from fixtures, honours resize requests, arbitrates display modes, and tees every message to the log. It is a real host implementation with a fixture file where a server would be, and the capability checks in it are the same checks a real host makes. Resolving a view is the part worth reading, because it is the sequence Chapter 3 describes and nothing about it is simulated: Extracted from from emulator/host.js const uri = descriptor?._meta?.ui?.resourceUri; if (!uri) { throw new Error(`${toolName} has no _meta.ui.resourceUri, so a host has ` + "nothing to render"); } The view is never named by anyone. The host looks up the tool the model called, reads the binding off its descriptor, and reads that resource. A tool without the field is not an error condition to recover from; it is an ordinary tool, and the host renders its text. The fixtures come from real servers. tools/record_fixtures.mjs starts each recipe’s actual MCP server over stdio, calls the tools listed in its record.json , and writes the responses to fixtures.json . So the sentence this book makes is true: the view in the live pane receives what the code in the server pane produces. The demonstration is honest even though the server is not executing in your browser. Everything regenerates. make rebuilds the pages, make fixtures re-records the server responses, and make check runs the ten checks Chapter 27 describes. A contributor who changes a recipe’s server and forgets to re-record gets a fixture diff in the same commit, and a contributor who changes a recipe’s behaviour and forgets to update its entry gets a transcript diff. Neither failure can reach the published site quietly.

sections.t: The Missing Primitive Loop, and the Live Book
sections.x: The thirty demonstrations on this site are two different things, and the difference matters when you read their transcripts. One group starts before the view exists and shows you how it came to exist. The other starts at the moment the view is already loaded, because what it has to show happens after that point and a prologue would be theatre. The thirteen recipes model the whole lifecycle. Each has a real MCP server with a ui:// resource and a tool carrying _meta.ui.resourceUri . The host emulator resolves the view the way a host does: tools/list , read the resource URI off the descriptor, resources/read , render what comes back. Their transcripts open with four host-to-server lines before the view has run a single statement, and the frame above them is rendering the document that arrived on line four. The seventeen capability labs start after the binding. They have no server, no tool and no resource, because each exists to demonstrate one chapter’s capabilities. Chapter 7’s lab is about ui/notifications/size-changed , and prefixing it with a tool call it does not have would be scenery. Their transcripts open at ui/initialize . That split is deliberate, and stating it is the point: a lab that loaded itself by URL while the book insisted hosts never know a URL would be the same defect this chapter exists to guard against.

sections.t: The Missing Primitive Loop, and the Live Book
sections.h: What the transcript pane is for
sections.x: It is a teaching device and a test artifact at the same time, and the second use is what keeps the first honest. The log you see on a page is the same log tools/check_demos.mjs records into conformance/transcripts/ when it drives the same page in headless Chrome, so Layer 1 of Chapter 27 is literally the thing on screen. When a recipe entry says “selecting a row sends exactly one ui/update-model-context ”, you can verify it by selecting a row, and the build verifies it by diffing a file. A pane that only illustrated would drift within a month; this one cannot, because a drift is a failing build.

sections.t: The Missing Primitive Loop, and the Live Book
sections.x: The claim that these demonstrations are honest rests on one chain, and the chain is short enough to state completely and check yourself. It has four links: a real server, a recorder that runs it, a fixture file nobody edits, and a host configuration that reads only that file. Break any link and the numbers on the page stop corresponding to the code in the tab beside them, which is why each link has a check behind it. Each recipe has a server.js that is a real MCP server over stdio. It answers initialize by declaring the UI extension, tools/list with descriptors carrying _meta.ui.resourceUri , tools/call by running the tool, and resources/read by returning the view’s HTML with its content security policy attached. tools/record_fixtures.mjs starts that server as a child process, sends the calls listed in the recipe’s record.json , and writes the responses to fixtures.json . Nothing in that file is hand-written and nothing is edited afterwards, and make fixtures regenerates all thirteen on every build, so a server whose output changes produces a fixture diff in the same commit. The whole recorder is one handshake and a loop over the plan: Extracted from from tools/record_fixtures.mjs const write = (message) => child.stdin.write(`${JSON.stringify(message)}\n`); write({ jsonrpc: "2.0", id: 0, method: "initialize", params: { protocolVersion: "2026-07-28", clientInfo: { name: "fixture-recorder", version: "1.0.0" }, capabilities: { extensions: { "io.modelcontextprotocol/ui": { mimeTypes: ["text/html;profile=mcp-app"] } } }, } }); calls.forEach((call, i) => write({ jsonrpc: "2.0", id: i + 1, method: "tools/call", params: { name: call.tool, arguments: call.arguments ?? {} }, })); Newline-delimited JSON over the child process’s stdin, which is exactly what a host does over stdio. The recorder declares the UI extension in its initialize so the server answers as it would to a real host, and there is no mode flag anywhere in a recipe’s server that behaves differently under recording. The demonstration’s host configuration imports fixtures.json and answers tools/call from it. So when the Data Explorer renders eight deployments with a worst p95 of 1290ms, those numbers came out of the server whose source is in the next tab. What is not true is that the server is running in your browser. It is not, and it could not be: a static site has no process to run it in. The fixture is a recording, and the check that keeps the recording current is that make fixtures regenerates it from the server on every build.

sections.t: The Missing Primitive Loop, and the Live Book
sections.x: The suite is deliberately unexotic, and porting it to another host is smaller than it looks. The demonstrations do not depend on the emulator’s internals. They depend on a host that answers ui/initialize , applies capability rules honestly, and can be told to do host-side things on command: change the container, withdraw a display mode, deliver a tool result, start a teardown. Any host with a development mode can expose those four, and a host that cannot withdraw a display mode on command cannot be tested against Chapter 7 by anybody, including its own authors. The harness depends on three things: a page it can load, a way to observe the message log, and a way to click host-side controls. In this repository the log is in the DOM because the demo widget puts it there, and check_demos.mjs reads it with a page.evaluate call. In another host it would more likely be a hook that receives every message, which is easier: reading structured objects out of a callback beats scraping list items out of a page, and it removes the one part of this harness that is coupled to how the book is presented. What does not port, and is the honest limit from Chapter 27, is driving the view’s own interface. That needs either the view’s registered tools or a host willing to grant allow-same-origin in a test configuration, and the first is the better answer because it is the same mechanism agents and accessibility tools use.

sections.t: The Missing Primitive Loop, and the Live Book
sections.x: Three things to do once, in any demonstration on this site. Between them they make the whole architecture visible in about a minute, they need nothing installed, and they work in whatever browser you are already reading this in. Do them on Recipe 1 if you want the fullest version, because it is the only one that exercises all four host-to-server lines and then renders eight rows from the result. Open Messages and reload the view. Watch ui/initialize go out, the result come back with hostCapabilities and hostContext in it, ui/notifications/initialized follow, and then ui/notifications/size-changed carrying the height the document turned out to need. Four lines, in that order, and every MCP application on any host starts the same way. Nothing after line four is guaranteed by the specification. Press a control in the grey strip. Those are the things only a host can do, which is why they sit outside the frame: resizing the container, changing the theme, withdrawing a capability, delivering a tool result. The page does them on the host’s behalf, and each one produces a message you can expand and read in full, including the ones your view is expected to ignore. Then open the index.html tab and find the code that handled it. The file the tab shows is the file the frame above is running, fetched from the same URL, which is the one guarantee that makes a book about a protocol worth reading two months after it was written.

sections.t: The Missing Primitive Loop, and the Live Book
sections.h: What this book does not do
sections.x: Two escalations beyond what is here exist, and neither is built. Both would make the demonstrations editable in the browser instead of merely runnable, and both are additive: neither changes anything the book claims, and neither is a prerequisite for anything in it. They are listed because the absence is a choice, and a reader who wants either now can build it without waiting for this book to change. Small client-only examples can be made editable in place with an in-browser bundler, so a reader can change app.tsx and watch the iframe re-render. That needs a custom template carrying the bridge shim, and it is the obvious next step for the labs. Full server-plus-view examples can open in a browser-based Node runtime, which boots the actual MCP server in a tab and runs it against a real host. That is how the extension’s own examples run locally against its reference host, and it would turn the recipes from demonstrations into things a reader can fork without installing anything. Neither is here. What is here is thirty applications that run, their sources, their transcripts, and a repository where all of it regenerates with one command. That was the smallest thing that could make a book about a protocol checkable, and checkable was the requirement. Previous 28. The Coverage Matrix and the Checklists Next Appendix A. Capability Index
The four layers, the vocabulary, the labels on every entry, and the one question the whole book is trying to answer.

The four layers, and the direction each part of the book travels through them The book has one shape and it repeats at every scale. Atomic capability. The smallest independently useful operation, with a namespaced identifier. surface.resize . input.selection . tool.invoke . Flat names are not used, because the namespace is what makes the index navigable once there are eighty of them. Reusable component. Capabilities composed into something with a name a designer would recognise. A combobox is input.keyboard plus input.selection plus focus management plus an ARIA pattern. A component entry lists which capabilities it composes, which agent interactions it participates in, and which Authoring Practices Guide pattern governs its keyboard behaviour. Application recipe. Components composed into an application: a data explorer, a spreadsheet, an approval queue. Each recipe declares a capability delta , the primitives it exercises that no earlier recipe does. A recipe with an empty delta gets merged or deleted, because it is not teaching anything and not testing anything. Capability validation. The recipes run as tests. A host either passes them or does not, and the coverage matrix in Appendix A is generated from the test annotations.

Host The application the user is actually in: a chat client, an IDE, a console. It connects to MCP servers, allocates surfaces, and mediates everything privileged. There is no way around it and no way to see past it. Surface The region the host gives your application. Inline card, side panel, modal, fullscreen. You do not own it, you are lent it, and the terms change without warning. Application, or view The UI your server delivers as a ui:// resource and the host renders in a sandboxed iframe. The specification calls it the View. This book uses both words, and means the same thing by them. Agent The model-driven participant. It can call tools, receive context, and hold the conversation the user is in the middle of. Atomic capability The smallest independently useful UI or host-interaction operation, with a stable namespaced identifier. Agent boundary The line between interactions handled locally and interactions that involve the model, tools, or external state. Chapter 4 is entirely about where to draw it. Golden transcript The recorded JSON-RPC message log for a scenario. Replaying the scenario and diffing the transcript is how this book proves anything.

sections.h: How do I read a capability entry?
sections.x: Every entry in Parts II and III opens with a block like this one: surface.resize Core Level 1 On the wire Report content size so the host can size the frame around it. Messages ui/notifications/size-changed containerDimensions Ground The MCP Apps extension defines a message for it. Recipes Data Explorer , Dashboard , Monitoring Console Demo lab-surface The badges are not decoration and they are not opinion. Each is generated from the registry, and the build fails if any of them stops being true. Level 1 to 4 places the capability on the conformance ladder in Chapter 1. Levels are cumulative: a Level 3 host supports everything at Levels 1 and 2. Core or Extended says whether the capability is mandatory at its level. Core capabilities are the promise a host makes by claiming the level. Extended capabilities are optional at any level, which means your application must handle their absence, because a modern host may still not have them. The ground badge is the most useful thing on the page, and the labels mean exactly this: On the wire means the MCP Apps extension defines a message for it, and the entry names the message. You send it, the host answers it, and the transcript pane shows it. Core MCP means the base protocol defines it and views inherit it. Cancellation and progress work this way. Platform means the browser inside the sandbox already does it and there is no host round trip at all. Pointer events, text selection, and the date picker are in this group. Looking for a protocol feature here is a way to waste an afternoon. Yours to build means the view implements it and nobody else can. Undo is the clearest case: no host can undo your document model for you. Not standardised means there is no mechanism, anywhere, today. Sixteen capabilities carry this label. Each entry says what you can do instead, and Appendix B collects them into one table, because a list of the things a platform cannot yet do is the most actionable page in a book like this. Draft only appears when a message exists in the current specification draft but not in the last dated release, 2026-01-26 . If you are writing against a host that shipped early, those are the messages most likely to be missing.

Entries that have a live demonstration embed it directly: The live application needs JavaScript. Its source is in the repository under apps/ . Click something in the frame. The transcript underneath fills with the actual messages, in order, with direction arrows. The buttons in the grey strip are things only a host can do, so the page does them on the host’s behalf: change the container size, withdraw a display mode, start a teardown. The tab strip switches between the message log and the exact file the frame is running. That last point carries weight. The frame loads demos/lab-surface/index.html ; the code tab fetches demos/lab-surface/index.html . They cannot disagree.

You arrived with a specific problem. Appendix A is the index. Find the capability, read its ground badge first, and the entry will tell you in one line whether you are looking for a message, a browser feature, or an afternoon’s work. You arrived with an application to build. Part V. Find the recipe closest to what you are building, read its local and agentic split, then read its host dependency table. That table is the list of things that can go wrong in a host you have not tested against. You are implementing a host. Chapter 1 for the ladder, Chapter 2 for the wire, Appendix C for the checklist, and then Chapter 28’s ordering advice, which is that the handshake, surface.resize and the teardown handshake are worth more than everything else put together. You want to know what is missing. Appendix B, which is fourteen entries long and is the most actionable page here.

Enough HTML, CSS and JavaScript to build a small interface without a framework, because every application here is built that way and none of them uses one. Enough of MCP to know what a tool and a resource are. Nothing about the Apps extension, which Chapter 2 covers completely in one sitting. It does not assume you have a host to test against, which is why the demonstrations run on this page.

Everything here exists to answer one question: Can a host construct conventional, native-like applications entirely from a small, well defined set of reusable UI capabilities? If a recipe needs host behaviour that the primitives in Parts II and III cannot express, the recipe has found a missing capability, and that finding belongs upstream in the specification. If the recipes run unmodified across several hosts, the capability model is evidence. Part VI describes the machinery that makes both outcomes observable. Previous What This Book Is Next 1. The Capability Model

From atomic UI capabilities to native-like applications An MCP application is a sandboxed iframe that speaks JSON-RPC to a host it does not trust, on behalf of a user it can see and a model it cannot. This book takes that surface apart: 89 atomic capabilities, the components they compose into, 13 application recipes that put them under load, and a conformance suite that decides whether a host really supports what it claims. Every capability entry says where its behaviour comes from: 29 are messages in the MCP Apps extension, 4 come from core MCP, 21 are the browser inside the sandbox, 19 are yours to build, and 16 have no standard mechanism at all. The last group is the most interesting part of the book. Pinned to core protocol 2026-07-28 , the MCP Apps extension io.modelcontextprotocol/ui , and SDK 1.7.5 . The applications on these pages are running, not recorded. Repository .

What This Book Is 87 capabilities, 30 applications that run on this site, and a build that fails when a sentence stops being true. How to Read This Book The four layers, the vocabulary, the labels on every entry, and the one question the whole book is trying to answer.

Chapter 1 The Capability Model Eighty-nine named operations, four conformance levels, five kinds of ground, and one question you have to ask before using any of them. Chapter 2 What Crosses the Boundary The whole wire protocol in one chapter: the handshake, the twenty messages, the double iframe, and the four ways a view finds out what it was rendered for. Chapter 3 One View at a Time The unit of rendering is the tool call. There is no page, nothing owns a screen, and two views cannot share one. Most of the hard problems in this book descend from that. Chapter 4 The Local-First Principle Sorting a column is not a conversation. Where the agent boundary goes, why it goes there, and what it costs when it goes somewhere else. Chapter 5 The Sandbox and What It Costs You An opaque origin, a content security policy your server declares and the host enforces, four permissions, and the surprising consequences of all of it. Chapter 6 Entries, Recipes, and the Discipline of Degradation The two templates the rest of the book is written to, the five failure modes every capability has, and why the failure section is the one that earns its keep.

Chapter 7 Surfaces and Geometry How to size your view, read the space you were given, go fullscreen, and ask to be closed. Most embedded layout bugs are in this chapter. Chapter 8 Focus and Scroll Inside the frame, focus and scrolling work exactly as they always have. Across the frame boundary, neither of them works at all, and the protocol has nothing to say about it. Chapter 9 Dialogs and Attention Six capabilities, no messages, one broken browser API, and a decision procedure for how loudly to interrupt somebody. Chapter 10 Keyboard, Pointer and Selection Nine capabilities, one message between them. The browser does almost all of this, which is why the two places it stops are worth naming. Chapter 11 Clipboard, Files and System Integration Two messages that exist because the sandbox closed a door, one permission, and three capabilities with no route at all. Chapter 12 Pickers and Dropzones Three inputs the browser has already built for every platform and locale, and one picker that has to come through the host because the view holds no connection. Chapter 13 Host Environment and Theming A theming contract in three layers, seven environment signals, and the reason your view must define every colour it uses even though the host is going to send them. Chapter 14 Accessibility Three preferences the host never sends, one live region you have to build, and the reason an embedded frame makes all of this harder than a page. Chapter 15 Lifecycle and Connectivity Your view will be destroyed without warning, hidden without notice, and disconnected without an event. One request in the whole protocol gives you time to react. Chapter 16 Persistence and History The sandbox took away your storage and the extension has not replaced it. Undo, on the other hand, was always yours, and in an agentic application it matters more than it ever did in a page. Chapter 17 Media, Progress, Cancellation and Errors Playback the platform gives you, immersion the host gives you, and four capabilities about work that takes long enough for somebody to change their mind.

Chapter 18 UI to Agent Three ways for a view to reach the conversation, one of which is quiet, one of which starts a turn, and one of which skips the conversation entirely. Chapter 19 Agent to UI The host cannot see inside your frame, so an agent that wants to act on your interface has to be given a vocabulary. Registering tools is that vocabulary, and it turns out to be the same mechanism accessibility and testing need. Chapter 20 Tool Invocation and Streaming The view can call server tools without the model's involvement, receive arguments before they finish arriving, and take delivery of a result it was rendered for. Chapter 21 State Ownership and Concurrency Two parties can write to the same document and neither knows what the other is doing. Declare who owns what before it happens, because afterwards there is no good default. Chapter 22 Approval, Elicitation and the Context Boundary Two capabilities the extension does not have, one principle it depends on, and an argument about what the model should never be told.

Chapter 23 Components I: Overlays, Controls and Text What each component composes, which ARIA pattern governs it, and the embedded-specific detail that makes it different from the version you have built before. Chapter 24 Components II: Navigation, Data and Visualization Structure without a URL bar, tables that survive streaming, and charts in a frame that cannot load a charting library. Chapter 25 Components III: Spatial, Media and Agent-Native Canvases in a small frame, transports you should probably not replace, and five components that exist only because there is a model in the room.

Recipe 1 Data Explorer The baseline recipe. A table you can sort, filter, page and select, and one button that turns a selection into a question. Recipe 2 Dashboard Tiles, sparklines, drill-down, and values that keep changing while you look at them. Recipe 3 File Explorer A tree, a context menu, drag to move, and a deletion that is both confirmed and undoable. Recipe 4 Document Editor The recipe where the agent writes too. Undo, autosave through a tool, a teardown that flushes, and a rewrite that has to be proposed rather than applied. Recipe 5 Spreadsheet A grid with a formula evaluator, range selection, and a clipboard format chosen for where the data is going. Recipe 6 Image Annotator A canvas with pointer capture, zoom about the cursor, a dropzone that validates, and an export that degrades to the clipboard. Recipe 7 Workflow Builder A node graph the agent can edit through tools, with validation that runs continuously and an undo stack that covers both parties. Recipe 8 Code and Diff Reviewer A unified diff where a range of lines is the unit of conversation, and where the model is asked about exactly what the reviewer selected. Recipe 9 Monitoring Console Sustained streaming, a selection that survives it, connectivity reported honestly, and an error that happens while nobody is looking. Recipe 10 Approval Center A queue of actions waiting for a person, with the provenance that makes approval meaningful and a tool interface that refuses to approve anything. Recipe 11 Agent Control Center Tasks that stream in before they exist, progress against a running request, cancellation that admits how far it got, and a retry that does not make you start over. Recipe 12 Media Viewer A transport, a caption track, an immersion request that goes through the host, and a share button for a capability that does not exist. Recipe 13 Settings and Preferences A form, done properly. Native pickers, validation that waits until you have finished typing, save and discard that mean what they say, and a dirty guard on teardown.

Chapter 26 Why Recipes Are the Test Suite Capabilities pass in isolation and fail in composition. The thirteen applications exist to find out which, and the completeness test is what they answer. Chapter 27 The Verification Layers Six layers, from a schema to a cross-host dashboard, and an honest account of which of them this repository actually runs. Chapter 28 The Coverage Matrix and the Checklists What eighty-nine capabilities by thirteen recipes actually shows, why the matrix is generated, and what a host is claiming when it claims a level. Chapter 29 The Missing Primitive Loop, and the Live Book How a gap gets found, what a good proposal looks like, and how a static site runs thirty applications next to their own source without hosting anything.

Appendix B The Gaps Sixteen capabilities with no standard mechanism, what each one costs, and the shape a proposal would take. Appendix C Conformance Checklists What a host is claiming when it claims a level, phrased as things a test can assert. Appendix D Glossary The terms this book uses in a specific way, each with the message, field or file it corresponds to. Appendix E Prior Art and Sources Where each part of this book is anchored, and every specification, guide and tool it depends on.

87 capabilities, 30 applications that run on this site, and a build that fails when a sentence stops being true. An MCP application is HTML in a sandboxed iframe that speaks JSON-RPC to a host over postMessage . About twenty methods, four permissions, no storage, no address bar. You write that HTML. The model does not generate it. Your server registers it as a predeclared ui:// resource, your tools point at it with _meta.ui.resourceUri , and the model’s only job is deciding when to call the tool and with what arguments. The interface is a file in your repository, which is what makes everything in Part VI possible. This book cuts that surface into 87 named capabilities, then builds 13 applications out of nothing but those pieces. If the pieces are enough, the applications work. If one is missing, an application breaks in a specific place, and Appendix B lists the 16 places where that happened.

You are writing a view. Start at Appendix A, find the capability, and read its ground badge first. It tells you in one line whether input.contextmenu is a protocol message, a browser feature, or your afternoon. You are writing a host. Chapter 2 is the entire wire protocol. Appendix C is a checklist of what each conformance level obliges you to do. Chapter 28 says which three to implement first.

Every demonstration on this site is a real application in a real sandboxed iframe, driven by a host emulator that implements the host half of the bridge. The panel underneath prints the JSON-RPC traffic as it happens. The source drawer shows the same file the frame is running, fetched from the same URL, so the two cannot drift. Thirteen of them have a working MCP server behind them. Run node apps/recipes/r01-data-explorer/server.js and it speaks stdio to any MCP client. The numbers in the Data Explorer come out of that server, recorded by make fixtures . None of this needs a model. A host connects to servers, allocates surfaces and mediates privileged operations, and none of that requires an LLM. That is why make render can start each server, render the view it delivers, and assert on the resulting DOM.

Ten checks run on every build. The six that catch real errors: Check Fails when check_claims.py A message name in the registry is not in the pinned spec check_identifiers.py An identifier in the prose exists nowhere check_web_claims.py A CSP directive, ARIA name or WCAG number is wrong check_listings.py A listing marked extracted no longer matches its file check_counts.py A number the prose asserts is out of date check_render.mjs A recipe’s real server stops rendering what it should check_web_claims.py earned itself immediately. The draft said hit targets need 44 CSS pixels; WCAG 2.2 requires 24 at AA, and 44 is the AAA criterion.

It runs against one host. The emulator here was written by the same person as the applications, which is the condition under which a capability model looks more general than it is. Chapter 27 calls cross-host conformance the missing layer. No usability sessions were run. Chapter 4’s local-first principle is an argument, not a finding. Eight message names are draft-only. ui/download-file , sampling/createMessage , updateModelContext , ui/notifications/request-teardown , notifications/tools/list_changed , downloadFile , resource_link and isError are in the current draft and not in the 2026-01-26 release. Those entries carry a badge.

Every code block says where it came from: extracted from a file the tests run, captured from a real run, or illustrative and executed by nothing. Capability identifiers are in code and every one appears in Appendix A. Message names are quoted exactly as the specification writes them, and the build greps the specification for all 68 of them. No em dashes anywhere, enforced by tools/lint_prose.py . Next How to Read This Book

Nothing here consults a model about how to sort.

One column at any width. A toolbar with a search field, an environment filter and three actions; a scrolling table with six columns; a pager. It reports its height and lets the host grow the frame, up to whatever maximum the host allows.
Toolbar, search field, dropdown, table with selection, pagination, toast, banner for the error state. All from apps/lib/view.css .

The view is rendered because list_deployments was called, so the rows arrive in ui/notifications/tool-result . It also calls the same tool itself, on mount and from the reload button, through tools/call . Both paths land in the same render function. That duality is worth designing for deliberately. The first arrival is free and comes with the view; every later one costs a round trip and needs a loading state. The demonstration’s “Deliver the tool result” control pushes a fresh result down the notification path so you can watch the table update without a call.

Selection, as structured data, and nothing else. Illustrative, not run { "selected": [ { "id": "d5", "service": "billing", "env": "production", "version": "9.2.4", "p95": 1290, "errors": 143 } ] } Not the sort order, not the filter, not the page, not the hover. Press “Show what the model was told” with nothing selected and the answer is that nothing has been published. Select two rows and it fills in. The server’s side of the same discipline is in summarise() : the model gets “8 deployments. Worst p95 is 1290ms on billing.” and the eight full records go to the view in structuredContent .

Select two rows, then press “Show what the model was told”. The payload is the selection as structured data and nothing else. Select a third and press it again: the payload was replaced, not appended to. Press “Break the server”, then “Reload from the server”. The table keeps its rows, a banner explains that the data is from the previous successful call, and the reload button still works. Press “Fix the server” and reload again. Press “Switch to ja-JP / Tokyo”. Every timestamp and number re-renders. The selection survives, because formatting is a render concern and selection is state. Open the server.js tab and find summarise . That one function is the whole two-channel argument: the model gets its sentence, the view gets the eight records.

sections.h: What happens when things go wrong
sections.x: The tool fails. Press “Break the server”. The table keeps the rows it had, a banner explains that the data is from the previous successful call, and the reload button still works. An empty table with an error above it would have thrown away the information the user still needed. The host cannot save files. The export button is not rendered. Copy is offered instead, which puts CSV on the clipboard through whichever of the two paths works. The host refuses a save it advertised. A different failure, and it needs a different answer. downloadFile was present at ui/initialize , so the button is rendered, and the host declines when it is pressed. The control reports the host’s own message and stays enabled: Extracted from from apps/recipes/r01-data-explorer/index.html try { const result = await bridge.downloadFile({ contents: [{ type: "resource", resource: { uri: "file:///deployments.csv", mimeType: "text/csv", text: csv() } }] }); if (result?.isError) { toast("The host declined to save that file."); return; } toast("Handed to the host"); } catch (error) { toast(`No answer from the host. ${error.message}`); } The isError check is the load-bearing line and the one most implementations leave out. McpUiDownloadFileResult carries isError for a host that declined or a user who cancelled the save dialog, so that promise resolves . Code that only catches reports “Handed to the host” for a file that was never written, which is worse than an error message: the user believes they have it. A rejection means something different again, that no answer arrived at all. The render harness withdraws downloadFile mid-session and asserts the toast, because silence was this button’s actual behaviour until the harness could withdraw a capability. The locale changes mid-session. Press “Switch to ja-JP / Tokyo”. Numbers and timestamps re-render; the underlying data does not change; the selection survives.

The table is a grid with aria-selected on each row and tabindex="0" for keyboard activation. Space toggles selection, and the selected count is announced once per change. Sortable headers carry aria-sort . The error banner is a live region. Every column that is numeric is right-aligned with tabular figures, which is a legibility requirement and is the sort of thing that gets dropped first.

The view sends ui/initialize and ui/notifications/initialized . It sends ui/notifications/size-changed with a positive height. tools/call for list_deployments succeeds and the table has eight rows. Sorting by a column changes row order and sends no message. Selecting a row sends exactly one ui/update-model-context . Selecting a second row replaces the context. With downloadFile withdrawn, the export control is absent. With serverTools withdrawn, the view still renders the initial result. Previous 25. Recipe 2 Tiles, sparklines, drill-down, and values that keep changing while you look at them. r02 Dashboard Needs level 4 At-a-glance monitoring with drill-down. Capability delta surface.compose surface.displayMode env.reducedMotion op.progress op.retry lifecycle.visibility ui.navigate All capabilities surface.compose surface.resize surface.viewport surface.displayMode env.theme env.reducedMotion tool.invoke tool.result op.progress op.retry lifecycle.visibility agent.contextUpdate ui.navigate A dashboard is a data explorer that will not hold still. Its capability delta is entirely about that: values updating in place, a drill-down that does not lose them, and a motion preference that has to be respected by something other than a CSS rule. The live application needs JavaScript. Its source is in the repository under apps/ .

Normally local Worth crossing Open a tile’s detail panel “What caused the error spike?” Compare two tiles “Compare this week to last” Change the time window “Is this normal for a Tuesday?” Refresh Refresh looks like a crossing and is not. The view calls service_health itself through tools/call ; no model is involved in a button meaning “get the current numbers”.

A responsive grid of tiles, minimum 150 pixels each, so the same view is one column in a narrow panel and four across in a wide one. A drill-down panel opens under the grid, because a modal in a four hundred pixel frame covers everything.

The tile is not rebuilt when its value changes. The text node and the sparkline are replaced; the tile element, its focus and its position stay. Illustrative, not run const tile = $("#tiles").firstChild; tile.querySelector(".v").textContent = `${format.number(m.value)} ${m.unit}`; tile.querySelector("svg")?.replaceWith(spark(m.series)); Rebuilding the grid on every tick would move focus out of whatever the user was on, twice a second. This is the same discipline Recipe 9 needs at a hundred times the rate.

The chart is inline SVG built with createElementNS , eleven lines, stroked with var(--color-text-info) so it follows the host’s theme. The view declares an empty CSP, because it loads nothing. Chapter 24 has the argument for why this is usually the right answer in an embedded frame.

sections.h: Reduced motion changes the poll, not just the transition
sections.x: Illustrative, not run setInterval(() => { /* ... */ }, reduced.matches ? 4000 : 1400); A stylesheet rule that disables transitions does nothing for a value that repaints continuously. Under a reduced motion preference the dashboard slows down, which is a different response from removing an animation and the correct one for something that is moving.

Watch the first tile for ten seconds. The value and the sparkline change; the tile element does not. Tab to it while it is updating and the focus stays put, which is the entire reason it patches instead of rebuilding. Open a tile, then press “Show the model context”. The model is told which panel is open, not which tiles were hovered on the way there. Press “Withdraw fullscreen”, then press Expand. The view checks availableDisplayModes before asking and reports that the mode is gone, instead of sending a request that would be refused.

sections.x: Fullscreen withdrawn mid-session. Press “Withdraw fullscreen”. The next press of Expand finds the mode absent from availableDisplayModes and says so, and sends no request that would be refused. The refresh fails. The tiles keep their last values and the freshness chip stops advancing, which is the honest signal: a dashboard whose numbers are wrong is worse than one that admits its numbers are old.

Each tile is a button with an aria-label that states the metric and its value, so a screen reader user gets “Checkout p95, 412 milliseconds” in one node. Sparklines are aria-hidden="true" and the note under each tile carries the trend in words. Opening a drill-down announces it. The grid is keyboard navigable by tab, and Enter opens.

Handshake completes and a size is reported. service_health returns four metrics and four tiles render. A pushed ui/notifications/tool-result updates values without a call. Opening a tile sends one ui/update-model-context . ui/request-display-mode returns the mode the host actually set. With fullscreen withdrawn, no display mode request is sent. Two panes side by side above 480 pixels, stacked below. A tree on the left, a property list on the right, a toolbar above both. The context menu is absolutely positioned inside the frame and closes on outside click or Escape.

The delete path confirms, and the confirmation says the action can be undone. Illustrative, not run const yes = await confirmDialog({ title: `Delete ${node.name}?`, body: "You can undo this from the toolbar.", confirm: "Delete", destructive: true }); if (!yes) return; apply({ label: `delete ${node.name}`, forward: () => parent.children.splice(index, 1), back: () => parent.children.splice(index, 0, node) }); Chapter 9 argues that a confirmation without undo trains people to click through it, and that undo without confirmation loses a folder before anyone notices. Doing both costs four lines and the confirmation stops being ritual.
Dragging a node onto a folder is one transaction that remembers the index it came from, so undo puts it back where it was. That detail is invisible when it works and obvious when it does not.

Drag notes.txt onto the documents folder, then press Undo. It returns to its original position in its original parent, because the transaction recorded the index and the parent. Right click any node. The menu is drawn by the view, positioned inside the frame, and closes on Escape with focus restored. Select a file and press Delete. The confirmation says the action can be undone, which is what makes the confirmation honest. Tab into the tree, then use the arrow keys. The whole tree is one tab stop. Select notes.txt , then cover.png . The detail pane previews the first as text and the second as an image, and neither preview is a placeholder: the text is the file’s own bytes and the PNG is a real image the server generated. Both arrive through one read_file call and are cached per file, so selecting a file twice costs one round trip. Change the preview size to Small and back to Large. No tool call is made. The bytes are already in the view and only the rendering changes, which is the whole reason size belongs to the caller instead of to the server.

role="tree" with role="treeitem" children and one roving tabindex, so a hundred-file tree is one tab stop. aria-expanded on folders, aria-selected on the current node. F2 renames, Delete deletes, Cmd/Ctrl+Z undoes. The context menu is reachable from the keyboard and moves focus to its first item. Every action announces its outcome, including undo.

Handshake and size report. list_files returns a tree and it renders with three top-level entries. Arrow keys move selection without changing the tab stop count. Delete opens a dialog; Escape cancels it and nothing is removed. Confirming removes the node and enables Undo. Undo restores the node at its original index. Dragging a file onto a folder moves it; dragging onto a file does nothing. Selecting a text file renders its contents; selecting an image renders an with an alt naming the file, and no text pane. Changing the preview size sends no message and keeps the same content. A read_file that returns isError shows the server’s message in the preview’s place and leaves the tree intact. Undo, autosave through a tool, a teardown that flushes, and a rewrite that has to be proposed rather than applied. r04 Document Editor Needs level 4 Authoring with agent-assisted rewriting. It is also the clearest demonstration of why undo is the safety mechanism that makes agentic editing acceptable. The live application needs JavaScript. Its source is in the repository under apps/ .

Normally local Worth crossing Type, format, undo, redo “Rewrite this to be shorter” Autosave “Check these dates against the ticket” Find “Draft a reply to the vendor” Accept or decline a proposal Accepting a proposal is local. The agent’s text enters the document only when a human presses Accept, and that press pushes one undo transaction.
Region Owner Policy Document body Shared Agent proposes, human accepts, one transaction Selection and caret User Agent never touches Save state View Autosave on pause, flush on teardown

There is no state.save message, so the document lives on the server and the view calls save_document with visibility: ["app"] . The model neither sees that tool nor can call it, which means the model cannot save a document it has not been asked to save. Autosave fires 900 milliseconds after typing stops, which is also when the undo transaction is committed. One pause, one save, one undo step.

Illustrative, not run bridge.on("teardown", async ({ reason }) => { $("#log").textContent = `Host is closing this view: ${reason}`; if (dirty) { $("#log").textContent += " Flushing unsaved changes first."; await save(); } }); This is the only window in the protocol where a view can finish something. Press “Close the view” in the demonstration: the control reports how long the view took to answer, which is exactly the measurement a conformance test makes to find out whether a host really waits.

The agent’s propose_rewrite tool does not touch the document. It shows the proposed text with Accept and Decline, and returns “Shown to the user. Not applied.” so the agent does not report a change that has not happened. Accepting is one transaction. One Cmd+Z puts the human’s words back, which is the entire safety argument for letting a model near a document.

Type in the document and watch the chip. Amber on the first keystroke, green about 900 milliseconds after you stop, with a save_document call in the transcript between the two. Press “Agent proposes a rewrite”. The document is untouched; the proposal appears below it. Press Accept, then Cmd/Ctrl+Z once. Your words are back. Type something, then immediately press “Close the view”. The note in the transcript reports how many milliseconds the view took to answer ui/resource-teardown , and the save happened inside that window. Press “Agent reads the document”. The tool reports the text and the dirty flag, which is the pull half of the pair whose push half is ui/update-model-context .

sections.h: What happens when things go wrong
sections.x: The host does not wait for the teardown response. Indistinguishable from the inside. Autosave is what makes it survivable: at worst 900 milliseconds of typing is lost. The save fails. The dirty flag stays set, the chip stays amber, the tool’s own message appears under the document, and the next autosave retries. Both failure shapes are handled: a result carrying isError: true , which means the tool ran and refused, and a rejected call, which means it never ran. The document is never marked saved on a failure, and the render harness asserts it by refusing one save and checking that the chip still reads “unsaved”. The agent proposes while the user is typing. The proposal appears below rather than replacing anything, so there is no race. Chapter 21’s lab shows the harder version of this, where the agent writes directly into a shared field.

The editable region is role="textbox" with aria-multiline . Undo and redo announce their labels. The proposal card is a live region so its arrival is announced, and its buttons are reachable in tab order immediately after the document. Formatting shortcuts are duplicated as toolbar buttons.

load_document populates the editor. Typing sets the dirty state; a pause clears it via save_document . ui/resource-teardown receives a response, and the response comes after a save when the document was dirty. propose_rewrite does not modify the document. Recipe 5 A grid with a formula evaluator, range selection, and a clipboard format chosen for where the data is going. r05 Spreadsheet Needs level 3 Editable grid computation. Capability delta clipboard.read All capabilities input.selection input.keyboard input.shortcut clipboard.write clipboard.read history.transaction history.undo state.save a11y.announce op.error The smallest program that needs a real dependency graph. A spreadsheet has cells that refer to other cells, which means it can have cycles, which means it needs an evaluator that detects them and an interface that reports them without losing the user’s text. The live application needs JavaScript. Its source is in the repository under apps/ .

Normally local Worth crossing Move, select ranges, type “What is driving the West number down?” Evaluate formulas “Add a column for margin” Copy a range “Check these prices against the catalogue” Undo Formula evaluation is emphatically local. A grid that asked a model to compute =SUM(B2:B5) would be slower, more expensive and occasionally wrong.

Numbers, cell references, arithmetic and SUM over a range, in about twenty lines, with a seen set threaded through the recursion to catch cycles. Illustrative, not run function evaluate(ref, seen = new Set()) { const raw = cells.get(ref) ?? ""; if (!String(raw).startsWith("=")) return Number(raw) || (raw === "" ? 0 : NaN); if (seen.has(ref)) throw new Error(`Circular reference at ${ref}`); seen.add(ref); /* ... expand SUM, then references, then evaluate ... */ } The guard is a whitelist regular expression before the expression is evaluated, so a cell containing arbitrary text cannot become arbitrary code. That is not paranoia about the user; the cells can be populated from a tool result, which came from a server.

A cycle shows #CYCLE in the grid and leaves the raw text in the cell and in the formula bar, with a banner explaining what happened. Clearing the user’s input because it was invalid is the failure mode that makes people distrust a grid.

Anchor and head, shift to extend, arrows to move, and the selected range is highlighted rather than just the active cell. Copy produces tab-separated values with newlines, which is what every other spreadsheet reads. Chapter 11 has the general rule: CSV for a file, TSV for the clipboard. A range copied as prose is a range nobody can paste.

Type =B2*C2*2 into D2. The column recomputes, and so does the total in D6, because evaluation is recursive. Type =D2 into B2. The grid shows #CYCLE , the cell keeps your text, and the banner explains. Nothing is cleared. Shift with the arrow keys, then press Copy. The clipboard holds tab-separated values, which is what a spreadsheet expects and what prose is not.

There is no clipboard read anywhere, so importing a range from another spreadsheet means pasting into a focused cell and letting the browser deliver it, which works for one cell and not for a range. Chapter 11 has the gap; this recipe is where it costs the most. A formula referring to an empty cell. Evaluates to zero, which is what every spreadsheet does and what users expect.

Every cell is an <input> with an aria-label carrying its reference, so a screen reader user hears “B4, 1601” and never “edit text”. Arrows move, shift extends, and the formula bar shows the raw content of the head cell. Changes announce the cell and its new value. The grid is not virtualised, which is a deliberate limit: six rows by four columns, because a virtualised grid with correct accessibility is a much larger piece of work than this recipe is trying to demonstrate.

load_sheet populates twenty cells including four formulas. Column D shows computed products, not formula text. Editing B2 changes D2 and B6 in the same frame. Entering a self-reference shows #CYCLE and keeps the typed text. Shift with arrows extends the highlighted range. Copy places tab-separated text on the clipboard. A fixed-height stage with a transformed world inside it. The image is inline SVG drawn by the view, which is why the recipe declares an empty CSP: a JPEG from a CDN would need resourceDomains and a host willing to allow it.

Illustrative, not run const before = scale; scale = Math.min(6, Math.max(0.4, scale * (event.deltaY < 0 ? 1.12 : 0.89))); const rect = stage.getBoundingClientRect(); const px = event.clientX - rect.left, py = event.clientY - rect.top; panX = px - ((px - panX) / before) * scale; panY = py - ((py - panY) / before) * scale; Six lines, and they are the difference between a canvas that feels right and one that fights. Zooming about the origin moves whatever the user was looking at off screen, every time.

sections.h: Pointer capture for the draw gesture
sections.x: The stage captures the pointer on pointerdown , so a drag that leaves the stage still produces a correctly sized box. Without capture, dragging past the edge stops the gesture and leaves a half-drawn rectangle. touch-action: none on the stage stops the browser interpreting a drag as a scroll, which otherwise makes drawing impossible on a touch device.

sections.h: The dropzone that says what it wants
sections.x: The zone states “Drop a file here” in its resting state and rejects anything that is not JSON with a message naming the file. A dropzone that silently ignores a bad file is indistinguishable from a broken one.

sections.h: Export, and what happens without it
sections.x: Illustrative, not run if (!bridge.hostCapabilities.downloadFile) { await navigator.clipboard.writeText(payload).catch(() => {}); toast("No download capability, so the JSON went to the clipboard"); return; } Press “Refuse downloads” in the demonstration. The button stays, its behaviour changes, and the toast says why. This is the one place in Part V where a missing capability changes what a control does, and it is defensible because the underlying user need, getting the annotations out, has an alternative that works.

Zoom with the wheel while the pointer is over the burr. The point under the cursor stays under the cursor. Zooming about the origin is the version that feels wrong, and the six lines that fix it are in Chapter 10. Draw a box, then drag past the edge of the stage. Pointer capture keeps the gesture alive, so the box is the size you drew. Press “Refuse downloads”, then Export. The button stays and its behaviour changes: the JSON goes to the clipboard and the toast says why.

sections.x: A tiny box. Drags under six pixels in either dimension are discarded, so a click on the canvas does not leave an invisible annotation. A JSON file that is not annotations. Caught by the try around the parse, reported by name, and the existing boxes are untouched.

The stage is focusable and carries role="application" , which is the one context where that role is correct: arrow keys have to reach this code instead of a screen reader’s browse mode. Arrows move a visible caret by ten pixels, Shift by one, Enter sets the first corner and then commits the box, and Escape abandons one in progress. Extracted from from apps/recipes/r06-image-annotator/index.html if (event.key !== "Enter") return; event.preventDefault(); if (!anchor) { anchor = { ...caret }; drawCaret(); announce(`Corner set at ${Math.round(anchor.x)}, ${Math.round(anchor.y)}`); return; } That is press, drag and release taken apart into three separate keystrokes, which is what every keyboard equivalent of a drag ends up being. The caret is drawn rather than implied, because a drawing surface with no visible cursor is one a keyboard user cannot aim. The zoom and pan have button equivalents through Fit, the existing boxes are announced when loaded, and the label and colour controls are ordinary form fields.

load_annotations returns two boxes and both render. A drag creates a box whose dimensions match the drag. Wheel zoom keeps the point under the cursor stationary within a pixel. Fit returns the plate to the visible stage. Undo removes the most recently added box. With downloadFile present, export sends ui/download-file . With it absent, export sends no message and reports the clipboard fallback. Previous Recipe 5. Spreadsheet Next Recipe 7. Workflow Builder
