Recipe 7 A node graph the agent can edit through tools, with validation that runs continuously and an undo stack that covers both parties. r07 Workflow Builder Needs level 4 Build and edit a node graph. Capability delta app.tools agent.intent All capabilities input.zoompan input.dragdrop input.selection input.contextmenu history.transaction history.undo ui.highlight ui.navigate app.tools agent.intent op.error state.ownership The recipe where the agent is a first-class editor. Everything the mouse can do to this graph, a tool can do, and everything a tool does is one undoable transaction. The topology explorer some applications need is this same surface in read-only mode. The live application needs JavaScript. Its source is in the repository under apps/ .

Normally local Worth crossing Drag nodes, pan, zoom “Build me a triage workflow” Connect two selected steps “What is wrong with this graph?” Add and delete steps “Add error handling to this” Undo The second column is the interesting one. All three of those are the agent calling the same operations the mouse calls, which is why they are safe.

Four tools: add_step , connect_steps , highlight_step , and get_workflow . Three of them mutate and are annotated readOnlyHint: false ; the fourth reads. Illustrative, not run bridge.registerTool({ name: "connect_steps", description: "Connect two steps by name", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { from: { type: "string" }, to: { type: "string" } }, required: ["from", "to"] }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: false }, }, async ({ from, to }) => { const a = graph.nodes.find((n) => n.name === from); const b = graph.nodes.find((n) => n.name === to); if (!a || !b) { return { isError: true, content: [{ type: "text", text: `No step called ${a ? to : from}.` }] }; } connect(a.id, b.id); return { content: [{ type: "text", text: `Connected ${from} to ${to}.` }] }; }); Two design decisions in that snippet. The tool takes names, because names are what appear in the conversation. And it fails with a message naming the step that does not exist, so the agent can correct itself. Press “Agent: connect to a step that is not there” in the demonstration to see the failure path.

The graph is validated on every change and the result is a chip: valid, or a count of problems. Nodes with problems get a red border. The initial graph loads with a disconnected Notify node, so the recipe starts invalid on purpose. get_workflow returns the problems as structured data, which is what makes “what is wrong with this graph” answerable without the model reading pixels.

Every mutation goes through the same apply() , whether it came from a pointer or from a tool. The agent adds a step; one Cmd+Z removes it. Chapter 21 argues this is what makes agent editing acceptable, and this recipe is the clearest case: a graph an agent can restructure and a human cannot un-restructure is a graph nobody will let an agent near.
Eleven lines of canvas drawing, showing node positions and the current viewport rectangle. It is the cheapest orientation aid available and the first thing users miss on a pannable surface.

Press “Agent: what is wrong with this?”. The reply is a count of structural problems, computed from the graph. Press “Agent: connect Assign owner to Notify”. An edge appears, the chip goes from “2 problem(s)” to “valid”, and one Cmd/Ctrl+Z removes it. Press “Agent: connect to a step that is not there”. The tool fails with the missing name in the message, so the agent can correct itself. Drag a node, then press Undo. One transaction for the whole drag, not sixty.

sections.h: What happens when things go wrong
sections.x: The agent names a step that does not exist. The tool returns isError: true with the missing name, and the graph is unchanged. A node is dragged outside the world. The world is 1200 by 800 and the transform does not clamp, so a node can be dragged out of view. The minimap is how the user finds it again, which is a mitigation.

Each node is a role="button" with aria-pressed carrying its selection state and an accessible name of “name, kind”. Enter selects, Shift+Enter adds to the selection, and the arrow keys move the focused node by ten pixels or by one with Shift. Connecting is then the ordinary Connect button, which enables itself at two selected nodes. A focusable div is silent about all of this by default. tabindex makes it reachable and nothing more: Enter does not fire click the way it does on a button, so a canvas whose nodes are divs with onclick is a canvas that cannot be operated at all without a pointer, and it looks fine in every screenshot. That was this recipe’s defect until the render harness gained key dispatch and could be pointed at it. Arrow-key moves coalesce into one transaction per run, on the reasoning Chapter 16 gives for typing: undo that steps back ten pixels at a time is undo nobody uses. The tool interface remains, and it is still the better route for an agent, because naming a step beats describing where it sits.

load_workflow returns four nodes and two edges. The validation chip reports two problems on load. connect_steps with valid names adds an edge and clears one problem. connect_steps with an invalid name returns isError: true . Undo removes an agent-created edge. get_workflow returns the same problem count the chip shows. Dragging a node produces exactly one undo transaction. Previous Recipe 6. Image Annotator Next Recipe 8. Code and Diff Reviewer

Recipe 8 A unified diff where a range of lines is the unit of conversation, and where the model is asked about exactly what the reviewer selected. r08 Code and Diff Reviewer Needs level 4 Review changes with agent context. Capability delta surface.scroll link.open All capabilities input.selection input.keyboard clipboard.write agent.escalate agent.contextUpdate ui.highlight surface.displayMode surface.scroll env.theme link.open The recipe that makes the strongest case for structured escalation. A reviewer looking at a diff has a precise question about a precise range, and the difference between sending that range and sending a description of it is the difference between a useful answer and a plausible one. The live application needs JavaScript. Its source is in the repository under apps/ .

Normally local Worth crossing Select a line, extend a range “Explain this change” Add a comment “Is this backoff correct?” Scroll, navigate hunks “What else depends on this constant?” Copy the hunk “Open the file on the server”

Click sets the anchor, shift-click extends, arrows move and shift-arrows extend. The selected range is published as structured content, with line numbers and kinds: Illustrative, not run { "file": "src/transport/retry.ts", "lines": [ { "no": 44, "kind": "del", "text": " return base * 2 ** attempt + jitter;" }, { "no": 44, "kind": "add", "text": " const capped = Math.min(base * 2 ** attempt, 30_000);" } ] } The model receives line numbers, the file path, and whether each line was added or removed. Compare that with a screenshot, or with “the user is looking at the retry file”, and the difference in what can be answered is large.
“Explain this change” sends the selected lines with their diff markers as a ui/message . Not the whole file, not the whole hunk, and not a summary: the lines the reviewer pointed at.
A comment is attached to a line and rendered under it, and it never leaves the view unless the reviewer escalates. That is the right default: a review comment is a note to a colleague, not a prompt.

Click line 42, then shift-click line 45. The published context is those four lines with their numbers and their kinds, which is what makes “explain this change” answerable precisely. Press “Explain this change”. The message carries the selected lines with their diff markers, not a description of them. Press “Refuse to open links”, then “Open on the server”. The refusal is reported, which is the correct handling for a capability that was present at initialisation and declined at use.

sections.x: The host refuses to open links. Press “Refuse to open links”. The button reports the refusal, which is the right response for a capability that was present at initialisation and declined at use. A very wide line. The diff pane scrolls horizontally, because a wrapped diff line breaks the alignment between the number gutter and the content. In a four hundred pixel frame this means horizontal scrolling, which is the least bad option.

The diff is a labelled group with keyboard navigation by arrow keys, and shift extends. Each line’s kind is carried by a + or - character in the text, and not by colour alone, so it survives forced colours. Comments are announced when added. The selection count and range are available to a screen reader through the live region.

Recipe 9 Sustained streaming, a selection that survives it, connectivity reported honestly, and an error that happens while nobody is looking. r09 Monitoring Console Needs level 4 Live operational awareness. Capability delta tool.partialOutput lifecycle.connectivity lifecycle.suspend notify.attention notify.banner All capabilities tool.partialOutput tool.result lifecycle.connectivity lifecycle.visibility lifecycle.suspend notify.attention notify.banner op.retry input.selection surface.resize The recipe that runs over time, and the one that exposes tool.partialOutput as the most consequential gap in Part III. Everything in it is about staying correct while data keeps arriving. The live application needs JavaScript. Its source is in the repository under apps/ .

Normally local Worth crossing Follow the tail, or stop following “What caused this burst of resets?” Select a line “Is this error related to the deploy?” Filter by service “Summarise the last ten minutes” Reconnect

The single most important line in this recipe is the one that is not there: the list is never replaced. Illustrative, not run $("#log").append(node); while ($("#log").children.length > 220) $("#log").firstChild.remove(); if ($("#follow").checked) $("#log").scrollTop = $("#log").scrollHeight; Appending and trimming preserves selection, focus and scroll position. Replacing the container’s children destroys all three, and at five lines a second the user notices immediately. Press “Stream 40 more lines” with a line selected: the selection stays.
Follow the tail until the user scrolls up, then stop and leave the checkbox unticked. Every terminal has taught people this behaviour, and it is the kind of thing nobody notices when it is right.

There is no partial tool result. What this recipe does is receive repeated ui/notifications/tool-result notifications, each carrying a batch, which works and is not something the specification promises. Chapter 20 has the gap and the three workarounds. This recipe uses the one that produces the best interface and is the least portable, and says so.

Three states: live, reconnecting, offline. The critical design decision is what happens to the data in the last two. The console keeps the lines it has and raises a banner saying the view is showing the last lines that arrived, which is not the current state. A console that clears itself when the connection drops has destroyed the evidence at the exact moment somebody needs it.

When an error line arrives while document.hidden is true, the console raises a banner that survives until the user comes back, and publishes the alert to the model’s context. Neither is a substitute for notify.attention , which does not exist. Both are what you can do instead.

Select a log line, then press “Stream 40 more lines”. The selection survives, because the list appends and trims and never rebuilds. Scroll up while lines are arriving. Following stops and the checkbox unticks itself, which is the behaviour every terminal has taught people. Watch the rate chip. It is the only honest signal that the buffer is dropping lines during a burst.

sections.x: Level Needs Without it 1 Render, resize, theme Nothing works 3 lifecycle.visibility The console cannot tell it was backgrounded 3 notify.attention Gap; the banner-on-return is the fallback 4 tool.invoke No log to tail 4 tool.partialOutput Gap; repeated results are the fallback 4 agent.contextUpdate The model does not learn about alerts

sections.h: What happens when things go wrong
sections.x: The frame is hidden by CSS. No visibilitychange fires, the console keeps rendering, and nothing tells it otherwise. Chapter 15 has this gap; the mitigation here is that rendering a log line is cheap. A burst larger than the buffer. The buffer is 220 lines, so a burst of a thousand loses the oldest. The rate chip is what tells the user this is happening.

The log carries role="log" for its semantics and aria-live="off" to silence it. A log region is politely live by default, so every arriving line would be read out, and at five lines a second a screen reader user hears nothing but the log. The announcement rate is a property of the interface and not of the data, so the recipe announces a summary every five seconds instead: Extracted from from apps/recipes/r09-monitoring-console/index.html setInterval(() => { if (!unannounced) return; const errors = unannouncedErrors ? `, ${unannouncedErrors} error${unannouncedErrors === 1 ? "" : "s"}` : ""; announce(`${unannounced} new line${unannounced === 1 ? "" : "s"}${errors}`); unannounced = 0; unannouncedErrors = 0; }, SUMMARY_MS); “Twelve new lines, two errors” is one utterance carrying what a person needs to decide whether to look. Nothing is announced when nothing arrived, so an idle console is silent. Lines carry their level in text as well as colour. The selected line carries aria-current , not aria-selected . aria-selected is only allowed on elements with a role that defines a selection, and a div inside a log region has none, so the attribute was invalid and axe-core reported it as critical. aria-current is permitted anywhere and says what is meant. The log itself carries tabindex="0" , because a scrolling region that cannot take focus cannot be scrolled from a keyboard at all.

tail_logs returns 24 lines and all render. A selected line stays selected after 40 more lines arrive. Scrolling up unticks Follow; scrolling to the bottom does not re-tick it. Going offline raises a banner and keeps the existing lines. An error line arriving while hidden raises a banner visible on return. The buffer never exceeds 220 elements. Previous Recipe 8. Normally local Worth crossing Read the queue, expand provenance “What is this refund for?” Approve or deny “Has this customer been refunded before?” Review the audit trail “Explain the retention rule behind this” Approving is local. A person presses a button; the approve tool exists only to refuse the agent.

sections.h: Provenance, or it is not an approval
sections.x: Every card carries five fields: who asked, on whose behalf, which tool, which arguments, and what has been approved before. Chapter 22 argues that a card without them is a dialog with a lever attached, and that people learn to pull levers. The version with them lets a reviewer notice that this is the first refund ever approved for this customer, which is the fact that changes the decision.

The view cannot enforce anything. It is untrusted HTML in a sandbox and its Approve button is an ordinary button. The enforceable arrangement is: The server queues. A refund tool returns a queue id and does nothing else. A second tool performs the refund, requires the queue id, and is visibility: ["app"] so the model cannot call it. The view calls it after a human presses Approve. That is a convention, and its weakness is that a compromised view could call the second tool without a human. Closing that needs ui/request-approval , which is in Appendix B.

Illustrative, not run bridge.registerTool({ name: "approve", description: "Approve a queued action", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { title: { type: "string" } } }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: false }, }, async () => ({ isError: true, content: [{ type: "text", text: "Approval requires a person. This view does not accept approvals over " + "the tool interface." }], })); Registering a tool in order to refuse it looks strange until you consider the alternative: an agent that finds no approval tool tries something else, and what it tries may not have a gate. Press “Agent tries to approve it itself” in the demonstration.
Decisions, and nothing else. Not which cards were expanded, not how long the person took, not the order they read them in. The audit trail is local; the context update carries the outcomes.

Read the provenance on the refund card before deciding. Five fields, and the one that changes the decision is “prior approvals: none for this customer”. Press “Agent queues a deletion”, then “Agent tries to approve it itself”. The tool refuses and says why. Registering a tool in order to decline it is the point of the recipe. Approve the deletion, then press “Show the audit trail”. The decision is recorded locally and published to the model; how long you took and which cards you expanded are not.

sections.h: A task that exists before it exists
sections.x: The row appears while the model is still writing the arguments. Illustrative, not run bridge.on("toolinputpartial", ({ arguments: args }) => { const task = tasks.get("pending") ?? { id: "pending", name: "…", steps: [], percent: 0, done: 0, total: 5, state: "queued" }; task.name = args?.name ?? task.name; task.steps = [`arguments arriving: ${JSON.stringify(args ?? {})}`]; tasks.set("pending", task); draw(); }); Press “Agent streams a task in” and watch "Reindex sh" become "Reindex shard 9" before the task starts. This is the difference between an interface that feels immediate and one that shows a spinner for as long as the model takes to write JSON. The pending row is keyed separately and replaced when ui/notifications/tool-input arrives, so a partial row never becomes a real task by accident.

notifications/progress carries a step count and a message, and each message is appended to the task’s step list. The bar moves; the last three step names are visible. A phase name is worth more than a percentage, because it tells the user whether the slow part is the part they expected to be slow.

Illustrative, not run task.error = `Stopped after ${task.done} of ${task.total} steps. ` + "Completed steps were not rolled back."; Resetting the bar to zero would say nothing happened, which is false. Leaving it at sixty percent would suggest the work is still there, which is also false. Saying where it stopped and what state that leaves is the only honest option, and it is one sentence.

The failed task keeps its name and its configuration, and Retry re-runs the same call. The user does not rebuild anything. Chapter 17 argues that a failure that clears the form is the same failure plus a punishment.

Press “Agent streams a task in”. The row appears while the name is still Reindex sh , then fills in when ui/notifications/tool-input arrives. Start a task and cancel it halfway. The task reports the step it reached and says that completed steps were not rolled back, which is unglamorous and true. Press “Make the next task fail”, then start one. The failure keeps its step history, explains what state it left, and offers Retry with the same arguments.

sections.h: Why the controls are custom here, and why yours should not be
sections.x: The native <video> controls handle keyboard, screen readers, captions, picture in picture, playback rate and every platform convention, in less code than the transport in this recipe. This one is custom because the recipe needs to demonstrate the transport as a component and because it has no media file to ship: the frames are inline SVG, which is also how it avoids declaring any external origin. If you have real media and no unusual requirement, use the native controls.

Element.requestFullscreen() needs the fullscreen permission policy, which is not in the extension’s set of four. The route that works is ui/request-display-mode , and the answer is authoritative: Illustrative, not run const target = bridge.hostContext.displayMode === "fullscreen" ? "inline" : "fullscreen"; const { mode } = await bridge.requestDisplayMode(target); $("#note").textContent = mode === target ? `Host granted ${mode}.` : `Host refused and kept ${mode}.`; Press “Offer picture in picture” and then “Withdraw fullscreen” to see the view react to both.

Audio continuing from a frame nobody can see is genuinely alarming, and it is the fastest way to make somebody close a conversation. The player checks document.hidden on every tick and pauses with a note saying why.

sections.h: A share button with nothing behind it
sections.x: navigator.share needs the web-share permission policy, which the extension does not have. system.share is a gap. What the recipe does instead is ask the host to open a canonical link, and fall back to putting that link on the clipboard, and say which it did. That is the general shape for a missing capability with a real user need behind it: find the nearest thing the host will do, do that, and be explicit about the substitution.

Press Play, then press “Withdraw fullscreen” and the Fullscreen button. The view reports the mode the host actually kept, having assumed nothing about the request. Press Share with links allowed, then press “Refuse to open links” and press it again. The first goes through ui/open-link ; the second falls back to the clipboard and says so. There is no share capability to fall back from. Turn captions on and scrub. The caption line follows the position, and the toggle carries aria-pressed and no colour change.

sections.h: What happens when things go wrong
sections.x: Fullscreen refused. The note reports the mode the host kept. The player keeps working at inline size. Autoplay. The player never attempts it. Everything starts paused, which is both a policy requirement and good manners. Captions with no track selected. The caption line is hidden.

Play carries an aria-label that changes with state. The seek slider has a real name, the captions toggle has aria-pressed , the frame has an aria-label naming the clip, and the thumbnail strip is a tab list with aria-current . The seek bar carries aria-valuetext in minutes and seconds, so it announces “1:20 of 2:14” and never “80”. A range input announces its raw value otherwise, which is the most common defect in custom transports.

list_clips returns three clips and the strip renders three thumbnails. Play advances the clock and Pause stops it. Hiding the frame pauses playback. ui/request-display-mode returns the mode the host set. With fullscreen withdrawn, the button reports the refusal. Share sends ui/open-link when openLinks is present and does not when it is absent. Previous Recipe 11. Agent Control Center Next Recipe 13. Settings and Preferences

Recipe 13 A form, done properly. Native pickers, validation that waits until you have finished typing, save and discard that mean what they say, and a dirty guard on teardown. r13 Settings and Preferences Needs level 3 Forms, done properly. Capability delta picker.date picker.time env.textScale env.inputMode env.fonts All capabilities picker.date picker.time picker.color env.textScale env.contrast env.reducedMotion a11y.announce surface.focus lifecycle.dirty dialog.confirm op.error state.save env.inputMode env.fonts The last recipe is the most ordinary and the one most applications need. Its delta is the full picker set and the accessibility requirements of Chapter 14 as the primary subject. The live application needs JavaScript. Its source is in the repository under apps/ .

Normally local Worth crossing Fill in fields, validate “What do these quiet hours mean for the digest?” Save, discard “Set this up like the platform team’s” Preview the accent colour Almost nothing crosses. A settings form that consults a model is a settings form with a latency problem.

<input type="date"> , type="time"> and type="color"> do the collecting. Intl with hostContext.locale and hostContext.timeZone does the displaying. Press “Switch to ja-JP / Tokyo”: the stored values do not change and everything rendered does. That separation is the whole of Chapter 12. The picker’s value is an ISO string; the user’s understanding of it is a formatted one; the host is the only source for which format is right.

Illustrative, not run const email = /^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$/.test(values.email); if (!email && (!live || $("#email").dataset.touched)) { /* show the error */ } A touched flag per field, set on blur. The error appears after the user has left the field once, and updates live from then on. Telling somebody their address is invalid while they are typing the at sign is the fastest way to make a form feel hostile.

sections.h: Save and discard mean what they say
sections.x: Both are disabled until something changes. Discard confirms, because it destroys work. Save validates first, focuses the first invalid field if there is one, and announces the failure so a screen reader user learns about it at the same moment a sighted user does. The server validates again and can reject. Press Save with a bad address after editing it past the client check: the server’s message is shown and the form stays dirty. Client-side validation is a courtesy; the server’s is the rule.

On ui/resource-teardown , if the form is dirty, it saves before answering. Chapter 15 explains why that window is the only chance, and Recipe 4 explains why the flush has to be small enough to finish.
Changing the accent colour or the density updates the view immediately, and the change is not saved until Save is pressed. Preview is not commitment, and a form that saves as you type has no discard.

Clear the email field and click away. The error appears on blur, not on the keystroke that made it invalid. Type an obviously invalid address and press Save. Focus moves to the field, the error is announced, and no tool call is sent. Edit something, then press “Close with unsaved changes”. The form saves inside the teardown window before answering the host. Press “Switch to ja-JP / Tokyo”. The stored values do not change and everything rendered does, which is the whole of Chapter 12 in one button.

sections.h: What it needs from the host
sections.x: Level Needs Without it 1 Render, resize, theme, locale, timezone Formatting falls back to the machine 2 picker.date , picker.time , picker.color Platform; always present 2 lifecycle.beforeClose Unsaved changes are lost on teardown 4 tool.invoke Nothing loads and nothing saves

sections.h: What happens when things go wrong
sections.x: The server rejects a value the client accepted. The message is shown, the form stays dirty, and nothing is marked saved. Teardown with unsaved changes. The view saves inside the teardown window and then answers. A host that sends no locale. Intl falls back to the machine’s default, which is wrong but functional, and the note in the view says which timezone it is using so the discrepancy is at least visible.

Every field has a real <label> with a for . Errors are associated through aria-describedby and marked with aria-invalid , so a screen reader reads the error as part of the field. Fieldsets group related controls with legends. Save failure moves focus to the first invalid field and announces the reason. The whole form is operable from the keyboard, which for a form built from native elements means it was operable from the keyboard before anybody thought about it. The recipe also registers focus_field , which moves focus to a named field and refuses a name it does not have. That is the workaround for surface.focusHandoff in Appendix B, built rather than described, and it is worth being exact about what it covers: an agent can move focus, and an assistive technology driving through an agent can move focus. A host still cannot, because no message exists, and someone working by keyboard alone gains nothing from it. The entry in Appendix B stays where it is.

load_preferences populates every field. Editing enables Save and Discard and sets the dirty chip. Blurring an invalid email shows an error; typing an invalid one does not. Save with an invalid email focuses the field and sends no tool call. A server rejection leaves the form dirty and shows the server’s text. Discard confirms, then restores the loaded values. Teardown with unsaved changes sends save_preferences before responding. Changing the host locale re-renders the formatted values. Previous Recipe 12. Media Viewer Next 26.
